News.title: Heroic girl, 9, stops wildfire after blaze breaks out at cricket club
News.content:
Heroic girl, 9, stops wildfire after blaze breaks out at cricket club

Images how fire ripping through trees and bushes at Stockport Cricket Club which was first noted by a nine-year-old girl who ran to get help with the the game halted

View 3 Images The fire ripping through trees and bushes (Image: FACEBOOK)

A nine-year-old girl's quick-thinking stopped a wildfire from spreading after a blaze broke out at a cricket club in Stockport.

‌



Bar manager Rebecca Evans, at Stockport Cricket Club, said her daughter, who plays junior cricket, came inside to tell her of the blaze while she was serving customers on July 18.

‌



Images show the fire ripping through bushes and trees on the edge of the cricket ground, which borders Cale Green Park, and spectators to be moved away with the game stopped for 45 minutes.

‌



And club officials have reportedly said that it is only the latest in a series of incidents where it has been targeted by fires and vandalism.

View 3 Images The game at the cricket club had to he halted due to the fire (Image: FACEBOOK)

‌



Ms Evans said that after her daughter alerted her to the fire she called 999 and could see the fire growing. "I went out and it was just a fire," she told the BBC. "I started walking towards it while I was phoning 999 and it was just getting bigger and bigger."

She told how her daughter had been "scared" with children moved to the clubhouse to ensure they were safe as everyone waited for the fire brigade to arrive.

It appears that the edge of the cricket pitch backs onto a bushes in Cale Green Park and people often gather behind where it is difficult to see them.

‌



It comes as extreme temperatures have hit the country this summer with blazes breaking out up and down the country due to tinder dry vegetation.

View 3 Images Stockport Cricket Club have reported several cases of vandalism (Image: FACEBOOK)

The club has reported incidents in recent years of damage to benches and walls, fires, trespassing and racist graffiti.

‌



And Greater Manchester Police confirmed it has received a series of reports of incidents at the club. These include a number of alleged antisocial behaviour involving fireworks, cannabis and fires started.

One report they received last year involved "damage to club house and fire started in park".

Club treasurer Herman Schurink reportedly said cases of vandalism are increasing over recent years and that up to £700 has had to spent on repairing a wall. And he added that if it wasn't for volunteers that work would have cost thousands of pounds.

‌



"We've got to sell 1,000 pints of beer to make that money back," he said, while he believes that the answer is to have more secure fencing put up.

And a post on Stockport Cricket Club Bar & Function Room from July 18 read: "The corner of Cale Green park that backs onto our property has caused us problems for well over a year now.

"It’s quite a big open space once you get through the bushes. Kids cause so much trouble for us here last year they were throwing lit cans over the wall at our cricketers. Climbing over and breaking our benches they even knocked down this wall that’s behind the fire pictured.

‌



"They’ve cost us so much money in damages, repairs and vandal paint to try and stop it. This was today at 5:40pm while the cricket was on. Obviously the game had to be stopped this fire was quite big and actually on our side of the wall not the parks. My guess is aerosol cans lit and thrown (just going off what I’ve previously seen).

"Now all it would take to deter this is getting rid of a lot of the bushes in this corner and ploughing the soil so the whole corner is an open space and not a hidden place for kids to set fire. Only two months ago I had to call the fire brigade out to a large fire on the parks property on the opposite side of this wall.

"It’s just so sad to see all the time and it’s getting worse and im honestly scared one of these kids will get seriously hurt one day!"

Article continues below

The Mirror has contacted Stockport Council for comment.

News.title: UB40's Robin Campbell on bitter feud with brother Ali and the moment he 'prepared to die'
News.content:
Formed under Thatcher’s Britain, as UB40’s critically acclaimed album Rat in the Kitchen turns 40 this week, the Brummie band still has an anarchic streak. Reflecting on a career that’s seen them headline Glastonbury, enjoy three number one singles and even be inducted into the Māori nation during a 1980s New Zealand tour, founder member Robin Campbell, 71, looks pensive.

Of the Māori honour, he says: “The last person for that to happen to was King Charles. I'm not a royalist, but he wrote me a nice letter thanking me for my involvement in the Prince’s [now King’s] Trust. Though I must say, if I had an invite to the Palace, I would politely turn it down.”

This rebellious spirit was what led to the UB40 name, when the band formed in 1978. Thatcherism had its hold on the country and UB40 was the name given to the unemployment benefit form - at a time when approximately 1.46 million Brits were on the dole. Robin formed the pop-reggae band with his brother, Ali Campbell and their mates Jimmy Brown, Earl Falconer, Norman Hassan, Brian Travers, Yomi Babayemi and Jimmy Lynn - most of whom were unemployed at the time.

View 5 Images (Image: L J Van Houten/Shutterstock)

‌



Now an 11-piece outfit, UB40 have sold more than 100 million records and will be playing an Electric Paradise gig on August 8 at Milton Keynes Bowl. Robin says: “UB40 formed at the height of Thatcher in the 70s - it was an awful time. High unemployment levels. It was quite frightening. We were echoing the voices of our contemporaries in our songs.”

Their 1981 hit, One in Ten, examining the social neglect they saw all around them, famously referenced the fraction of the workforce out of a job. Robin continues: “Flash forward to 2026. Not much has changed. I'm hoping Andy Burnham will prove to be the Labour we need. And I hope he condemns Israel's actions in Palestine.”

UB40 have had more than 50 singles in the UK Singles Chart, including their chart toppers, Red Red Wine, I Got You Babe and (I Can't Help) Falling in Love with You. And they’ve made 21 studio albums, 19 compilation albums, six live albums and four remix albums. Robin says: “When we started, we thought we'd have 10 years if we were lucky. The fact that we can still go around the world and sell out gigs is just amazing to me. As long as I'm enjoying this, I'm going to just keep doing it. My intention is to bop till I drop. I'll be performing at 100 if I make it that far.”

And a UB40 show is now a family affair, according to Robin, who lives in Meriden, near Birmingham, with his wife, Luci, who he married in 2020, but has been with for more than 20 years. He says: “Our fans have grown up, they bring their kids. I have my kid on stage with me too!”

‌



View 5 Images Robin Campbell performs in Vancouver, Canada, in 2019 (Image: Getty Images)

Robin, who has two children from a previous relationship, Amy and Matt, now performs with his son on backing vocals. As well as him and Matt, the band now includes founder members Jimmy Brown, Earl Falconer, Norman Lamont Hassan, plus newcomers Matt Doyle, Martin Meredith, Laurence Parry, Ian Thompson, Jahred Gordon and Gilly G.

Clearly proud of the Rat in the Kitchen album, which reached number 8 in the UK Albums Chart, it included the track Sing Our Own Song, written by Robin as a direct protest against the apartheid regime in South Africa. It famously incorporates the African National Congress (ANC) rallying cry Amandla Awethu (meaning "Power To The People") and was subsequently censored by the governing authorities in South Africa.

UB40 performed a historic tour of the country in 1994, following the end of apartheid and the election of President Nelson Mandela, playing to a record breaking crowd of roughly 250,000 people over three days. Robin says: “Perhaps the biggest highlight of my whole career for me was playing South Africa after apartheid. We had observed the cultural boycott. We made anti-apartheid songs and then when Mandela was released, he invited us to perform. I still get goosebumps thinking about it. It was all I could do not to cry. Music matters. We still hold the live record in South Africa. They were singing all the songs that had been banned.”

‌



View 5 Images Robin and Ali Campbell singing together in 2006 at 'Night of the Proms' in Rotterdam (Image: Redferns)

But it’s not been plain sailing for UB40. In 2008, Robin’s brother Ali quit the band, blaming the acrimonious split after 30 years on a row about time off. Their third brother, Duncan, replaced him. Then Ali’s rival touring group, UB40 featuring Ali, Astro and Mickey, led to a public family estrangement and High Court name disputes.

Fortunately, a practical working agreement was reached. But Robin and Ali still don’t speak. Robin says: “It's sad - but it's his choice. “ And that’s not the only storm the band has weathered. In 1999, UB40 had to stop a gig in Northern Ireland after an attempted assassination. Robin says: “There was a shooting, that was quite frightening. A loyalist terrorist was shot in the head. He was a fan... I believe he survived. But it certainly shook us all up!”

Earlier, in the late 80s, the band also survived a near plane crash, while flying from Germany to the UK. Robin says: “Over the Channel everything fell silent. All the engines stopped working, they'd frozen. It was probably the most frightened I've ever been. Everyone on board shook hands and prepared to die. Then the engines started again. But as a band you have to catch so many flights, you just can't be afraid. Later, in Hawaii, a pilot took us on a helicopter fun ride which scared the life out of us too, under waterfalls. The next week he crashed and killed everyone on board. So there’s two lucky escapes for you.”

‌



View 5 Images UB40 as they are today (Image: Phillipa Jane Photography)

In 1983, UB40 headlined Glastonbury, when tickets cost just £12. Regulars on the festival scene to this day, Robin says he and the rest of the band still love making music. And he is careful to take a leaf out of the book of his musical heroes, by keeping his feet firmly on the ground. Describing Paul McCartney as a “class act” he says: “He’s just so down to earth. We were doing a photo session with his then wife, Linda. She said, ‘Would you like to meet Paul?’ And we went, ‘Yeah, of course we would.’

“He was at Abbey Road laying down a drum track at the time. When we walked in he threw his sticks in the air. It turned out that he's a UB40 fan. He turns up to our shows unannounced. When we played Wembley, the security guy used to come in and say, ‘Uh, Paul McCartney's out the back and he wants to know if he can come in.’

“After I'd met him the first time, he sent me a cassette with some music on and a little letter with it saying, ‘I hear you are going on tour. I just thought I'd send you some music to listen to that I'm working on at the moment while you're away.’ I love the man. He’s a class act.”

‌



But for true inspiration, he looks to Stevie Wonder. He says: “I've met him several times now and he's always been delightful. “Stevie Wonder is as important to music as Beethoven or Mozart. “

News.title: Warped relationship of vile mum and paedophile boyfriend who murdered two-year-old Isabelle
News.content:
Warped relationship of vile mum and paedophile boyfriend who murdered two-year-old Isabelle

WARNING: DISTRESSING CONTENT. EXCLUSIVE: As Alexandra Walker and Harrison Simpson are jailed for the murder of two-year-old Isabelle Rose Welsh, questions are being raised about how the vile couple could commit such horrors behind closed doors

Footage released of Isabelle Welsh as mum and partner found guilty of murder

Bright and bubbly with an infectious smile, little Isabelle Rose Welsh's life was cut short in circumstances that are near impossible to comprehend.

‌



The two-year-old suffered a campaign of heinous abuse at the hands of her mother Alexandra Walker and boyfriend Harrison Simpson. Eventually, it became too much for Isabelle's little body to fight. After a violent assault, the tot collapsed from severe injuries in her home in Thornaby, near Middlesbrough - with careless Walker taking hours to raise the alarm with medics. She died in hospital the following day.

‌



"For weeks this child had been violently assaulted, and her death - by that terrible head injury - was simply the end point in that campaign of violence to which she had been subjected," prosecutor Richard Wright KC told Teeside Crown Court.

‌



This week, the deplorable couple were sentenced to life imprisonment for murder, with minimum terms of 22 and 28 years respectively. Jurors unanimously convicted Simpson of murder, while Walker was convicted by a majority of 11 to one, with both convicted of child cruelty. Paedophile Simpson was also found guilty of sexual assault of a child, a charge which Walker was cleared of.

View 8 Images Alexandra Walker and Harrison SImpson have been jailed for Isabelle's murder (Image: Cleveland Police)

The court heard that Walker had concerns about her partner Simpson when they began their relationship. So much so that she looked up his name on the Sex Offenders Register. But she disturbingly ignored the signs.

‌



The pair met in the summer of 2025 on Facebook and entered into a warped relationship, where drugs, alcohol, 'attention seeking' and child cruelty were front and centre. Walker had been subjected to domestic violence in a previous relationship, the court heard.

Simpson wasted no time in luring his way into Walker's home to prey on Isabelle. This isn't uncommon in predatory abusers, Stacey Ashman, a therapist trained in forensic psychology, tells the Mirror. "Nobody falls in love faster than an abuser looking for their next victim.

"They're very, very quick with the love bombing, and if they figure out that somebody is already vulnerable, i.e., as with Walker, she has just come out of or has been in a long-term abusive relationship. They know exactly what they're doing."

‌



View 8 Images Isabelle was described as 'full of smiles'

Within weeks of Simpson entering Walker's life, those who knew and loved Isabelle began to notice worrying differences in the once happy and bubbly toddler.

Following one visit, Isabelle's concerned maternal grandmother said that the tot, whose leg was broken, "looks like she is being abused". The true horrors of the suffering came to light on September 13.

‌



After receiving a 999 call from Walker, paramedics arrived at the two-bedroom house to find that Isabelle was covered in bruises. She wasn't breathing and was already cold to the touch.

Despite valiant efforts on behalf of the paramedics, the following day, Isabelle died from her grave injuries, the extent of which became apparent after a post-mortem was carried out. The little girl had suffered 21 broken bones in the weeks before her collapse and had sustained a catastrophic head injury, with a shattered skull and brain damage. She'd also been sexually assaulted.

View 8 Images Walker had voiced concerns that Simpson might be a paedophile, but chose not to act on them (Image: Facebook)

‌



There was, the court would later hear, no way that any mother could have missed what was going on. In the beginning of their relationship, Walker found Simpson's preference to see her and Isabelle together "weird".

In other messages exchanged with her mother, Walker described Simpson as "a homeless romance scammer". But despite all the signs, she didn't call things off.

Reflecting on this unthinkable decision, Stacey, who has worked with survivors of trauma, says: "Her threshold for what she counts as alarming has already been worn down before she met him."

‌



She added: "I don't feel like that this is a case of a mother who simply failed to notice what was happening. I think it's a case that shows how a predator walks into an already vulnerable home situation, exploits it, and there will be very little resistance from the person that's vulnerable—the mother.

"He didn't really need to work too hard on overpowering her, and she was already a victim of trauma in her previous relationship. That had already done the work for him."

8 View 8 Images The little girl had suffered 21 broken bones in the weeks before her collapse (Image: Cleveland Police ) 8 View 8 Images She had sustained a catastrophic head injury (Image: Cleveland Police )

‌



On social media, Simpson portrayed himself as a family man intent on setting a good example for young children. In reality, he was a depraved peadophile.

One post, seen by the Mirror, shows an image of a man telling a young boy: "Gangsta isn't fighting, stealing or killing. Gangsta is handling your business, taking care of you and your family. That's a real G!". Another post showed a man walking along with a child, above a list entitled, 'Rules to teach your son'.

This lengthy list of 32 'rules' included advice such as, 'Hold your heroes to a higher standard', and "Stand up to Bullies. Protect those bullied." The final point says: "In all things lead by example, not explanation."

‌



This online persona doesn't surprise Stacey, who says: "This kind of predator wants to appear to be a great dad because what they're doing is they're micromanaging what everyone's vision of him is.

"So, he can not be looked at as the person who has caused the damage or the pain. Because, 'Hey, look, guys, this is how good I am. This is how good a father I am. I'm going to teach my child that'.

"We look at it, and we can see that it's problematic, but in his mind, he thinks he's micromanipulating everybody. It's appearance. The only people who really know what this person's capable of are the people who are living with him. What he portrays to everybody else is very different."

‌



In other posts, Simpson appeared to adopt a victim mentality, seemingly believing he was being judged for past mistakes. In one, he shared a message shared by another Facebook user, which read: "Don't rub my past in my face cuz we all did s*** we ain't proud of." In another, he alluded to steering clear of unspecified "drama", with a quote misattributed to the late rapper Tupac Shakur: "I'm at a point in my life where I just want my family happy, my health good, my mind right, my finances flowing and no drama".

View 8 Images Harrison Simpson met Walker on Facebook dating

In another post, which now appears eerie considering his fate, the paedophile shared a post from Visit Shropshire, advertising 'A Night Behind Bars' experience at Shrewsbury Prison. The  enthuses: "You may choose to head off in search of spirits or simply experience sleeping in a real prison cell. It's your night, so it's your choice."

‌



The offline Simpson could not have been more different to his sanctimonious and defensive online persona. While he and Walker were only together for one month, it was enough time to destroy and ultimately end Isabelle's brief life under the most harrowing circumstances imaginable.

Their short, grim relationship was marred by substance abuse and violence. The two at-home cameras installed by Walker, one of which overlooked the rear of the house, captured evidence reflected in a back window, giving a glimpse of the couple's sordid domestic life.

As shown in camera footage, Walker would sometimes down as many as 10 cans of Stella Artois, while Simpson was a habitual cannabis smoker. Disturbing images show an intoxicated Walker jabbing herself with a knife, while she was supposed to be looking after Isabelle.

‌



View 8 Images Flowers and teddies laid at the scene

At times, the pair would sell cannabis, with Walker explaining how her self-harming, captured on CCTV, was an attempt to wriggle out of such dealings. CCTV footage also showed that Isabelle had suffered a broken leg while being cared for solely by Simpson, who had also bathed the child without permission while her mother attended a doctor's appointment.

But even as Simpson's campaign of terror became impossible to ignore, Walker did nothing to stop him. On September 2, 11 days before Isabelle's death, Walker took her daughter to North Tees Hospital's emergency department, claiming she'd hurt herself by poking her leg through her cot. By this point, Isabelle's leg had been broken for days without treatment.

‌



An X-ray determined that the little girl had suffered a spiral fracture to her tibia, with her injuries sparking concerns among nurses and paediatric staff. Wright, prosecuting, told the court: " The response of Walker was not the response that you might expect in a concerned mother who had just been informed that her daughter had a broken leg that had gone untreated for several days or weeks.

"Instead, Walker became aggressive and stood up to challenge the nurse. She told her that it was unnecessary and over the top for her daughter to be admitted. She demanded to see another doctor and then declared that she was taking her home anyway."

View 8 Images In a statement, Isabelle's family said: "Rest in peace Isabelle, fly high little girl. Forever two." (Image: Cleveland Police )

‌



This callous approach was repeated when Isabelle lay dying. Walker didn't immediately ring 999 as it became clear her daughter was in a serious condition. Instead, she first smoked a cigarette in her kitchen while Googling "why would my toddler be bleeding".

Walker also first called her stepfather to come over. It was only upon his instruction that she finally called emergency services. Commenting on this behaviour, Stacey said: "This is not the normal kind of motherly mindset. This is somebody who is extremely vulnerable, knowing that she's let her child down, not wanting to admit that, and not wanting to get herself in trouble, which she did."

Walker and Simpson both denied murder, allowing the death of a child, sexual assault and child cruelty. In court, they turned on each other, with Simpson's barrister, Nicholas Lumley KC, arguing that it was "trotting out the old stereotype" to blame the man, not the woman.

‌



Meanwhile, Walker's barrister, Mark McKone KC, argued she "would not and did not" harm Isabelle, claiming she'd been unaware her daughter was being abused.

Mr Wright said Walker did not protect her daughter, saying: "On the contrary, she delayed, she deflected, and she failed to act when action was most urgently required."

Following his arrest, Simpson refused to answer police questions and did not testify at trial. Meanwhile, Ms Justice Norton asserted that Walker was "a fantasist and an attention-seeker" who'd "lied from start to finish".

‌



Addressing Walker, she said: "Right to the very end, your interest was not in Isabelle, but in yourself."

If you've been the victim of sexual assault, you can access help and resources via www.rapecrisis.org.uk or calling the national telephone helpline on 0808 802 9999

If you are 18 or under and have been affected by this story, you can contact Childline, confidentially on 0800 1111. You can also contact the NSPCC Helpline by phoning 0808 800 500 or emailing help@nspcc.org.uk. If a child is in immediate danger, call 999.

Article continues below

For mental health support, contact the Samaritans on 116 123, email them at jo@samaritans.org or visit samaritans.org to find your nearest branch.

Do you have a story to share? Email me at julia.banim@reachplc.com

News.title: Meghan Markle's family pictures from UK visit shows 'she wants world to remember' royal connections
News.content:
Meghan Markle’s 'baffling' behind-the-scenes holiday snaps showed she wanted “the world to remember” her royal connections, according to an expert.

The Duchess of Sussex surprised her 4.7million Instagram followers by opening up her family album and sharing a string of photos from her recent trip to the UK and Portugal along with Prince Harry and their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. One snap that stood out from the 12 that were shared was a photo that appeared to have been taken at Althorp - the vast Northamptonshire estate, where Harry’s late mother Princess Diana is buried.

In it, Lilibet, five, is seen walking through the estate’s famous tree-lined gardens, while Harry and seven-year-old Archie walk ahead carrying bouquets of flowers.

Meghan Markle will never leave California despite Harry reunion, royal expert claims READ MORE :

Prince Harry sees rise in approval ratings after reunion with King Charles READ MORE :

7 View 7 Images Meghan shares a photo of Harry, Archie and Lilibet visiting Althorp (Image: Meghan/Instagram) 7 View 7 Images Meghan shared 12 photos from the family's trip to Portugal and the UK (Image: Meghan/Instagram)

‌



It came after details about the trip had previously been kept firmly under wraps, with security concerns cited as the reason why Meghan and their children did not travel to London during the visit with Harry. And for royal expert Jennie Bond, showing the family did visit Althorp is a reminder of their connection to Diana - and indeed the wider Royal Family.

She told the Mirror: “I think it shows that she wants the world to remember that her children are part of the royal family. I think she’s proud of her connection to the royal family – hence her continued use of her title of Duchess and their decision to use their children’s titles.

“I’m rather confused by Meghan’s decision to post such private pictures. Of course she’s perfectly entitled to do just as she pleases, but it seems strange to me when the family is so desperate for privacy. I’m sure it meant a huge amount to Harry to be able to show the children his mother's childhood home as well as her burial place.

View 7 Images Harry flips Lilibet as they play in a swimming pool (Image: Meghan/Instagram)

‌



“It was a very important moment in their lives, and I’m glad they were able to be there. I’m just not sure why the rest of us should have been included in that very personal visit.”

Other photos posted by Meghan and set to the Cliff Richard tune ‘Summer Holiday’, show the Sussexes in swimwear spending time at the beach, as well as Harry throwing his daughter up in the air as they play in a swimming pool and enjoying time in Portugal, where they had been enjoying a holiday before heading to the UK.

It has previously been reported that the Sussexes have a holiday home on the country’s Atlantic coast, close to where Princess Eugenie and husband Jack Brooksbank spend some of their time.

And in one photo, Meghan appears to share an image of the front of fish restaurant, O Melidense, in Melidese - in the same Alentejo region of Portugal.

‌



Meghan is also photographed on a sun lounger beside a pool and in the background are a man and woman that have a striking resemblance to Harry's uncle Charles and his new wife, Cat Jarman.

7 View 7 Images The Sussexes enjoy a day at the beach (Image: Meghan/Instagram) 7 View 7 Images Meghan pets a dog as she relaxes on a sunlounger (Image: Meghan/Instagram)

In another sweet snap, Archie is seen in the cockpit of a plane wearing a pilot's hat, while the three staff members surround him as he is shown the controls.

‌



None of the photographs shows Archie or Lilibet's faces - a move by Harry and Meghan to protect their children’s privacy. In all of the photos that Meghan has shared on social media of her children, she does not show their faces.

And Jennie added: “As for the rest of the holiday pictures – they were all very charming although shrouded in the usual mystery of where they were and what the children really look like.

“I still don’t quite understand why Meghan includes the children in so many posts when they are so concerned about privacy, security and the dangers of the digital world.

View 7 Images Meghan with King Charles and Queen Camilla at a Buckingham Palace garden party (Image: AFP/Getty Images)

‌



“William and Catherine issue pictures of their children at milestones in their lives, such as birthdays or first days at school because there is a genuine public and historical interest in the future King, George, and his siblings. The same is not true of Archie and Lilibet. But it’s lovely to see them.”

However, the string of pictures did not contain any photos of the Sussexes’ family reunion with the King and Queen at Highgrove three weeks ago.

Harry and Meghan took their children to see their grandfather at his country retreat for the first time in four years earlier this month after the Duke previously said his security arrangements in the UK made it too dangerous to bring his family to his home country. The children had last seen their grandfather on their previous visit to the UK for the late Queen's Platinum Jubilee celebrations in 2022.

‌



Harry had planned to bring his family to the UK while he undertook a week-long series of events earlier this month, promoting charities and organisations close to his heart including the Invictus Games he founded.

Security issues prevented Meghan and the children from travelling with him to London but it appears concerns over safety were mitigated to allow the visit to Highgrove, as well as Althorp, to take place later in the week.

News.title: Prince George can learn 'instrumental' lesson from Mike and Zara Tindall, says expert
News.content:
Prince George can learn 'instrumental' lesson from Mike and Zara Tindall, says expert

With the future king just weeks away from starting his secondary schooling, an expert says there are two important people in his life who he turns to for down-to-earth guidance

View 4 Images George recently turned 13, and is preparing for secondary school (Image: PSNEWZ/SIPA/Shutterstock)

Prince George is just weeks away from embarking on the next chapter when he begins at his new school of Eton College.

‌



The future King is following in the footsteps of his father Prince William by attending the prestigious school, with the rest of his life likely to consist of a stint in the military before years of royal duty.

‌



And while his parents, the Prince and Princess of Wales, will be gently guide him, there could also be two other people who could prove to be instrumental to George as he grows up. George's godmother Zara Tindall and her husband Mike could be there to offer their grounded advice as they live their lives away from the royal spotlight, according to an expert.

‌



Prince Edward melts hearts as rare public moment is caught on camera READ MORE :

View 4 Images Prince George is heading to Eton in a matter of weeks (Image: Getty Images)

Zara and Mike have always had a close relationship with William and Kate, as they have often been seen talking and laughing together at royal events. William and Zara, who are first cousins, are particularly close, and while Zara isn’t a working royal, she is often seen supporting William’s work for the Firm.

And while William and Zara share a special bond, that relationship has seemingly also been passed down to Prince George, who recently celebrated his 13th birthday. Royal expert Robert Jobson told the Daily Mail that Zara and Mike, who are content with their life away from the limelight, have been instrumental in keeping George grounded.

‌



He said: “Watch Zara with George, and there is no difference in it. She teases him. He is easy with her the way children are easy with adults who want nothing from them.

“Then there is Mike, who is not a godparent and has become something better. He talks to him about losing, the one subject nobody else raises, because everybody else is invested in the boy winning.

View 4 Images Prince William and Zara Tindall, with her godson Prince George (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The royal expert added: “George is growing up among adults who are either dazzled by the institution or depend on it. What he needs are grown-ups who won something on their own terms and then treat the whole business lightly. Like Mike and Zara.”

George is also just a few months older than his cousin, Zara and Mike’s eldest child Mia, with the pair being spotted together walking to church at Sandringham on Christmas Day.

Former BBC royal correspondent Jennie Bond believes that the Wales’ and the Tindall’s would have very similar home lives: fun, slightly chaotic, and most importantly, private. She said: “I think the Tindalls run a very similar household to the Waleses: allowing the children a pretty free rein, with lots of noise and laughter along the way. With their rugby-playing dad, I’m sure there’s been a lot of rough and tumble, and plenty of fun.”

‌



She also previously told the Mirror: “Zaran and Mike, remain very close to William and Catherine and I’m sure they will both be called on to help out at events like garden parties for many years to come.”

View 4 Images Zara and Mike Tindall (Image: Max Mumby/Indigo, Getty Images)

Article continues below

“So I think we can expect to see Zara popping up every year at events like garden parties, throwing her arms around her uncle, the King, at occasions like Royal Ascot, and being part of the family celebrations at Christmas.”

The same closeness is shared with Zara’s husband Mike, as Jennie said: “I think the rest of the family regard Mike as a huge asset, and a solid character who has helped William through some tough times. He’s immensely likeable and seems like a great husband and super fun dad.”

News.title: Man brandishes claw hammer in road rage incident witnessed by terrified children
News.content:
Man brandishes claw hammer in road rage incident witnessed by terrified children

Neil Jones fled Coliseum Shopping Park after he trapped a man between two cars in a terrifying road rage incident witnessed by young children out with their families

View 2 Images Jones, of Morningside Road, Liverpool, was sentenced after pleading guilty to dangerous driving, assault by beating, common assault, and threatening a person with an offensive weapon in a public place. (Image: Liverpool Echo)

A man who assaulted shoppers and narrowly avoided mowing down children during a road rage incident at a retail park just two days before Christmas has been jailed.

‌



At around 3pm on 23 December 2025 a family had been walking across the pedestrian crossing at the Coliseum Shopping Park off Coliseum Way when Neil Jones, of Morningside Road, Liverpool, sped towards them narrowly missing one of the children.

‌



One of the adults shouted at the car to slow down and threw two soft toys which hit the back of the car.

‌



View 2 Images The retail park was busy with families just days before Christmas (Image: MEN)

Angered by the exchange Jones pulled into a disabled parking bay and got out of his vehicle. He shouted at the man accusing him of damaging his car and squaring up to him. Jones then pushed him in the chest.

The man pushed him back to create space and two members of the public approached to try and diffuse the situation. Jones then went to the boot of his car to retrieve a red claw hammer and brandished it at the man he had assaulted and then turned on another member of the public.

‌



He then went back to his car and locked himself inside. Other members of the public surrounded the vehicle to try and prevent him from leaving while a security guard tried to break Jones’s door window to try and get him out.

Jones reversed his vehicle and crashed into another trapping a man between two vehicles. He then managed to drive away.

A witness was able to give officers who turned up at the scene the car’s registration number and Jones was subsequently stopped by Roads and Crime Unit officers. They spotted the damage to the rear of the car and he was arrested.

‌



Jones, of Morningside Road, Liverpool, appeared at Liverpool Crown Court on Tuesday 28 July 2026 to be sentenced after pleading guilty to dangerous driving, assault by beating, common assault, and threatening a person with an offensive weapon in a public place.

The 48-year-old was jailed for two years and three months. He was also sentenced to an additional two years for an unrelated Merseyside Police case of causing death by careless driving, meaning his total sentence is one of 51 months.

DC Jason Smith said: "Jones was prepared to go to trial but once the jury was sworn in there must have been a dawning realisation that despite his protests of innocence his outrageous behaviour was witnessed by many and he had no choice but to change his plea to guilty.

Article continues below

“Thankfully, no one was seriously injured in this highly volatile situation, but for all those involved it was a frightening experience where they had no idea whether this was going to escalate into a dangerously violent conclusion. It is not what you should have to expect to encounter when Christmas shopping with your family.”

News.title: Three killed after bomb detonated at Moscow restaurant, state media say
News.content:
At least three people have been killed and 21 injured after a homemade explosive device was detonated at an Italian restaurant in Moscow, Russian state media reports, quoting security officials.

The blast happened at about 20:00 local time (17:00 GMT) on Kudrinskaya square near the city centre.

The National Anti-Terrorist Committee said a woman carrying the explosives tried to enter the restaurant but was stopped by a security guard.

The device detonated, killing the woman, the guard and a visitor to the Balzi Rossi restaurant, which had been holding a private function.

Authorities have not said who they believe was the target, but many Muscovites will suspect a link to the war in Ukraine.

In recent years, several senior Russian military figures have been assassinated in and around the Russian capital. Moscow has blamed Kyiv for those attacks.

Initial reports said the blast happened in the establishment's kitchen but the restaurant later issued a statement saying "there was a problem outside".

The restaurant is located in one of Moscow's famous Stalin-era skyscrapers, with roads around the square briefly closed.

Dozens of cyclists had been gathering nearby for an evening ride through the city but the event was cancelled.

Video released by Russia's RIA news agency showed heavily armed law enforcement officers at the scene, which had been closed off to members of the public.

News.title: Emotional Kerr delivers moment Glasgow 2026 has waited for with men's mile gold
News.content:
There were no pacers. No wave lights. No declarations about what time he would run or what record he would beat. This was a Saturday night scrap - Glasgow rules - and Josh Kerr wasn't going to let anyone beat him in that fight.

Not his childhood pal and Scotland team-mate Jake Wightman. Not the Australian prodigy Cam Myers. Not the former Olympic silver medallist Timothy Cheruiyot.

This Commonwealth Games men's mile was his race, in his country, in front of his people. This gold medal really meant something.

Kerr's explosion of joy after he crossed the line and swaddled himself in a Saltire - having conducted the crowd during his final few strides - made that clear.

And so did his halting attempts to sing along with Flower of Scotland, the 28-year-old repeatedly stopping to bite his lip before wiping away tears from each eye.

"We rush through these moments so quickly," Kerr told BBC Sport Scotland, having spent the best part of 45 minutes doing selfies and signatures. "So I was just telling myself to slow down.

"In my head, I was flashing through all the hard moments and realising that I've come a long way. And to have Flower of Scotland playing versus the GB national anthem, it's just different. Not many times in my career I'll ever have that."

News.title: Love Island has a problem, say fans - 'there hasn't been much love'
News.content:
What's your dream Love Island series on paper?

Some watch for the heartwarming romances, like Molly-Mae Hague and Tommy Fury falling for each other back in 2019, while others prefer intense dramas - we see you 2022 winners Ekin-Su CÃ¼lcÃ¼loÄlu and Davide Sanclimenti.

Others tune in for exciting challenges like Snog, Marry, Pie or the ones which literally send heart rates soaring.

For most, it's a mix of all of the above, and it's a balance TV producers have been trying to strike for years with the original UK series, as well as a host of spin-offs and international editions.

It's no secret that Love Island UK linear viewing figures have dropped from their 2019 heyday, with streaming and social media becoming more of a focus.

Across the pond the US edition has been reaching new heights, with the latest eighth series ranked as the number one reality show for five weeks in the States across all streaming platforms, according to its streamer Peacock. , external

It also had an injection of star power as US celebrity fans, including Lizzo, Demi Lovato and Kesha, sent messages of support to the finalists, while rapper Megan Thee Stallion has become a regular guest.

BBC Newsbeat has been speaking to fans, commentators and an ex-Islander to see what they feel the UK edition could learn from the US version to regain its spark.

News.title: Why I don't regret choosing a vasectomy in my 20s
News.content:
Because he was asking for a vasectomy at such a young age, Sam had prepared for the questions his doctor was going to ask him: Don't you think you're too young to know you don't want kids? Could you change your mind in future? You do know reversals are expensive and aren't always successful?

"[The doctor] actually said he had very recently changed his view," says Sam. "And that, if I had come in half a year earlier, he would have turned me away instantly."

His vasectomy took place a couple of months after he first contacted the clinic.

The questions from Sam's doctor were designed to ensure he was making a decision he could live with; men under 30 are more likely to regret a vasectomy, according to guidance from NHS Scotland, external.

Dr Sarah Salkeld, a former GP who is now a medical director for MSI Reproductive Choices, a group of clinics offering various contraceptives to NHS and private patients, says a vasectomy is "very safe and effective".

But she cautions it is important for men to "really think about" whether a vasectomy is right for them.

"We offer everyone counselling to talk about it if they want to, just toâ¦ make sure they've got all the information they need to make that decision."

She says reversals are not routinely available on the NHS as there are strict criteria for having one.

The NHS website points out that other forms of contraception, external are available to men, including condoms and the fertility awareness method - avoiding sex or using condoms on the days when their female partner is most fertile.

Sam told his doctor that, while he loved kids and had a happy childhood himself, he wanted to stay focused on his job as a sound designer for video games.

News.title: Solitude as a new aspirational lifestyle: 'We are not lonely'
News.content:
It's a Friday night. A young woman trudges back to her apartment after a day of work. She enters a spotless kitchen, unloads a bag of groceries, and unwraps a frozen pizza before sliding it in the oven.

What follows is a nightly routine that is almost meditative in its mundanity: she lights a candle and gazes briefly at the snow-covered landscape outside her window, piles a premade salad onto a plate with the pizza, and settles on her sofa to eat in front of the TV.

The tagline that accompanies the scene reads: "POV you're a childfree and single girl that has no friends and lives alone so this is how you spend your Friday night."

At the centre of the video â which has amassed seven million views on TikTok â is Lana Isa, a software sales manager in her 20s based in Toronto.

In addition to chronicling her nightly self-care routines, she takes her almost 400,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram on late-night fast food drives, reading sessions perched on a rock by the lake, even a saga of getting locked out of her apartment in the middle of the night.

Isa is part of a growing, albeit niche corner of the internet where content creators, many of them women, share their daily rituals of living alone, choosing to spotlight a lifestyle that prioritises peace and solitude - the antithesis of social media excess.

For Isa, unveiling the "no friends" aspect of her life was less of a tagline, but the "reality" she had been living for several years.

News.title: Spider-Man fans hail Brand New Day as Holland's best yet
News.content:
Fans have been queuing outside cinemas to catch the latest Spider-Man film, with many hailing it as a spectacular return for the web-slinging superhero.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day marks Tom Holland's fourth standalone adventure as the protagonist and hero Peter Parker.

Picking up after the events of Spider-Man: No Way Home, the film follows Parker as he devotes his time to protecting New York City while adjusting to a life in which everyone, including his closest friends, has forgotten who he is.

The fourth Spider-Man film is director Destin Daniel Cretton's second project in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), having previously been at the helm of Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings.

Appearing together in the same film for a second time this summer, Holland reprises the role alongside his wife Zendaya, who stars once again as MJ.

There is also a return for Jon Bernthal's Punisher, making his first appearance in an MCU feature film, and an introduction to the MCU for Sadie Sink, whose role in the plot has been kept firmly under wraps.

News.title: Ginger hair portraits show unexpected 'golden thread' connecting Americans
News.content:
For Kieran Dodds, photographing people with red hair has become something of an obsession over the past decade.

The 45-year-old, from Edinburgh, who is himself a "proud ginger", began taking pictures in his homeland in 2013 as part of a series examining Scottish identity.

His interest in the subject soon took him to other ginger hotspots such the Russian city of Perm and Jamaica's Treasure Beach.

His 2020 book Gingers spanned the world but after its release he notice there was a "huge gap".

"I realised I didn't have any American citizens," Kieran told the BBC.

"Then all these people got in touch."

News.title: How Australia combines modern tech and Indigenous knowledge to fight wildfires
News.content:
The wildfires currently ravaging Europe feel close to home for Professor Marta Yebra, despite being on the other side of the world.

Originally from Spain, the Canberra-based bushfire expert has spent years developing ways for Australia - home to some of the most fire-prone landscapes in the world - to battle its own blazes.

She heads up the Bushfire Research Centre of Excellence, which was set up in the aftermath of Australia's worst fire season on record: the Black Summer fires of 2019-20, which razed a combined area about the size of the UK.

Her team looks at how technology such as satellites, drones and AI can be used to better detect fires, alongside the knowledge of experienced firefighters.

Equally important, though, is the knowledge and experience that has accrued in Australia over thousands of years, and has been passed down through generations.

This is where Australia has an advantage.

The use of fire has been part of the country's Indigenous culture since long before Europeans arrived in the 18th century - but the value of this ingrained knowledge has only been truly realised in recent years.

News.title: Peak District's rebrand deal brings in cash - but also criticism
News.content:
A deal between Peak District bosses and car firm Skoda to put up temporary signs welcoming tourists to "the Peaq District" in honour of the firm's new electric model has given the park authority's coffers a welcome boost.

However, it has also sparked protests from campaigners and residents unhappy about the commercial aspect of the arrangement.

One campaigner said: "If national parks are prepared to sell their very name to the highest bidder, then we're already on the path to industrial extraction of the most protected landscapes."

Park bosses have defended the "fantastic" deal and said the partnership brought in extra funds for conservation and heritage work.

With national parks continuing to grapple with funding pressures, could the partnership be a sign of things to come for the Peak District and beyond?

News.title: Trust, grief and betrayal: Inside the Legacy funeral case
News.content:
This story contains details some might find distressing.

I've reported on many criminal cases before, but nothing like that of undertaker Robert Bush.

Now the case is over, we can report on what it was like to follow a story that began when whistleblowers raised concerns about Legacy Independent Funeral Directors with Humberside Police in March 2024.

Bush, the former owner of Legacy in Hull, admitted 67 offences, including fraudulent trading, denying 30 people a decent and proper burial, and giving some bereaved relatives the ashes of strangers.

The scale of Bush's offending was extraordinary. Police identified 300 victims.

Some were families who had paid Bush for funeral plans and services.

Others were relatives left questioning whether the ashes they had received really belonged to their loved ones.

There were also the deceased, whose bodies he had been trusted to bury or cremate with dignity.

Bush's scores of victims meant seats in courtroom four at Hull Crown Court for his five-day sentencing were in high demand.

Every day, diligent ushers stood like bouncers at the court's heavy, soundproof doors. They ensured families were given priority to see the man who wronged their loved ones face justice.

Court staff escorted them in with boxes of tissues, paper cups of water and a kind hand on their arms. Some were wiping away tears before they even walked into the room.

Fearful of what they were about to hear.

Their worries were not misplaced. The details of Bush's crimes were harrowing.

Among them, discarding stillborn premature baby Sunny Beverley-Conlin on the floor in a paper bag, and abandoning one victim naked on the floor to "let nature take its course".

They are descriptions one grieving mother said "will never leave me".

News.title: Mountaineer Nirmal Purja killed in Pakistan avalanche, his company says
News.content:
Purja's death was also confirmed by Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who said that "the tragic death of six Nepalese and four other foreign climbers, including world record holder Nirmal Purja, in the Karakoram mountain range of Pakistan, has shocked us".

"The history of their courage, dedication, and contributions will always remain inspiring," the prime minister added.

In a statement, Purja's older brother Kamal wrote: "It is with the heaviest heart that I share the devastating news that my beloved younger brother, Nirmal 'Nimsdai' Purja, and the other climbers are no longer with us.

"Although our hearts are broken, we are incredibly proud of you. Your legacy will live forever," he added.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a post on X: "Incredibly sad to learn of the passing of Nirmal (Nims) Purja and those he was climbing with.

"He was an inspirational man who served in our Armed Forces for many years - and whose incredible mountaineering adventures are known the world over."

Naila Kiani, a spokesperson for the Alpine Club of Pakistan which is involved in the rescue efforts, told BBC's Newshour programme that Purja had led many expeditions that she was on.

Praising his leadership skills, she described him as a "very experienced climber and fearless".

Kiani said the Alpine Club would only announce his death once the body has been recovered - but she added that "we are fearing them all dead".

She also said rescuers had seen some bodies - but were yet to reach them.

Teams in Pakistan have been searching for the climbers on the world's 12th-highest summit after an avalanche on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak in the Karakoram range.

Pakistani officials earlier said the bodies of three climbers from his expedition - American Mallory Geis, Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy from Oman and Pur Bahadur Gurung from Nepal - had been recovered.

The multinational climbing group was being led by Purja. Also known as Nims, he rose to prominence in 2019 when he climbed all 14 of the world's mountains with peaks above 8,000m in 189 days - smashing the previous record by more than seven years.

He became widely known following a Netflix documentary chronicling his journey, 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible, released two years later.

At the time, he said: "It has been a gruelling but humbling six months, and I hope to have proven that anything is possible with some determination, self-belief and positivity."

Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievement in extreme high-altitude mountaineering.

Purja, who lived with his wife and three-year-old daughter in Hampshire in southern England, said he was also the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military.

In his last post on X, published on Monday, he said he had not intended to climb Broad Peak.

"Initially, the plan was to climb just G2," Purja wrote, referring to Gasherbrum II, another peak in the Karakoram mountain range.

But right before he set off for Pakistan, he realised that if he also managed to climb Broad Peak while he was there, he would have only one more mountain to conquer before becoming the "first person in history to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice. Without oxygen."

An eight-thousander is a mountain that rises more than 8,000m above sea level.

"This wasn't planned," Purja wrote. "But opportunities don't scream: they whisper to those already working in silence."

"Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down. I take zero mountains for granted," he wrote.

Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit.

Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives.

One of Broad Peak's deadliest years was 2013, when at least six fatalities were recorded.

News.title: Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism row defends his work
News.content:
A Cambridge University professor has defended his academic work after finding himself at the centre of a plagiarism row.

The row erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in Prof Jason Arday's work and questioned some of his stated achievements.

While some critics say the treatment of Arday, who is black, has been motivated by racism, others have said the claims of plagiarism were legitimate.

Arday admitted errors in his work, telling the Times, external in an interview on Saturday that he was accountable for those mistakes but that "what I am not is a liar".

He told the newspaper: "There has been, since I arrived at Cambridge, a very well orchestrated and co-ordinated campaign to unseat me from my position."

He argued this was "racially motivated" and that he had become a "lightning rod" for criticism of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policy.

Arday said some errors in his early academic work was because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information, and that similar scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics.

"We're talking about academia here. I didn't murder somebody. I think the cruelty that I've experienced and the positioning of me as this kind of liar and fantasist is totally unacceptable," he told the newspaper.

In 2023, the then 37-year-old sociologist became the youngest ever black professor at Cambridge, telling the BBC at the time his work focused on neurodivergence and race in education.

He was diagnosed with autism and global development delay in his early years, to which his being unable to speak until the age of 11 and unable to read or write until 18 was attributed.

Arday worked as a PE teacher before earning his doctorate at Liverpool John Moores University and going on to teach at Roehampton, Durham and Glasgow.

News.title: Son of Wicker Man maker dies just weeks before his sequel to film premieres
News.content:
British filmmaker Justin Hardy, who directed a sequel to his late father Robin's 1973 cult horror classic The Wicker Man, has died aged 61.

His family said Hardy died on Friday night after suffering a heart attack, remembering him as "a man of family, of boundless creativity" and "so full of life right to the end".

A Bafta and Emmy nominated writer and director, Hardy was known for the documentary Children of the Wicker Man in 2024, made with his brother Dominic, which chronicled the legacy of their father's iconic film.

He had just completed production on Wrath of the Gods, the concluding chapter to the Wicker Man trilogy, which was due to premiere in London later this month.

Hardy also directed historical films and documentaries for the BBC, Channel 4 and CNN, including Princes In The Tower, Trafalgar Battle Surgeon, The Relief Of Belsen and Spanish Flu: The Forgotten Fallen.

His family said they were "devastated" by his death and "heartbroken" Hardy would not be able to see Wrath of the Gods open.

Dominic described his brother as having "an incredible appetite for life".

"We've lost him and we've lost that larger-than-life presence looking over us all," he said. "He really became a filmmaker his own right."

Dominic also praised Hardy's work on his last film as "incredibly beautiful", adding it was "a great satisfaction to him" to have made something new.

The Wicker Man, starring Edward Woodward and Christopher Lee, is the story of a police officer sent to a remote Scottish island community to investigate the disappearance of a local girl.

Wrath of the Gods was inspired by recently discovered scripts and storyboards by Hardy's late father Robin, marking the end of the trilogy that began with The Wicker Man and the 2011 follow-up The Wicker Tree.

Hardy, who also taught screenwriting at University College London, is survived by his wife Larissa, and their four children.

News.title: Ballot paper for Clacton by-election is longest in British electoral history
News.content:
The longest ballot paper in British political history is costing four times as much to print than regular ballot papers, the local council has said.

The list for the Clacton parliamentary by-election, which was prompted by the resignation of Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, is 90cm (3ft) long.

When people unfold the paper, they will find it is longer than most adults' arms.

Tendring District Council chief executive Ian Davidson - who is the acting returning officer for the by-election in the Essex constituency - said organising the vote had been "manic".

People have already started returning postal votes to town hall and most registered voters will go to polling stations on 13 August.

Davidson said: "We've logistically been looking at the size of the ballot paper, how we fold it to get it into the envelope so we can send it out to our postal voters [and] how we manage the polling stations."

News.title: Manhunt after prisoner escapes from van outside court
News.content:
A manhunt is under way after a prisoner escaped from a van taking him to a court appearance.

Stephen Grzyb, 22, was being transported by contractor GEOAmey from Belle Vale custody suite to Liverpool Magistrates' Court to face burglary charges on Saturday.

As the van arrived outside the court building, at around 10:00 BST, Grzyb was able to flee and ran off down Red Cross Street towards the Strand.

Merseyside Police said: "Assisting him in any way will bring police to your own door, so it is not an association worth keeping."

News.title: William and Kate bring children to second last day of Commonwealth Games
News.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have brought their three children to watch some of the final sporting events at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Cheering crowds at the city's OVO Hydro were treated to exhilarating performances in the netball semi-finals where the family watched New Zealand's 61-54 win over England.

Known as the Duke and Duchess of Rothesay while in Scotland, the couple also spent time meeting athletes, staff and volunteers during a slightly blustery visit to the venue on the River Clyde.

They then made their way to the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome - where they chatted to British cyclist Dame Laura Kenny and sat one row behind another Olympic cycling champion, Sir Chris.

News.content:
Inside Uefa’s extraordinary World Cup boycott plans – and what Fifa might do next

Manchester United are considering a shock move for Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly as Michael Carrick targets versatile options to bolster his squad. Former England rugby captain Phil Vickery has pledged to donate his brain for research into the damage caused by head injuries having been diagnosed with probable chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

Vickery, part of the side that won the 2003 Rugby World Cup, was given a probable diagnosis two years ago, though CTE – believed to be caused by repeated brain injuries – can only be confirmed after death.

The 50-year-old is part of the concussion lawsuit involving more than 1,000 players that accuses World Rugby, England’s Rugby Football Union (RFU), the Welsh Rugby Union and the Rugby Football League of failing in their duty of care to protect those involved in the game.

open image in gallery Phil Vickery toured twice with the British and Irish Lions ( PA )

Vickery, who toured twice with the British and Irish Lions and won 73 caps for England, has admitted he has considered taking his own life but wants to ensure his brain can be used to further research into neurodegenerative diseases.

“Is that gonna make someone stand up?” Vickery said in an interview with The Observer. “I don’t know. What a horrible thing to say. But what does it have to take?

“With the knowledge that we have now, it makes you wanna cry. Because it’s f****** awful. Brain injuries are with you all the time, 24/7, 365 days a year, and it weighs heavy, and it grinds at you all the time. It won’t beat me. You know, I keep going.”

Vickery retired in 2010 having captained England at the 2007 World Cup four years on from starting the final win over Australia.

Steve Thompson, another member of that side, has been diagnosed with early onset dementia and probable CTE, and has said that he has no memory of the World Cup win.

The lawsuit has reached a key juncture with hundreds of cases at risk of being struck out due to a failure in disclosure and an allegation that the solicitor who had led the case, Richard Boardman of Rylands Garth, had provided “misleading evidence” to the court. Boardman’s representation has now been terminated by the claimants.

Senior Master Jeremy Cook has reserved judgement on the strike out decision.

Despite his brain injuries, Vickery insists he would still do his career all over again if given the choice.

open image in gallery Phil Vickery retired in 2010 ( Getty )

“The sport’s f****** amazing. Rugby’s an amazing sport. You know, the sad reality is I sit here today – would I do it all again? Oh my God, I would. I’m f****** mental, but I would because it’s amazing,” he said.

“I also sit here knowing there are lots of people out there, I believe, who are suffering because of the sport. And it’s not about blaming the sport and about getting all nasty and horrible. Let’s just f****** help people. There are people suffering, so let’s help them.”

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

Delta Goodrem is set to grace the Strictly Come Dancing stage in September – and has one request about the professional partner she’s paired up with.

Months after representing Australia at the 2026 Eurovision Song Contest, the actor-turned-singer was announced as a contestant on the all-new version of the BBC competition, which is shaking things up behind and in front of the camera.

In a new interview with The Independent, Goodrem said she was “excited to dive into” the Strictly glitz and glamour.

While the “Born to Try” singer said she did not have a preference as to which professional dancer she would compete alongside, she did say she would “love to be” paired with someone taller than her because she “doesn’t really want to be the one that has to lift people”.

open image in gallery Delta Goodrem is a contestant on this year’s ‘Strictly Come Dancing’ ( BBC )

Goodrem is 5 feet 10 inches tall, and if she got her wish, she would most likely be coupled with either Kai Widdrington or Aljaž Škorjanec, both of whom are over six feet tall.

Earlier this month, five new professional dancers were announced to be joining the series alongside the old familiars, including Amy Dowden, Carlos Gu, Dianne Buswell, Jowita Przystal, Katya Jones, Lauren Oakley, Nancy Xu, Neil Jones, Nikita Kuzmin, Vito Coppola, and last year’s new arrivals Alexis Warr and Julian Caillon.

The newcomers are Maddie Ingoldsby, Aleksandra Isaeva, Mark Karmalita, Lethabo Monametsi, and Cristian Priori. They will replace outgoing pros Nadiya Bychkova, Karen Hauer, Gorka Marquez, Luba Mushtuk, and Michelle Tsiakkas.

This celebrity line-up is slowly coming together, too, with football pro Shaun Wright-Phillips the latest to be announced. He joins Goodrem, Dani Dyer, House of the Dragon star Bethany Antonia, actor Jaime Winstone, Paralympian cyclist Dame Sarah Storey, TV presenter Will Best, reality star Cacheral Mercer, hair stylist Chris Appleton, and more.

Speaking about her appointment, former Neighbours star Goodrem said she is “thrilled” to be adding the Strictly stage to the many she’s performed on throughout her career.

open image in gallery Delta Goodrem at Eurovision in May 2026 ( Getty )

“I’ve been incredibly honoured to perform on many different stages throughout my career – from TV, theatre, film sets, to touring my own shows around the world,” she said.

“There is, however, one stage I’ve never stepped onto and that is the ballroom floor. I’m absolutely thrilled to be joining Strictly and can’t wait to get started.”

Goodrem has also been a judge on The Voice Australia and competed for the country at the Eurovision Song Contest, finishing fourth earlier this year.

The new series of Strictly Come Dancing will be hosted by trio Emma Willis, Johannes Radebe and Josh Widdicombe, who are taking over from Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman. It returns to BBC One and iPlayer in September.

News.title: Blackjack rules: How to play blackjack
News.content:
As one of the more traditional alternatives to card games such as poker, blackjack continues to be one of the most popular games at casino sites worldwide.

On the best blackjack sites, punters can choose from a huge range of standard blackjack games that are available to play online, as well as variations such as live games, Spanish 21 and European blackjack.

Part of the game’s appeal is that it is easy to learn, and though it does require both luck and strategy, it pays to learn the rules before you start playing online or in-person.

In simple terms, blackjack is a card game in which players compete against the dealer to have a hand closer to the value of 21, without going over that number.

In this guide, we will expand on that explanation, as well as detailing blackjack rules, player strategies, and tips for success when using the best casino apps.

How each hand of blackjack works

In this section, we briefly explain how every hand works, according to basic blackjack rules. You’ll find the same setup across both established operators and new casino sites for a regular game of blackjack. If using a variation the system may be different.

Initial setup

At first, players are dealt two cards face up, while the dealer receives one card face up and one face down (this is known as the hole card).

The goal is to have a hand total closer to 21 than the dealer, without exceeding 21. If you exceed 21, this is known as ‘going bust’, or ‘busting’.

Card values

Cards have different values in blackjack – some are self-explanatory, while others require learning and memorising.

Number cards (anything between 2 and 10) are worth their face value. Face cards (Jack, Queen, King) are worth 10 too.

Aces can be worth 1 or 11, depending on what benefits the hand.

Blackjack (natural 21)

A player automatically wins if they are dealt a ‘blackjack’, which as also known as a natural 21. This would consist of an Ace and a card with a value of 10.

However, you do not win if the dealer also has blackjack, in which case it’s a tie (this situation is also known as a ‘push’).

Player options

In this section, we will discuss what options each player has during their respective turns in blackjack.

Hit

A hit is when a player opts to take additional cards in order to get closer to 21. Of course, choosing to hit comes with the risk of busting if the total exceeds 21.

Stand

A player can choose to stand, meaning they keep their current hand and do not take additional cards, thereby staying on the current value.

Double down

A double down is the name given to the option to double the original bet and receive one additional card. This is a common move when the player has a hand total of 9, 10, or 11, as it is less likely that they will go bust.

Split

When a player has two cards of the same value, they can split them into two separate hands by placing an additional bet.

Once you split the cards into two hands, you’ll place your original bet with one hand and place an equal bet on the second hand. You will play the hand to your right first.

Surrender

Players also have the option to surrender, which is when a player forfeits half of their bet and ends their participation in the hand. This is typically used when the player has a weak hand against a strong dealer upcard.

Side bets in blackjack

Blackjack card game rules include side bets, which operate as optional wagers placed alongside the main blackjack game. They are usually staked at the beginning of the round, before the cards have been dealt, and they are placed alongside regular bets.

Many side bets come with fixed odds that typically offer higher payouts than the standard 2:1 reward for beating the dealer.

We have provided some detail on popular side bets below.

Perfect pairs: This is a bet on whether the first two cards dealt to the player will form a pair.

This is a bet on whether the first two cards dealt to the player will form a pair. 21+3: This bet combines the player’s two cards and the dealer’s upcard into a three-card poker hand (such as a flush or straight).

This bet combines the player’s two cards and the dealer’s upcard into a three-card poker hand (such as a flush or straight). Insurance: A bet offered when the dealer’s upcard is an Ace, which then pays out if the dealer has blackjack.

Risk vs reward

While side bets can offer large payouts, they also carry a higher house edge and should be played with caution.

This is a strategy for a more advanced blackjack player and not someone who is still learning the rules – when starting out, it is better to simply stick to ‘normal’ blackjack in order to avoid any losses potentially piling up.

Basic blackjack strategy

Introduction to basic strategy

There are no guaranteed methods to win at blackjack. Basic blackjack strategy is based on statistical probabilities rather than anything a player can influence, and this helps players make the best decision for each hand.

Overall, the strategy is aimed at reducing the house edge and maximising the player’s odds of winning.

Strategy chart overview

Blackjack strategy charts are large charts that provide odds and probabilities based upon the value of your hand. They essentially recommend whether to hit, stand, double down, or split based on the player’s hand and the dealer’s upcard.

It is useful to memorise the different probabilities (for example, the chance of going bust) on different card values, though remember to use common sense too.

Budget control

Remember to manage your budget. Never get carried away with your success and never chase losses after a losing hand. New customers should also start with small bets before wagering larger amounts. Using casino bonus funds is a good way to avoid using your own funds when playing blackjack.

Key tips for blackjack players

Nevertheless, there are four key blackjack tips that can be easily remembered and incorporated into your game.

1. Always stand on a hard 17 or higher

2. Always hit on a hand of 8 or lower

3. Split Aces and 8s, but never split 10s or 5s

4. Double down on 11, or on 10 if the dealer has a weaker upcard (such as 9 or below)

Summary: Blackjack rules

Blackjack has become such a popular game because it is both easy to learn and play.

In some ways, the lack of concrete strategies, combined with the player’s inability to influence any events other than their own decision-making, have contributed to it becoming so widely enjoyed.

The simple goal for the player to beat the dealer by being closer to 21 makes the outcome straightforward.

Blackjack rules are arguably easier to understand than many other table games.

That said, memorising blackjack strategy charts will help you out while learning how to play blackjack to help you beat the dealer.

Make sure you have a solid understanding of the rules of blackjack before playing for real money.

Ensure you gamble responsibly when playing blackjack, and don’t hesitate to seek help if you need it.

Responsible gambling

Remember to gamble responsibly. Blackjack is only a form of entertainment, not a way to make money.

Gambling can addictive, so remember to never wager more than you can afford to lose, and take steps to remain in control of your budget.

The same apples whether you’re playing on blackjack sites, roulette sites, poker sites, betting sites or any other type of gambling medium.

Players should set limits before playing and to stick to them (whether they be limits on time, spending or both).

Setting a budget helps manage your time and spending, while also avoiding a situation in which you begin to chase your losses.

If necessary, you can make use of responsible gambling tools offered by gambling sites, such as deposit limits, loss limits, self-exclusion and time-outs.

If you want to seek help for gambling-related issues, there are several charities and healthcare providers who offer free support and information:

Blackjack rules FAQS

How do you win at blackjack?

According to the rules of blackjack, the player must try and beat the dealer by gaining a hand with a total value that is closer to 21 than the dealer’s hand. However, if the value of the hand exceeds 21, the player goes ‘bust’ and loses the hand.

What happens if both the player and dealer get 21?

If both the player and dealer get 21, this is known as a ‘push’. It is essentially a tie, as neither the player or the dealer wins the hand. Blackjack dealer rules say that if a player is dealt a perfect 21, also known as a blackjack, then they win unless the dealer has the same.

Can I split any pair of cards in blackjack?

The rules for playing blackjack state if you are dealt a pair of identically ranked initial cards, then you can split them into separate hands, but they must be a pair in order to split. Once you split the cards, you’ll place your original bet with one hand and place an equal bet on the second hand.

What is the house edge in blackjack?

House edge is the name given to the casino’s advantage over a player for a certain game. It also represents the profit that the casino expects to make on each game, and it is usually expressed as a percentage. The house edge for blackjack ranges between one per cent and two per cent.

What is insurance in blackjack?

An insurance bet is a type of side bet that can only be made when the dealer’s up-card is an Ace. This bet is essentially wagering that the dealer has a Blackjack – if they do, the insurance bet pays out at 2:1.

News.title: Hard Labour: Inside the global crisis killing mothers and babies
News.content:
For centuries, pregnancy and childbirth were among the world’s greatest dangers. Over the past 25 years, major advances in healthcare have helped reduce maternal deaths by 40 per cent. But that progress is now under threat.

Unprecedented international aid cuts, combined with the highest levels of conflict seen in a generation, are reversing years of hard-won gains.

In this powerful new documentary, Bel Trew travels to some of the world's most dangerous places for pregnancy and childbirth, meeting mothers, babies and frontline healthcare workers as they confront the devastating consequences of conflict, poverty and collapsing healthcare systems.
