Sports.title: Today on Sky Sports Racing: Blue Bolt and Precise clash again in Prix Rothschild
Sports.content:
We have a busy day's racing on Sunday with Flat action from Chester, Yarmouth and Deauville, live on Sky Sports Racing...

3.40 Deauville - Star fillies Blue Bolt and Precise lock horns again

A red-hot renewal of this Group One Prix Rothschild at Deauville where Blue Bolt and Precise renew their rivalry.

Andrew Balding's Blue Bolt saw off Precise when landing a first Group One success in the Falmouth at Newmarket last month and bids to confirm that form under Colin Keane. A dominant winner on that occasion, the market believes she can follow up and land a four-timer.

Balding said: "She seems in good nick and if she repeats the performance from Newmarket she will take a lot of beating.

"She's been a star this year and the only factor is she has never travelled far from home to run before. But if she takes the travel in her stride then she should hold every chance of continuing her winning run."

Aidan O'Brien saddles Precise, herself a four-time Group One scorer, with Ryan Moore in the plate. An impressive winner of the Irish 1000 Guineas, she took the Coronation Stakes at Royal Ascot before failing to land a blow on Blue Bolt. Sent off the odds-on favourite that day, it will be fascinating to see if she can reverse the form.

O'Brien said: "She's in good form, she was stood in the gates a little bit long the last day and lost a couple of lengths and turned her head a little bit.

"Hopefully she won't do that the next day and give away those lengths. It's hard to do that at somewhere like Newmarket, especially at the July meeting where you are going straight down. We're happy with everything she's doing and looking forward to seeing her again, she's been a special filly for us so far."

Moon Target has two lengths to find on her fourth behind Precise at the Royal meeting, while Green Spirit might appreciate the drop back to a mile.

A deep contest has several with each-way claims including Karl Burke's 1,000 Guineas runner-up Evolutionist.

3.20 Chester - Unbeaten Lifeplan heads the field

Declan Carroll's Lifeplan faces eight rivals as he bids to remain unbeaten in a cracking edition of the Listed Queensferry Stakes at Chester.

Last year's Gimcrack champion has not been seen since landing that prestigious prize back in August and his connections are hoping he can make up for lost time. Stall nine will make life a bit trickier for jockey Zak Wheatley however.

Song Of The Clyde is a top performer on his day and showed all his ability when taking the Listed Carnarvon Stakes at Newbury. Below his best the last twice, he will not want conditions to be too quick.

Hugo Palmer fields Fitzella and Ardisia who are both closely matched on the pick of their runs, while Calico Blue steps up in class for Roger Varian.

12.56 Deauville - Woot Woot, Nicely and Queen Of The Day clash

A strong edition of the Sky Sports Racing Prix Six Perfections where a host of in-form two-year-old clash over seven furlongs.

Christopher Head has never hidden his admiration for Woot Woot and she justified that reputation when winning impressively at Saint-Cloud and she warrants respect on this grade.

Queen Of The Day defeated Woot Woot on debut before chasing home the exciting Avec Toi on her second start and she will find this an easier task.

British raider Nicely stepped forward from her debut to win comfortably at Hamilton and adds further intrigue to this splendid opener.

Best of the rest

1.32 Deauville - Group Three contest with Light Of Dawn representing Wathnan Racing and Karl Burke. Jorolina and Kosuma look useful.

3.05 Deauville - Group Three where Elle Eclipse and Lefteye feature. Evita has good form behind Diamond Necklace. William Buick rides Symbol Of Majesty.

10.09 Saratoga - Grade Two Glen Falls - rescheduled with Survie and Gezora fancied.

3.52 Chester - Power Fizz and Monarch's Gold involved alongside Roman Dragon.

3.08 Yarmouth - Valuable novice.

Sports.title: Staveley-led consortium agrees deal for minority stake in West Ham
Sports.content:
Vanessa Gold has confirmed she has agreed to sell her stake in the club to a consortium led by former Newcastle co-owner Amanda Staveley.

Gold, who succeeded her father David as joint-chair of the Hammers following his death in 2023, has a deal in place with a group headed by Staveley, her husband Mehrdad Ghodoussi and PCP Capital Partners for her family's 25.1 per cent holding.

However, current shareholders will also be presented with the chance to buy out the Gold family under an ongoing process.

Image: Former Newcastle co-owner Staveley's consortium is set to buy a 25.1 per cent stake in the club

"Amanda Staveley, her husband Mehrdad Ghodoussi, PCP Capital Partners along with Ashland Forest Capital Partners can confirm they have agreed the purchase of the Gold family's 25.1 per cent stake in West Ham United," the Staveley-led consortium said in a statement.

"A legal binding agreement has been signed.

"This sale agreement, though, remains subject to a pre-emption process under which existing shareholders have the option to buy the shares instead.

"No further comment will be made whilst the ongoing legal process takes its course."

Sky Sports News further understands Staveley, Ghodoussi and their consortium have brought together considerable funds.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch highlights of West Ham's pre-season friendly against Stevenage

Gold said in a statement: "As the daughter of David Gold, it was a great honour to step into a joint-chair and director role at the club following his passing in 2023.

"Whether as a youth-team player, a lifelong fan or an owner, my father's priority was always to champion and protect this great club. Over the past three years I have taken huge personal pride in continuing that legacy and will always be hugely grateful to the staff, players and fans who allowed me to do so.

"On June 12, Daniel Kretinsky and I agreed a sale that would have made EP Group the single largest shareholder in West Ham. Unfortunately, since that time, the original deal and other alternatives that we have discussed could not be brought to fruition.

"In light of this, I have now reached an agreement to sell my family's shareholding to a consortium of PCP Capital Partners, led by Amanda Staveley and Mehrdad Ghodoussi, in partnership with Ashland Forest Capital Partners. This sale remains subject to a pre-emption process, under which existing shareholders have the option to buy the shares instead.

"While the process has not yet concluded, I wanted to be open with our fans about where things stand and my intentions.

"My ambition throughout this process has been to ensure the club has the right leadership and ownership to enable West Ham to achieve its potential and return to its rightful place in the Premier League.

Image: The consortium is led by Staveley and her husband Mehrdad Ghodoussi, alongside PCP Capital Partners

"Amanda Staveley, Mehrdad Ghodoussi and PCP Capital Partners will bring deep experience and understanding of what it takes to lead a successful football club, and I have every confidence in what she and her partners can bring to West Ham.

"While the sale process proceeds, I will continue to act in the club's best interests, as my father did and would expect of me."

Staveley brokered the deal which allowed a Saudi-backed consortium to buy out then Newcastle owner Mike Ashley in October 2021, and she and Ghodoussi oversaw the club's rise from Premier League relegation candidates to Champions League participants and, after their departure during the summer of 2024, Carabao Cup winners.

The Hammers dropped out of the top flight at the end of last season and will begin the process of attempting to secure a swift return at Burnley on August 16.

West Ham said in a statement: "West Ham United can confirm it is aware of the announcement from joint-chair Vanessa Gold that she has reached a provisional agreement to sell her shares to a consortium of PCP Capital Partners, led by Amanda Staveley and Mehrdad Ghodoussi, in partnership with Ashland Forest Capital Partners.

"The proposed transaction will now be subject to a pre-emption rights process. This provides all existing shareholders with the opportunity to acquire their proportional percentage of shares in round one, and any remaining shares in round two. This process will take approximately two months and, until it is completed, nothing will change regarding the ownership structure of the club.

"West Ham United would like to assure supporters that the day-to-day running of the football club is in no way affected by this situation. Preparations for the new season continue to take shape with diligence and focus, and we thank all fans for their continued loyal backing at this time.

"The club will be making no further comment while the pre-emption process runs its course."

Sports.title: Warrington go fourth as Wakefield move second, Saints beaten by York
Sports.content:
Super League: Warrington move into fourth with comprehensive win over Castleford, St Helens beaten by York in thriller, and Wakefield regain second

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights as Warrington Wolves wrapped up a big win over Castleford Tigers Highlights as Warrington Wolves wrapped up a big win over Castleford Tigers

Warrington Wolves moved up to fourth in the Betfred Super League table after recovering from a lacklustre start to claim a comprehensive 48-18 win at Castleford Tigers .

Having lost four of their last six matches, including three in a row on the road, Warrington were made to pay for an error-strewn first 20 minutes as the Tigers went 16-6 ahead at the OneBore Stadium.

But Matty Ashton, Toby King and Toafofoa Sipley touched down to turn the tide and put Warrington 24-18 in front at half-time, and James Harrison and Leon Hayes extended the Wolves' lead after the break.

Ashton scored again, taking his tally to five tries in two matches against Castleford this year having bagged a hat-trick when Warrington claimed a 72-6 victory in March, before Ben Currie scored.

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

Teenage scrum-half Ewan Irwin was excellent with the boot, splitting the posts with all eight conversions, to make it back-to-back defeats for Castleford.

While Castleford were stuffed by rivals Wakefield last weekend, they claimed a shock win over Leeds in their last home match and Warrington head coach Sam Burgess had warned they would be no pushovers.

On this occasion, they could not find the defensive intent required to stop Warrington on their push for a spot at the top end of the top six.

Sailor misses late kick as York edge thriller

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights as York Knights clinched a thrilling victory over St Helens Highlights as York Knights clinched a thrilling victory over St Helens

Oli Field's double further dented St Helens' play-off hopes despite Jack Welsby's try-of-the-season contender as York edged to a thrilling 34-32 victory at the LNER Community Stadium.

Saints got off to the perfect start when Welsby kicked through to allow Jake Davies to touch down, with Jackson Hastings adding the conversion.

York Knights inflicted a damning loss on St Helens

York hit back almost immediately when Toa Mata'Afa put Jon Bennison over in the corner, and although he was unable to convert his own score, he was successful after Field capitalised on Cody Hunter's well-timed pass with a neat step to make it 10-6.

The lead proved short-lived when Hunter was unable to claim Hastings' up and under and Shane Wright pounced to score a converted try, and the visitors surged further head when Welsby burst through Denive Balmforth's tackle after the fleet-footed Harry Robertson had raced down the right wing.

However, Balmforth swiftly made amends with a sniping finish and Bennison levelled it up at 16-16 at the break.

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

The Knights were temporarily reduced to 12 when Ata Hingana was sent to the bin for a high tackle on Davies, but it was they who regained the lead with 53 minutes gone when prop Paul Vaughan barged his way over and Bennison added the extra points.

They went 12 points ahead after Saints failed to deal with Hunter's lofted kick, Nikau Williams touching down and Bennison making it 28-16, but Robertson's brilliance allowed Tristan Sailor to feed Welsby to complete a length-of-the-field move which was converted by Hastings.

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

Field's second try and a fifth successful Bennison conversion gave the Knights breathing space, but late scores from Robertson and Jacob Douglas gave Saints a chance.

Regular goal kicker Hastings remained on the field but was holding his glute so Sailor had to deputise and missed the crucial kick to level the game.

Wakefield move back second with win over Catalans

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights as Wakefield Trinity sealed victory over Catalans Dragons Highlights as Wakefield Trinity sealed victory over Catalans Dragons

A crucial double from Isaiah Vagana helped Wakefield Trinity to a 32-12 win over Catalans Dragons to move back into second place in the Super League table.

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

The match was close at the break, Trinity leading by just four points, but a five-minute spell changed the game thanks to Vagana's quick efforts.

Jake Trueman and Cameron Scott had gone over early to give the visitors the lead before Catalans responded through Toby Sexton.

After Caleb Hamline-Uele and Matthieu Laguerre then put more points on the scoreboard for both outfits, Vagana's moment arrived with just 15 minutes remaining before Scott sealed the deal with his second.

Sports.title: Evening Saigon wins Stewards' Cup at Goodwood
Sports.content:
James Doyle picked the right one from three choices as his bosses at Wathnan Racing topped an amazing week at Glorious Goodwood with victory in the Coral Stewards' Cup with Evening Saigon.

The win was a feather in the cap for the owners, who target this fixture with a vengeance, but perhaps more telling it was a second major handicap of the week for Qatari-born trainer Hamad Al Jehani.

Having also won the Golden Mile with Archivist when Doyle picked the wrong one, Al Jehani was able to celebrate a famous victory with the whole team on this occasion.

Despite higher numbers being preferred at Thursday's draw, the finish was dominated by the eventual winner drawn in 10 beating Stratusnine in five. Jamie Spencer flew from the back on Mitbaahy for third but he was beaten a head and a short head. Completely Random was fourth.

"It's been a great week. Obviously I was very deflated last year with just one and we were really frustrated by that so the memo was we need to do better and that's everyone, including me as well," said Doyle.

"We've done a lot of work this week looking at different tactics and things like that, track position and stuff. All the guys back home in the office, these guys, Hamad has done an unbelievable job with this horse as well.

"He's not an easy conveyance, setting off he was that well in himself he tried to get rid of me the first few strides but that was great.

"We just had the perfect set-up. Dark Thirty was near me, I was able to draft in behind him and we didn't go that mad I didn't think for a Stewards' Cup so I was happy to pull him out before the two and set sail for home.

"I knew the second horse, I won on him the other day at York, he's a pretty decent horse too so it was a good tussle up to the line.

"Hamad and his team, it's nice that they have won the two big handicaps this week."

Al Jehani said: "I am very happy for Evening Saigon and very happy for the team. He performed very well at Royal Ascot and it was the right decision from the management to keep him for the Stewards' Cup.

"It's really important for us and it's a really important race for the season. I'm very happy and thanks to James for giving the horse a great ride.

"It's not easy to be competitive with the best trainers in the world but we try our best and I think we are building in a very good way, with great help from the management. Hopefully, we will improve year by year and we can make Wathnan be in the winner's enclosure more and more."

Wathnan's racing advisor Richard Brown added: "James had a bit of a hard choice but he was pretty firm on riding this lad in the end. Hamad has turned up and won two of the hardest handicaps to win all year. We plot these and work as a team - when these results come off, it's just fantastic for Wathnan and what Wathnan is all about.

"If you look at Hamad's statistics since he started training, they match up with the best trainers in the country. He's a phenomenal horseman and was a very good rider himself. He's very modest about it but he showjumped to a good level. He's a great horseman and he's formed a great team. We all work very closely together and to pull this off is huge for everybody involved."

Goodie Two Shoes sticks her neck out to edge Lillie Langtry battle

Goodie Two Shoes needed to be very brave as she added to Joseph O'Brien and Dylan Browne McMonagle's fantastic week at Goodwood in the Qatar Lillie Langtry Stakes.

With three winners already in the bag, the JP McManus-owned Goodie Two Shoes was sent off an 8/1 chance to bag a first victory of the season but looked to face a tough ask as Santorini Star kicked for home.

She still had ground to make up with 100 yards to the line but the seven-year-old stuck her neck out right where it mattered to get the verdict by a nose.

Image: Goodie Two Shoes (centre), ridden by Dylan Browne McMonagle, on the way to winning the Qatar Lillie Langtry Stakes at Goodwood

Goodie Two Shoes was second in the Melbourne Cup in November and a return to Australia will surely now be on the cards following this Group Two triumph.

The winning rider said: "She's a lovely filly, she's improving all the time since she started coming back this year, she's got better with each run.

"I was quietly confident she would get a lot closer to these fillies, she ran well last year [third] when the ground turned up soft but she would gallop down the road for you, she handles quick ground. I got a lovely split through them and she wanted to win.

"To be honest I didn't think I'd won but I looked back at the camera and she had her head stuck down for me at the right time; I did think Tom (Marquand) had won but we came out the right side of it.

"These are very, very special silks to put on. A big thanks to JP for putting me up and she's going to have a nice campaign through to the end of the season.

"I'm sure the Melbourne Cup is probably the main target, the boys will know that and Joseph and JP will discuss it but I'd probably guess that's the obvious target."

Sir Anthony McCoy, representing McManus, said: "I didn't think she had won but Jason Weaver said right on the nod, not before the line or after the line but right on the line, she put her head in the right place.

"She got a good ride - he was going to ride her for that bit of luck, down the inside, and he got a lot of luck. When you are as good as Dylan Browne McMonagle and you are riding for Joseph O'Brien, you seem to get a lot of luck.

"Dylan was over at mine a few times when he was 11 or 12. He is very mechanically correct, like Ryan Moore, and he's got that chip - that little thing where he could go the wrong way. I mean it in a good way. As Frankie found out one day at Ascot, he has that little edge to him.

"She was second in a Melbourne Cup and I thought she had been quite well handicapped for the Galway Plate if she ran there off 123. It's nice when you win races like this and hopefully she will be able to go back to the Melbourne Cup."

Sports.title: Welbeck completes move to Chelsea
Sports.content:
Chelsea have completed the signing of Danny Welbeck from Brighton for an undisclosed fee.

Chelsea have turned to Welbeck as they look to add experience to manager Xabi Alonso's squad.

The last time the west London club paid a transfer fee for a player over the age of 26 was four years ago, when they signed Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang from Barcelona.

Image: Welbeck is set for a medical ahead of a move to Chelsea

It has been two years since Chelsea selected a player over the age of 30 in any game.

Welbeck has continued to be a reliable goalscorer in the Premier League at 35. He scored 13 last season, and 10 during the campaign before that.

It would also place further doubt on the futures of strikers Nicolas Jackson, Liam Delap and Marc Guiu.

Chelsea have signed several players from Brighton in recent seasons, including their main striker Joao Pedro, plus Moises Caicedo, Marc Cucurella and Robert Sanchez.

Several Brighton staff members have also moved to Stamford Bridge over the past four years, including sporting directors Paul Winstanley and Sam Jewell.

"When you hear of the interest from Chelsea, it's something that fills you with such immense pride," said Welbeck.

"Knowing the history of Chelsea, it's a club that wants to win trophies and is pushing to do that every single season.

"I'm really honoured to come to a club of this stature at what feels like a really exciting time.

"I know a few of the boys already, and I've had fantastic conversations with the manager and already feel that connection.

"I've got that fire in my belly, and I'm ready to give it everything for this club to make everyone at Chelsea, and the supporters, proud.'

Neville backs Chelsea decision to sign PL experience

Gary Neville has said signing players like Welbeck and Jordan Henderson is exactly what Chelsea's young players need in order to gain more guidance.

The former Premier League-winning captain insists the decision to bring the veterans in is not a "magical" one, but rather an example of what all top teams need to compete.

"If you watched Chelsea for the last three, four or five years you'd say there's inexperience right throughout the football club," he said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Gary Neville says Chelsea have been crying out for Premier League experience in their squad, backing any decision to sign the likes of Welbeck and Henderson

"I think putting a spine in of good, senior professionals who act as guardians of good behaviour, responsibility and discipline in the dressing room is something that's not magic. It's something all top teams have had for many decades.

"Putting in Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck who know how to win Premier League titles, their jobs will be as much off the pitch as it will be on it. They're still good players who can contribute 25-35 games a season, but they will make sure the young players turn up every single day and give their all.

"I didn't think the young players at Chelsea have any real leadership or guidance on and off the pitch. They've now got people who can do that."

BlueCo's drastic change in transfer policy

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Sam Blitz explains why Chelsea's transfer policy U-turn - including potential signings Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson - makes sense.

Analysis from Sky Sports' Callum Bishop:

The BlueCo era at Chelsea has been defined by hoarding some of the best young talent on the planet and developing them in-house. That method has had some successes, but overall, it has not panned out.

Image: Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang was the last player over the age of 26 who Chelsea paid a transfer fee for

There is clearly some recognition and accountability from the top brass about that. In bringing in Alonso as manager, they know they have lucked out in getting one of the most sought-after tacticians in the game. The Spaniard has clearly identified the need for experience and the club are following his lead.

The interest in Granit Xhaka earlier in the summer was among the first signs of the shift. Even making a move for Lacroix is evidence of a change in approach.

The Welbeck move is surprising, but there is some logic that can be applied to it. Is he going to start every week? No. However, Chelsea's other four senior strikers have an average age of just 23. Combined, they have made 269 Premier League appearances and scored 74 goals.

Image: Thiago Silva was the last player over the age of 30 to play for Chelsea

The Brighton veteran has 400 appearances and 90 goals on his own. To have that as your back-up to the young guns you want to develop makes sense.

Henderson? That's a complete 180-degree turn. Caicedo and Enzo Fernandez are two of the more experienced players Alonso has. If you had to pick anywhere Chelsea needed a wise head, you would not say midfield.

Yet, they wanted Xhaka. They will soon have Henderson. Alonso may have been the man to oversee the blossoming of players like Florian Wirtz at Bayer Leverkusen. However, he clearly sees the values of opposite characters and knows Chelsea, and perhaps more importantly, he needs people ready now.

Sports.title: O'Leary stopped by Chamberlain in Dublin thriller
Sports.content:
Pierce O'Leary suffered his first professional defeat when he was stopped by Mark Chamberlain in a thrilling fight in Dublin.

O'Leary battled back to drop Chamberlain after being floored twice in the early rounds, but the hometown hero was dramatically halted in the 10th round of their super-lightweight fight at 3Arena.

Chamberlain had taken a firm grip on the fight from the second round when he floored O'Leary with a left hand.

O'Leary was on the brink of a swift stoppage loss when he was dropped again in the third, sinking to the canvas after an uppercut from Chamberlain.

Roared on by a vociferous crowd, O'Leary launched a spirited rally and a body shot sent Chamberlain crumpling to the floor by the ropes in the seventh.

Image: O'Leary's spirited fightback was ended in the 10th round

O'Leary's pursuit of a comeback win was ruthlessly ended by Chamberlain a few rounds later, though, as the Portsmouth fighter landed a huge right hand that prompted the referee to wave it off.

After his unbeaten record was ended, O'Leary called for a rematch: "I thought I was well back in the fight when it happened but it is what it is.

"Mark was the better man on the night. A fight like that, I think we all want to see a rematch."

Image: Chamberlain celebrates a thrilling victory

Chamberlain, who put his career back on track after a draw with Jack Rafferty last August, said: "I'm not a stranger to an away day, and anyone that knows me deep down knows I will fight anyone, anywhere.

"If it means I've got to go in the champion's back garden, I'll do that.

"But I take my hat off to Pierce because he's a true champion and he'll come again."

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino could face leadership challenge as Fifa Council members rebel
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino is facing a rebellion from members of the Fifa Council who are attempting to force an extraordinary general meeting (EGM) that could develop into a full blown leadership challenge.

The Guardian has learned that moves to call an EGM were already under way before the emergence of Infantino’s abortive plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup, with council members demanding an independent review into the unprecedented decision to lift Folarin Balogun’s suspension during the World Cup, which involved multiple phone calls from Donald Trump.

Fifa Council is the world governing body’s main decision-making forum composed of 28 representatives of the six confederations, eight vice presidents and Infantino. Under Fifa rules a motion from 50% or 19 of the 37 council members can trigger an EGM.

It is understood that the rebels had already reached double figures before it emerged that Infantino had secretly proposed to sell 20% of a new World Cup operating company to Thrive Capital, an investment company founded by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

The unhappy council members had been planning on calling for Infantino to resign if he refused to sanction an independent review of the Balogun affair, which led to the Norwegian FA filing an official complaint to the International Olympic Committee alleging Fifa had breached rules on political neutrality by bowing to pressure from Trump.

Fifa has insisted all along that it followed due process with the decision taken independently by its ethics committee, but has yet to publish a written report on the hearing.

The rebels are likely to have been emboldened by Infantino’s U-turn over the World Cup sell-off debacle, with the plan abandoned in a statement from Fifa in the early hours of Saturday morning after Uefa, North American confederation Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation denounced it.

Uefa and Concacaf both issued further statements condemning Infantino and calling for a thorough review of Fifa’s governance yesterday, but it is unclear if they have sufficient support from the rest of the world to oust him.

View image in fullscreen The rebels are likely to have been emboldened by Infantino’s U-turn over the World Cup sell-off debacle. Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPA

The Confederation of African Football and South American Conmebol remain fully behind Infantino, while the Qatar Football Association issued a statement yesterday backing him to stay as president.

Of the 37 council members 14 are from Europe and North America so support from Asia will be required to put real pressure on Infantino.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Fifa Council is not due to meet until November with the rebels attempting to move quickly to force an EGM, where Infantino would be asked to explain himself. A refusal to commission an external review into Balogun would lead to more active attempts to oust Infantino, with alternative presidential candidates already being sounded out.

Qatar’s stance has definitely ruled out a presidential bid from Paris Saint-Germain president, Nasser Al-Khelaifi, and much will depend on whether Victor Montagliani, the Canadian who is president of Concacaf, has the appetite to take on Infantino. A campaign from AFC president Sheikh Salman, who lost narrowly to Infantino in the 2016 Fifa election, would be difficult without the support of his own confederation.

Infantino has already secured more than 200 letters of support endorsing his re-election campaign, but they can be withdrawn and the deadline for other candidates to announce an intention to stand is not until 18 November.

Another potential vehicle for removing Infantino would be an emergency Fifa Congress to trigger a vote of no confidence in the president, which can be called if letters are submitted by 43 associations.

Sports.title: There can be no letup. Humiliated Infantino must stand down at Fifa or be removed | Nick Ames
Sports.content:
There is no time to dance around the subject. Gianni Infantino must stand down as Fifa president or otherwise be legally removed. No fresh chances can be made available for an official who has demolished trust in football’s integrity and governance, trashing all remaining credibility of the body that oversees the world’s most-cherished sport.

Infantino was forced into a humiliating climbdown on Saturday morning when he accepted the failure of his plan to sell off portions of the World Cup to private investment. He resolved to resume dialogue about football’s growth “in the spirit of shared interest in our game”. But such a naked attempt to save his own skin cannot hold. Every day Infantino remains in power is a fresh stain on an institution whose reputation is on the floor.

The overreach involved in unilaterally launching the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme – with its vision to place huge influence on football’s future in the palms of venture capitalists – would be enough to bring down most leaders. But Infantino’s rap sheet goes far beyond that. He has routinely made a mockery of Fifa’s own statutes and governance regulations, so nobody should be surprised that patience has finally snapped in corridors of power globally. Fifa’s “football unites the world” slogan has never looked more empty.

Article 10.3 of those regulations, which specifically pertains to the presidency, requires the incumbent to ensure “Fifa’s objectives, mission, strategic direction, policies and values are sustainably pursued, protected and implemented, and that a positive image of Fifa is fostered”. It stipulates “promoting friendly and peaceful relations within Fifa”, which is a nonsense given the degree to which federations and senior personnel have distanced themselves from Infantino in recent days.

The rules give no green light to the pursuit of multiple private projects that, most recently in lockstep with the current US administration or its tributaries, have been tabled with scant appetite for oversight or explanation.

Where to begin? The Folarin Balogun saga tipped many leading figures in football, particularly in Europe, towards the edge. There had already been widespread bafflement and disgust at Infantino’s presentation of the new Fifa peace prize to Donald Trump in December, with little background given about the process and highly contestable information provided about the US president’s qualifying achievements. Stakeholders were frustrated by a lack of consultation about the introduction of “hydration breaks”, which fundamentally toyed with the fabric of matches at this summer’s World Cup.

View image in fullscreen The saga involving Folarin Balogun after his ban for a red card was suspended tipped many leading figures in football towards the edge. Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters

The bizarre expedited bidding process for the 2034 tournament, which resulted in Saudi Arabia’s candidature being waved through in December 2024, also brought widespread criticism. This list only covers the past 20 months of controversies inflicted by Infantino, capped on Friday by revelations that plans for a 64-team World Cup are in full swing.

When a scathing statement from Uefa on Saturday called for an end to “secret schemes on fast track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game”, it was not only referring to the FFE project and its casual sidelining of other decision makers within Fifa.

A critical mass has been reached. Uefa took a decisive lead in following more than a year of harsh words with strong, united action in pledging to boycott future Fifa tournaments if Infantino did not withdraw his plan. It undoubtedly influenced the outcome and the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, secured an achievement that may define his own reign. But it will mean nothing if Infantino, who is understood to have deployed a major consultancy to smooth relations with federations in recent days, is given the oxygen to dangle fresh promises and turn heads back towards the status quo.

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino’s rap sheet goes far beyond attempting to launch the Fifa Forward Enterprise unilaterally. Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPA

There is an acknowledgment within Uefa and beyond that the pace must not let up. Senior figures are adamant Infantino must not survive the current scandal. Some insiders feel a crucial next step will be for member associations, the overwhelming majority of whom had formally pledged their support for Infantino’s re-election next March, to recall those letters.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Doing so requires a request to Fifa but could, in sufficient numbers, be a de facto vote of no confidence in Infantino. Fifa had lobbied aggressively for those submissions but many FAs would now be red faced if their expression of fealty towards Infantino was more widely publicised.

Member associations have a duty not to shrink in staving off existential threats to their sport otherwise they, like Infantino, are doing it an egregious disservice. Backing away now would mean leaving the job half done at best.

Uefa have pledged to devise a new method for distributing Fifa’s wealth, delving into its multibillion cash reserves without “selling the family silver”. Behind the scenes it continues to work with other confederations in an effort to find credible candidates for Infantino’s replacement, with a view to running in the election should the Swiss hold on until then. The present crisis can be used to reshape football for the better but only if Infantino is not in situ to impose the final say.

The alternative is that Fifa, and by extension the game, continue lurching from one disaster to the next. It is no laughing matter when the public conversation around football centres on one man, his ego and brazen ventures.

In December Zvonimir Boban, a former sidekick to Infantino as Fifa’s deputy secretary general, told the Guardian that “the way is lost” after the peace prize award to Trump. Fifa will not find a route back until Infantino plays no further part in its operation.

Sports.title: The five big beasts are gone: who will be the Premier League’s next alpha manager? | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
This used to be a land of giants. This used to be a land where big men fought. This used to be a land where Sir Alex Ferguson and Arsène Wenger tussled, then José Mourinho joined the fray. This used to be a land where Jürgen Klopp made Pep Guardiola reconsider, and he changed his style and won anyway.

Not any more. Next season will be the first since the inaugural Premier League in 1992 not to feature any of the five big managerial beasts – not Ferguson, not Wenger, not Mourinho, not Klopp and not Guardiola.

What’s come over our great land? The Premier League is still our home, but where have all the heroes gone? Where’s the man who ruled by fury? Or the man who made virtues of broccoli and sobriety? Where’s the man who made the conference room the pitch? Where’s the gegenpressingmeister, or the cold philosopher of the positional game? Now they take a man who instigated some interesting pressing patterns and they call him a regular hero. Where are the men who are willing to play the game?

You don’t have to be a nostalgist in the vein of Bill Anderson to think that the Premier League looks a little diminished. Régis Le Bris took over at Sunderland two summers ago and already he is the fourth longest-serving manager currently at a Premier League club. While his quiet authority impressed last season, the understated Breton is nobody’s idea of a main character. And it’ll take a while before the meeting of the two longest-servers, Mikel Arteta and Unai Emery, looks like a clash of the titans, even with the twist that Emery was Arteta’s predecessor at Arsenal.

Tottenham appointed Roberto De Zerbi in March and, the promoted sides excepted, he has already been a Premier League manager longer than 11 of his rivals. All long-running dramas go through this process. Major characters move on, new ones arise. At least they are easier to tell apart than in House of the Dragon: they don’t all have the same hair, and they are not all bafflingly interrelated. Still, it will take time for the new breed to become familiar. Quirks have to be learned, strengths and weaknesses understood.

View image in fullscreen Roberto De Zerbi has the charisma of a leading figure. Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/PA

The result is that this season looks as hard to call as any in living memory. Perhaps the Premier League has entered its Arsenal era and Arteta will soon squat like a giant toad across English football. But retaining the league is difficult, particularly given the emotional outpouring that inevitably comes with ending a lengthy drought. Neither Declan Rice nor Bukayo Saka looked especially fresh at the World Cup, while William Saliba damaged his back. It would be no great surprise if Arsenal started the season slowly.

But who is equipped to take advantage? The previous two league title winners are under new management. Enzo Maresca – Guardiola’s replacement at Manchester City – is a curious manager in that his record is rather better than the experience of watching his teams play. Although his reputation was enhanced by Chelsea’s decline after his departure, it shouldn’t be forgotten just how frustrated Leicester and Chelsea fans became at times with the cautious nature of his football. Arne Slot showed at Liverpool that it is, at least in the short term, possible to thrive when following one of the big beasts but it remains an enormous challenge to succeed somebody who has defined the personality of a club.

Andoni Iraola impressed at Rayo Vallecano and Bournemouth, but the truth is that it’s impossible to know how anybody will adapt to the greater scrutiny of a club like Liverpool, no matter how composed they may previously have appeared.

There’s a lingering doubt about his Bournemouth’s propensity to concede late goals. It may be that a deeper bench offers an immediate solution but equally that could indicate a problem with load management – and that is not going to be made any easier by involvement in the Champions League. Iraola has always relied on extremely physical training sessions, but they will have to be tempered, at least to an extent, by the demands of European football, which Iraola has never experienced.

Similar questions can be asked of Michael Carrick at Manchester United. He did enough last season that United effectively had to appoint him, without doing enough to offer overwhelming proof of his abilities. Signings so far seem to have addressed the right areas in the squad, but the big issue is whether he can handle the demands of playing in multiple competitions. United finished third last season without ever playing a team who had played fewer matches than them.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

So demanding is the modern calendar that fatigue may end up being a bigger factor than any manager. If you are a superclub, the key to having a bad season, as United have demonstrated, is to have one so bad that you don’t qualify for any form of European competition.

View image in fullscreen Xabi Alonso endured an awkward few months at Real Madrid but has the time to impose his ideas at Chelsea. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters

Which is extremely good news for Chelsea. Not only do they have, in Xabi Alonso, one of Europe’s most promising young managers but he has time to impose his ideas and his side will be fresher than their opponents in almost every game this season.

Emery’s domination of the Europa League has paradoxically given him a reputation of not quite being of the highest tier, but if Aston Villa can find a way of winning games beyond Morgan Rogers thrashing long-range efforts into the top corner, he has a great opportunity to impose himself. De Zerbi, who has the charisma of a leading figure, should also find himself in the Champions League qualification shake-up given Tottenham’s summer signings and their lack of European football.

The big beasts may have gone but that just means the Premier League is entering a new phase. What matters now is the battle to be the next alpha. Arteta is perhaps best placed, but the contenders are legion. The land awaits its next giant.

Sports.title: Scottish Premiership: Mayo and Nisbet strike late to help Aberdeen stun Hearts
Sports.content:
Hearts’ miserable summer continued as they conceded two late goals to lose 2-1 to Aberdeen in their Premiership opener at Pittodrie.

Wouter Vrancken and Hearts looked on course for a much-needed victory after a turbulent few months as they led through Oisin McEntee’s first-half goal. But just as they looked to be closing out a first win at Pittodrie for more than a decade, Lewis Mayo equalised in the 90th minute before Kevin Nisbet won it for Aberdeen with a stoppage-time penalty after Stuart Findlay was sent off for denying a goal-scoring opportunity.

It was a third consecutive defeat for Vrancken, who has endured a chastening start since replacing Derek McInnes in June.

The Aberdeen manager, Stephen Robinson, whose side had built up some momentum by winning each of their four Premier Sports Cup group-stage matches, pitched Chris Cadden straight into his starting lineup a day after he joined from Hibernian.

There were five changes to the Hearts side that lost Wednesday’s Champions League qualifier at home to Sturm Graz, with the goalkeeper Beau Reus and Laurent Mendy handed their debuts and Sabah Kerjota – more than a year after joining – and Amadou Ba-Sy given their first competitive starts.

In what was their first league match since being pipped to the title by Celtic in May, the 1,600-strong travelling support could be regularly heard singing anti-Scottish Football Association songs in protest at the contentious calls from officials in the closing matches of last season that they felt cost them dear in their quest for glory.

Following a summer of transition and a 6-0 aggregate defeat by Sturm Graz that had done little to improve the mood of the fans since that agonising end to the past campaign, there was a sense of trepidation in some quarters about the prospect of kicking off the new season at Pittodrie, where they had not won in their previous 14 visits.

Hearts’ makeshift defence – with the midfielder McEntee playing at centre-half following an injury to Malachi Fagan-Walcott – looked to have allowed the Aberdeen captain Nisbet to get clean through in the third minute but McEntee recovered well to scramble the ball behind for a corner.

Nisbet then glanced a header just wide from Connor Ronan’s corner in the 27th minute, although clear chances were generally at a premium.

Hearts made the breakthrough in the 35th minute after some pinball in the penalty area. Ba-Sy’s cutback from the left broke to Blair Spittal, whose shot was blocked by Nesta Guinness-Walker on the edge of the six-yard box and the fellow defender Dan Happe’s attempt to clear ran into the path of McEntee, who shot low into the net from seven yards.

The visitors generally looked comfortable for most of the second period, with Cláudio Braga spurning a good chance to double their lead.

Aberdeen had offered little as an attacking force but they levelled in the 90th minute when Mayo bundled in from close range after Happe headed Ronan’s free-kick back into the danger area.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The dramatic turnaround was completed in stoppage time when Toyosi Olusanya was hauled down by Findlay, who saw red, and Nisbet despatched the spot-kick.

The St Mirren manager, Craig McLeish, believes his team’s 2-0 win at Falkirk augurs well for a successful campaign.

McLeish is convinced his squad will improve on last season’s struggles before he steered Saints to safety when the interim head coach.

He has set a high bar of the top six and a European qualification bid this term, and a double from Killian Phillips helped St Mirren get off to a fine start at Falkirk Stadium.

“I thought the performance was excellent and if we can build on that we can go and achieve something as a group,” McLeish said. “I’m delighted for the group. We got the result our performance deserved. I thought we were excellent.”

Sports.title: Transfer news: Welbeck joins Chelsea, Brentford complete record Sangaré deal
Sports.content:
Chelsea have signed Brighton’s veteran striker Danny Welbeck in a deal worth a reported £5m. Welbeck has agreed a two-year contract and will link up with Xabi Alonso’s squad on their pre-season tour.

The 35-year-old’s move to Stamford Bridge is a break from Chelsea’s policy of signing younger players with the potential to be developed. It is the first time they have paid a transfer fee for a player over the age of 26 since they signed Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang from Barcelona in 2022 when the striker was 33.

“When you hear of interest from Chelsea, it’s something that fills you with such immense pride. Knowing the history of Chelsea, it’s a club that wants to win trophies and is pushing to do that every single season,” Welbeck said.

“I’m really honoured to come to a club of this stature at what feels like a really exciting time. I know a few of the boys already and I’ve had fantastic conversations with the manager and already feel that connection. I’ve got that fire in my belly and I’m ready to give it everything for this club to make everyone at Chelsea, and the supporters, proud.”

Alonso was keen to add experience to his squad after last season’s disappointing 10th-place finish in the Premier League. He opted for Welbeck after the former Manchester United and Arsenal forward enjoyed a memorable campaign with Brighton.

Welbeck, who has 42 caps for England, scored 13 goals in 37 Premier League games last term after netting 10 times in 2024-25.

Welbeck’s arrival in west London will raise questions about the future of Chelsea striker Liam Delap, who signed from Ipswich last season, as well as fellow forwards Nicolas Jackson and Marc Guiu.

Welbeck is the latest player to move from Brighton to Chelsea in recent years after João Pedro, Moisés Caicedo, Robert Sánchez and Marc Cucurella, who joined Real Madrid earlier this summer.

Chelsea spent a British record £117m to sign the England forward Morgan Rogers, 24, from Aston Villa in July. They also secured the France defender Maxence Lacroix, 26, from Crystal Palace for £52m earlier this week and signed Atalanta defender Marco Palestra, 21, for £43m.

Brentford seal record Sangaré deal

Brentford have signed the Mali international Mamadou Sangaré from ⁠Lens for a club-record fee, reported to be £39m. Sangaré, 24, joins Brentford on a five-year contract, with ⁠the option to extend for another year.

“Mamadou ​is someone ‌that we’ve tracked ‌for quite some time. He’s been on ‌our radar and was a player we were really keen to bring in,” the Brentford head coach Keith Andrews said. “He’s a humble young man, but he’s equally as ⁠determined to succeed in his career. He ​fits ​everything we want from ​a Brentford player, on and ​off the ‌pitch.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Sangaré left Austria’s Rapid Vienna to ‌join Lens last year, and featured prominently as they won the ​French Cup for the first time and finished second in Ligue 1.

View image in fullscreen Mamadou Sangaré has swapped RC Lens for Brentford in a £39m move. Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/Reuters

Bournemouth have announced the signing of António Silva from Benfica for a fee believed to be in the region of £25m. The 22-year-old defender becomes new manager Marco Rose’s second signing of the summer after the arrival of Álvaro Rodríguez earlier this week.

Silva made 235 senior appearances for Benfica and collected six major honours during his time in Portugal. He told the club website: “I am very happy to be here. It’s a pleasure to play for Bournemouth and in the Premier League.

“The mentality is always to win. I will try my best, and I will play for the fans. We have everything here that helps us perform on the pitch, and I can’t wait to get started.”

Sports.title: Faster, faster: Iraola in a rush to plug Liverpool gaps before Premier League starts
Sports.content:
“Faster, faster,” bellowed Andoni Iraola throughout the open training session Liverpool held in Chicago on Friday. His first pre-season tour as Liverpool head coach ends at the city’s famous Soldier Field Stadium on Sunday, with a friendly against Leeds, and “faster, faster” could apply to all aspects of the club’s preparations for a new Premier League campaign that begins in three weeks’ time.

Iraola was in his element as he immersed himself at the centre of every training drill that Liverpool performed at Chicago Fire’s Endeavor Health Performance Center, their base for the past two weeks in the US. “Faster, faster” was the new head coach’s instruction to his players as three teams of seven worked on their pressing games. He also shouted it when they walked over to a different pitch, recently vacated by Robert Lewandowski and his new Chicago Fire teammates, to work on offensive and defensive set-piece routines. Sprints were demanded following every rondo.

There is an urgency to Iraola’s situation at Liverpool as he works towards his first season in charge, not only to his style of football. Post World-Cup holidays have deprived him of eight first-team players so far, injuries of a further six.

It was telling that, after Liverpool’s open training session had ended, many of the fans invited headed to the gym for a look through its glass windows. Jérémy Jacquet, Liverpool’s £60m recruit from Rennes, was inside working on his recovery from a shoulder problem.

He was joined by Giovanni Leoni, who is rehabilitating from an anterior cruciate ligament rupture and appears to have doubled in chest size since sustaining the injury on his Liverpool debut last September. Nearby was Joe Gomez, who pulled up with a muscle injury eight minutes into the first friendly of the tour. All central defenders, all out.

The concentration of problems in one particular area was a recurring theme under Arne Slot last season and has not eased yet. Two 18-year-olds, Mor Talla Ndiaye and Ifeanyi Ndukwe, have impressed in their absence but Liverpool are looking to loan out the latter next season having been unable to secure a work permit.

Among the observers on Friday was Mike Gordon, the president of Liverpool’s owners, Fenway Sports Group, who has returned to a more hands-on role at the club after the departure of Michael Edwards as FSG’s chief executive of football.

View image in fullscreen Teenage defender Ifeanyi Ndukwe is likely to be loaned out by Liverppool. Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty Images

Gordon is expected to be in attendance at Soldier Field on Sunday when Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak should feature for the first time in pre-season. FSG will not be the only ones at Liverpool looking for a return on their combined £241m investment in the pair.

“We need a very good version of Florian,” Iraola said this week, when confirming he intends to play the Germany international “in that position behind the striker” rather than on the left, where he operated without reward at the World Cup, or in the variety of roles that Slot tried without success.

Wirtz supplying Isak and/or Hugo Ekitiké was always the intended plan of attack for Liverpool last season. The trio ultimately played only 119 minutes together as injuries struck. That stat was never lost on Slot as he was ushered to the exit after a turbulent and toxic campaign.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Liverpool need a very good version of Isak, too. The excuse of playing catch-up having missed pre-season, or almost four months of the season due to a fractured ankle and fibula, no longer washes for a striker who featured in all four games of Sweden’s World Cup. Isak has looked sharp in pre-season training. He not only has to sustain that sharpness next season but convince he is a suitable fit for this Liverpool team.

View image in fullscreen Florian Wirtz will be used behind the striker this season under Andoni Iraola for Liverpool. Photograph: Becky Oliver/LFC/Liverpool FC/Getty Images

Iraola’s options and vision for Liverpool will improve as senior names return but he undoubtedly requires more help through the transfer market. Work is under way on a move for Bradley Barcola, who is open to leaving Paris Saint-Germain for Anfield, but a deal for a winger who the European champions value at £145m is yet to be struck.

A lack of defensive cover cost Liverpool last season and remains a glaring issue, and there are doubts over the futures of Curtis Jones, Federico Chiesa and Harvey Elliott, among others.

Liverpool’s head coach has admitted he “hates this month of August” because of the uncertainty that surrounds players while the season starts. “It’s difficult to build a proper team with a lot of question marks,” he added. Between Soldier Field on Sunday and St James’ Park on 23 August, the building work must accelerate.

Sports.title: De Zerbi wants ‘lovely guy’ Richarlison to stay at Tottenham after winner sinks Chelsea
Sports.content:
Roberto De Zerbi wants Richarlison to stay at Tottenham, but says the striker, who has been linked with a move away, is still unsure about his future.

The Brazilian scored a last-gasp winner as 10-man Tottenham defeated Chelsea 2-1 in a pre-season friendly in Sydney, with Kevin Danso sent off just minutes after coming on as a half-time substitute.

Speaking after the game, De Zerbi said Richarlison had not clarified if he was going to depart this summer. “I don’t know, I didn’t understand well, because sometimes he said to stay, sometimes he leaves, we have to speak. Anyway, there is not any problem, he’s a lovely guy. All of us love him, the teammates, the club, the staff, because he works hard every day.”

Richarlison has less than a year left on his contract after joining Tottenham from Everton in 2022. He has struggled to find consistent form during his time in north London but De Zerbi said it would be difficult to replace his goals.

“For me he’s still an important player because it’s not so easy to find another striker as Richarlison, because Richarlison scored goals and he knows the way. The new striker, we don’t know, the other striker, we don’t know. He [Richarlison] scored 12 goals last season, not for luck, because he feels the way to score.”

Richarlison bagged a 92nd-minute winner for Tottenham against Chelsea in front of more than 80,000 fans at Sydney’s Accor Stadium. The Brazilian was the first player to react after Jamie Donley’s shot came back off a post, prodding the ball into an empty net to avert the need for a penalty shootout.

It was the first time that the two sides have met outside the UK and the match started in the spirit of a true London derby. Conor Gallagher flew into a challenge on Dário Essugo after 10 minutes, picking up a yellow card and a fair few heckles from the largely Chelsea-supporting crowd. Jan Paul van Hecke clattered into João Pedro, while Dominic Solanke and Levi Colwill tussled off the ball.

This fixture has had its fair share of red cards over the years and there was another one to add to the list, after Danso was sent off three minutes after coming off the bench. A poor surface got the better of the Spurs defender as he failed to control a backpass, allowing João Pedro to run on to the ball and through on goal. Danso lunged headfirst into the Chelsea forward, with the referee reaching straight for his pocket.

View image in fullscreen Kevin Danso is shown a red card three minutes after coming on as a substitute. Photograph: David Neilson/EPA

De Zerbi said the sending off made the game harder for both sides. “It was worse for us and for Chelsea, because if you consider the condition of the pitch, very bad. And if you consider we are starting from two weeks, maybe less than three weeks, the second half you start the fatigue and playing, attacking against 10 players behind the line of the ball is tough for every team.”

De Zerbi’s side were on top in the early stages and took a deserved lead on 17 minutes when the new signing Sandro Tonali scored his first goal for Tottenham. The midfielder’s side-footed effort from outside the area took a deflection, wrong-footing the Chelsea goalkeeper Teddy Sharman-Lowe before nestling into the bottom corner.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Spurs were only ahead for four minutes, as Estêvão Willian got the better of Andy Robertson to head home at the back post after some good work from Jamie Gittens down the left.

The game lost its competitive edge in the second half with both sides making a flurry of substitutions, before Richarlison settled it at the death.

Chelsea will now head to Hong Kong where they will be joined by Mykhailo Mudryk, who has been cleared to play again after the Football Association and the World Anti-Doping Agency resolved his appeal against a ban for failing a doping test. The Ukrainian winger was suspended for four years after failing a drug test in 2024. De Zerbi, who managed Mudryk at Shakhtar Donetsk, said he viewed the player as one of his “sons”.

“I’m very happy – he deserves to play, he’s a good guy, top player. Hopefully he can show what he suffered in the last two years, in the next season, maybe not against Tottenham, but he’s a lovely guy and he’s a very, very good player.”

Sports.title: Amanda Staveley consortium set to buy Gold family’s 25.1% stake in West Ham
Sports.content:
A consortium led by Amanda Staveley has reached an agreement to buy a ‌25.1% stake in West ⁠Ham after Vanessa Gold, daughter of the former chair David Gold, ⁠agreed to sell ⁠her ​family’s shares in the Championship club.

The move by the businesswoman who helped lead the Saudi consortium takeover of Newcastle comes after a previously agreed sale to fellow shareholder and Czech businessman ⁠Daniel Kretinsky fell through.

The Gold family ​trust owns the 25.1% stake in West Ham, ‌who were relegated from the Premier League last season just two seasons after winning the Europa Conference League in 2023. However, current shareholders will also be presented with the chance to buy out the Gold family under an ongoing process.

Gold said in a statement: “As the daughter of David Gold, it was a great honour to step into a joint chair and director role at the club following his passing in 2023. Whether as a youth team player, a lifelong fan or an owner, my father’s priority was always to champion and protect this great club. Over the past three years I have taken huge personal pride in continuing that legacy and will always be hugely grateful to the staff, players and fans who allowed me to do so.

“On June 12, Daniel Kretínsky and I agreed a sale that would have made EP Group the single largest shareholder in West Ham. Unfortunately, since that time, the original deal and other alternatives that we have discussed could not be brought to fruition.

View image in fullscreen West Ham were relegated from the Premier League last season. Photograph: Eddie Keogh/Reuters

“In light of this, I have now reached an agreement to sell my family’s shareholding to a consortium led by Amanda Staveley, Mehrdad Ghodoussi and PCP Capital Partners. This sale remains subject to a pre-emption process, under which existing shareholders have the option to buy the shares instead.

“While the process has not yet concluded, I wanted to be open with our fans about where things stand and my intentions. My ambition throughout this process has been to ensure the club has the right leadership and ownership to enable West Ham to achieve its potential and return to its rightful place in the Premier League.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“Amanda Staveley, Mehrdad Ghodoussi and PCP Capital Partners will bring deep experience and understanding of what it takes to lead a successful football club, and I have every confidence in what she and her partners can bring to West Ham. While the sale process proceeds, I will continue to act in the club’s best interests, as my father did and would expect of me.”



Staveley brokered the deal which allowed a Saudi-backed consortium to buy-out then Newcastle owner Mike Ashley in October 2021, and she and Ghodoussi oversaw the club’s rise from Premier League relegation candidates to Champions League participants and, after their departure during the summer of 2024, Carabao Cup winners.

The Hammers dropped out of the top flight at the end of last season and will begin the process of attempting to secure a swift return at Burnley on 16 August.

Sports.title: Inside the chaotic four days that has left Gianni Infantino fighting to stay in power, how arrogant FIFA president's gamble spectacularly backfired and the contenders looking to overthrow him after World Cup own goal
Sports.content:
Inside the chaotic four days that has left Gianni Infantino fighting to stay in power, how arrogant FIFA president's gamble spectacularly backfired and the contenders looking to overthrow him after World Cup own goal

Unlock more of the best of our journalism with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

It's only two weeks since Gianni Infantino joined President Donald Trump in handing over the Jules Rimet trophy to Spain in New Jersey, wearing a dark suit, blindingly white trainers and the self-satisfied grin of a man celebrating a World Cup triumph of his own.

The FIFA president declared the tournament - and its new 48-team format - a huge success after spending the previous six weeks flitting around North America in a private jet to see his vision become reality.

Anybody else might have been inclined to spend some time reflecting on a World Cup that produced more than its fair share of talking points, or even have some time off.

Not Infantino. He was already moving onto his next project; one that backfired spectacularly this week and has left the 56-year-old Swiss fighting to stay in power.

It took less than four days for his grand plan to sell off football’s crown jewel to private investors for £3.1billion to go up in smoke, from the bombshell news breaking at lunchtime on Tuesday to Infantino’s humiliating statement in the early hours of Saturday confirming it has been scrapped in the face of widespread opposition.

At the end of a seismic week for world football, it is hard to see how he can survive after leading confederations and even senior executives at FIFA turned on the embattled president, and UEFA made the first move towards removing him from office with a vote of no confidence on Saturday morning.

Just days after lauding the 2026 World Cup as a huge, almost personal, success Gianni Infantino saw his iron grip on FIFA's presidency unravel

Why did it unravel so quickly? How did Infantino, a skilled political figure, get it so horribly wrong?

It was clear this wasn’t going to end well from the immediate sense of shock and outrage when The Times revealed that Infantino wanted to create a subsidiary company called FIFA Forward Enterprise to run its flagship events, primarily the World Cup, in a deal that could be worth up to £15bn.

Private investors would have been able to buy stakes in FFE through a group led by Thrive Eternal, a US venture capital company founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared.

The 211 member associations were offered a £30m cut if they agreed with the proposals by September 19.

UEFA were the first to voice their opposition with a strongly worded statement agreed unanimously and co-signed by the English FA and Europe’s other 54 associations. They criticised Infantino for ‘a profound failure of leadership’ and presiding over ‘governance by intimidation’, adding: ‘None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA’s to sell.’

UEFA followed that up with a threat to boycott the World Cup if Infantino refused to back down and abandon his plans.

Two other Confederations then came out against Infantino on Thursday and Friday. CONCACAF, which represents 41 countries across North America, Central America and the Caribbean, rejected the proposal and expressed ‘deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal and the artificially short deadline imposed’.

The Asian Football Confederation followed, saying: ‘Football should never have been placed in such a position. It has exposed fundamental weaknesses in FIFA’S consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed.’

Infantino needed a majority of the 211 member nations to vote through his proposals, but already 136 of them were opposed to him.

He doubled down on Friday morning when FIFA issued a statement insisting that ‘nobody is selling football’ - but opposition was growing at an alarming rate.

New Prime Minister Andy Burnham weighed into the controversy, questioning whether Infantino is the right man to lead FIFA anymore.

‘This was an outrageous suggestion,’ said Burnham. ‘The idea that it could even be brought forward, in my view, shows that the FIFA president is the wrong man to lead the organisation.’

More damagingly for Infantino, two of his senior aides turned against him in the space of a few hours.

President of the US Soccer Federation Carlos Cordeiro was a key Infantino ally before he fell on his sword

CONCACAF president Victor Montagliani has emerged as an early contender to stand against Infantino in March

Carlos Cordeiro, who was FIFA’s representative on the White House taskforce for the World Cup and at Infantino’s side throughout, said: ‘As a senior adviser to the FIFA president, a former banker, and a lifelong football fan, I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup.

‘I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally. It is a bad deal for FIFA’s member associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game.

‘Selling a permanent stake in football’s most valuable asset to raise $4.2bn makes little sense. It is mortgaging football’s future without any compelling justification.’

If that wasn’t bad enough for Infantino, FIFA’s chief operating officer Kevin Lamour then quit, claiming that Infantino had ‘deceived’ his own administration and accusing him of a ‘lie by omission’. He blasted the plans as a ‘the project of one person’.

‘This (lie) and unilateral exercise of power are not trivial,’ added Lamour. ‘They are indicative of a lack of trust, a lack of transparency, a lack of discernment, a lack of good governance. And a serious lack of respect.

‘Not only must this project not go ahead, but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions.

‘My colleagues - some of whom have dedicated their lives to football - deserve better than contempt and intimidation.

‘The ball is now in the court of those who have the power to change things. I know I have a duty of loyalty to my employer. But I also, and above all, have a duty of loyalty to certain values and to the upbringing I have received, and a duty to support my colleagues. And if that means I lose my job, then so be it. I will understand and respect that decision. At least I’ll sleep well tonight.’

Shortly after midnight, Infantino inevitably bowed to the pressure and announced he was scrapping the proposals because ‘it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place’.

If he thought that would be the end of the matter, however, it quickly became clear on Saturday that the implications could be far greater when UEFA declared a vote of no confidence in him.

Europe’s governing body hit out at Infantino for the ‘shabby, back-room, opaque deal he hatched’ and promised to work with the other confederations in world football to ‘identify those responsible and hold them to account’.

It added: ‘This is a victory for the whole game. But it must not be the end of the story. The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in FIFA has only just begun.’

So what next for Infantino? He has been in power for 10 years and was expected to win re-election for a fourth term unopposed at the next FIFA congress in Morocco in March.

But with support dwindling fast and UEFA on the warpath, it looks increasingly likely that a rival candidate will stand against him.

CONCACAF president Victor Montagliani has emerged as an early contender, along with current FIFA general secretary Mattias Granstrom and Dariusz Mioduski, a vice-president of the European Football Clubs body.

Two weeks after he had the whole world in his hands, it feels as though Gianni Infantino’s time is almost up.

Sports.title: Why Rob Key picked Stephen Fleming over England's up-and-coming coaches: The coaching 'shift' that has swept cricket, why foreigners are judged through a different prism and the county coach who has been harshly overlooked
Sports.content:
There are many reasons that few Englishmen go on to coach England these days: the results of those that have gone before hang heavy, a mistrust of the country’s embedded coaching system has developed and so has an infatuation with star names.

This century only Peter Moores (twice) and Chris Silverwood have been given the privilege of calling themselves Test coach and between them they lost more matches than they won - the numbers being 24 and 23 respectively.

That might appear to be a tough yardstick to be judged by, but such statistics will have influenced Rob Key in his decision to appoint New Zealander Stephen Fleming despite a lack of first-class coaching experience, ahead of Richard Dawson, perhaps the brightest coaching talent in the country and one with silverware on his CV.

Some will argue, perhaps with justification that Dawson’s achievements with two unfashionable counties have not been given commensurate weighting in this selection process. Gloucestershire supporters look back on their Lord’s one-day cup final win in 2015 as one of the club’s finest achievements while he has Glamorgan as high as fourth in the County Championship after his first season in charge concluded with promotion last September.

In between those two jobs, there was the small matter of overseeing an eight-match England Lions tour of Australia in early 2020, returning home undefeated having won the four-day ‘Test’ against Australia A.

On Friday, Key spoke of ‘working on’ homegrown coaches to ‘upskill’ them, saying more experiences needed to be created for them overseas. That such development would not be a quick fix. Yet Dawson’s very positive experience of winning in Australia was six years ago. He has knowledge of lots of conditions around the world garnered from various England tours.

With the appointment of Stephen Fleming, there is the suggestion that England have overlooked attracting one of their own - such as Richard Dawson

Fleming (left, with ex-team-mate and former England coach Brendon McCullum in 2008) is a much starrier name

It feels like a case of disregard for the coaching path from which Dawson - whose standoffish demeanour should not detract from the fact he is an excellent coach well respected by the country’s leading players - has emerged.

Key has shown little regard for the traditional level four coaching qualification that the ECB has asked the country’s best coaches to complete for the past quarter of a century, instead appointing those with limited or no coaching backgrounds in the form of former playing greats Brendon McCullum and Andrew Flintoff to high position.

Investment has been in inspiration not perspiration. Overall, McCullum has proved to be a success across four years and three England teams, but said early on: ‘Don’t expect me to be on the tools.’ But Flintoff has proved more of a mentor than coach since taking over the Lions two years ago, and will skip some of next winter’s programme in South Africa to coach Sydney Thunder in the Big Bash League.

It is part of a wider culture of ‘image’ taking precedent over results. When the Hundred launched in 2021, not a single coach was English. The late Shane Warne was chosen by London Spirit; experienced international coaches like Andy Flower, Darren Lehmann and Gary Kirsten were signed; the two emerging coaches were New Zealander Daniel Vettori and Australian Simon Katich.

Key is part of a shifting cricket culture that places names over deeds and achievements abroad over ones here.

The last six County Championship titles have been claimed by teams with English coaches: Moores (Nottinghamshire), Gareth Batty (Surrey), Mark Robinson (Warwickshire) and Anthony McGrath (Yorkshire).

If we do not have confidence in our own production line, why should we expect others to? Work abroad has been limited: Silverwood and Paul Farbrace (both Sri Lanka), Bob Woolmer (Pakistan) and Jonathan Trott (Afghanistan) rare examples of those to have taken head coach jobs of Test-playing nations this century.

Vikram Solanki is the only Englishman to move from a county position to one at the Indian Premier League, as director of cricket at Gujarat Titans. Moores was the only English coach at the Big Bash League last winter.

However, there is evidence of a shift. Ian Bell has been on coaching staffs at both tournaments. Others have ventured to the BBL to gain experience through observational or backroom roles. Andrew Gale, formerly of Yorkshire, is making big waves as a coach with Tasmania and was promoted to work with Australia A last winter.

Peter Moores is one of few English coaches able to have the privilege of calling themselves England Test coach this century

But like his compatriot Chris Silverwood, Moores lost more Test matches than he won

Foreigners appear to be judged through a different prism. For all of Fleming’s widely acknowledged man-management skills, tactical acumen and calm, calculated persona, he has never won a trophy without MS Dhoni as his captain.

Marcus Trescothick, meanwhile, failed to make the shortlist this time despite four years of experience under McCullum in which his one major failing was insisting there had been no talk of the dangers of driving on the up after first Test defeat in Perth, in keeping with the regime’s off-the-cuff policy.

Trescothick did a sound job as McCullum’s stand-in on the limited-overs tour of the Caribbean two years ago, coming home with a rare series win over West Indies, and will step up again against Pakistan.

He has been produced by a country with a revered coaching system that has launched several individuals on the road to international head coach jobs around the world.
