Mexico – A Phantom Dissipates in the Boardroom

A strange, quiet jubilation settled over Mexican corporate law offices on Friday. The mood was not one of explosive victory, but of a deep, existential threat evaporating into thin air. The Rio Times reported that Orbia, the Mexican chemicals giant, had successfully escaped a $1.14 billion cartel lawsuit. A billion-dollar phantom, a legal Sword of Damocles that had hung over the company, was simply wiped away by a court ruling. The S&P/BMV IPC’s slight dip suggests the broader market was unmoved, but for Orbia, it was a rebirth by judicial decree.

This narrow escape contrasts with the broader, more pedestrian challenge highlighted by Expansión: the struggle to convert Mexico’s growing number of investment accounts into actual, lasting wealth. The democratization of finance is underway, but the mood is one of caution, a realization that opening an account is far easier than building a patrimony. The Orbia ruling, then, is a private miracle in a landscape where the real, daily miracle—turning savings into security—remains stubbornly elusive for the many.

Colombia – Holding Steady in a Political Storm

Colombia’s Friday felt like a tightrope walk performed with a straight spine. The Banco de la República, in a move of almost theatrical steadiness, held interest rates at 12% and announced it would start buying up reserves due to a cheap dollar, as reported by La República. The COLCAP soared by over 2%, a roar of approval from a market desperate for a technocratic anchor. The central bank stood as a pillar of orthodoxy, seemingly unmoved by the political weather.

But that weather is turbulent. Our reporting broke the news that Ricardo Roa, the recently departed CEO of Ecopetrol, is seeking a plea deal over alleged irregularities in President Gustavo Petro’s 2022 campaign, which he managed. It is a seismic political event wrapped in the quiet language of legal procedure. The contrast is dizzying: a stable, predictable monetary authority on one hand, and a state oil company’s former chief trying to negotiate his way out of a campaign finance scandal on the other. La República also noted Petro’s comments on gas imports, a reminder that energy sovereignty remains a live wire. The nation’s mood is a held breath, a bet that institutional gravity can withstand the pull of political chaos.

Argentina – The Weight of the Dollar and the Silence of the Showroom

In Buenos Aires, the mood is a brittle thing, a thin veneer of official celebration over a deep well of personal anxiety. iProfesional captured the dissonance perfectly: while Economy Minister Caputo celebrates that more dollars are entering the country than leaving, Argentine savers quietly bought up $2.4 billion in June alone. The people are voting with their wallets, and they are voting for the greenback, a deep-seated instinct that no macroeconomic statistic can soothe. The S&P Merval’s slight decline reflects a City that is, as iProfesional advises, recommending extreme caution for August.

The real economy is sending smoke signals. Car sales, a bellwether of middle-class confidence, suffered their worst collapse of the year, reshaping the very ranking of top brands. The story of a leading empanada business collapsing under 230 bounced checks and a billion pesos in debt is not just a business failure; it is a parable of the real cost of this transition. Our reporting on Argentina’s economy notes that inflation is down to 1.9% a month and poverty is at a seven-year low, but the showroom floors are empty and the empanada empire is in ruins. The ‘Milei miracle’ has a ledger, and on Friday, the debit column felt heavier.

Chile – A Faint Pulse in the Factory Floor

A cautious, almost superstitious hope flickered through Chile on Friday. After eight long months of decline, industrial production finally turned a corner, as Emol reported, reinforcing a fragile bet that the country might just dodge a technical recession. The sound of machinery stirring back to life is the most precious music in Santiago right now, a signal that the patient’s long fever might be breaking. The peso rallied, with the dollar falling sharply over the week, a sign of easing nerves.

Yet, the celebration is muted, a whispered prayer rather than a shout. Unemployment remains stubbornly high at 9.4%, a figure our own reporting confirmed, and Minister Rau could only offer the tentative hope that a ‘turning point’ has been reached. It is the language of the wince, not the victory cry. The joblessness is a cold, hard floor beneath the warm air of industrial output. Chile’s mood is that of a family watching a sick relative take their first spoonful of soup: desperately hopeful, but terrified of a relapse.

Peru – The Earth’s Reminder

Peru’s day was split in two: the solid, encouraging clink of construction steel, and the deep, terrifying growl of the earth. El Comercio reported that construction grew by a roaring 11.8% in the first half of the year, and Proinversión is accelerating a massive $40 billion infrastructure portfolio. The sol held steady, a quiet anchor of stability. The mood in Lima’s boardrooms was one of bullish, forward-looking momentum, a country building its way out of stagnation.

Then, the Amazon spoke. A magnitude 5.6 earthquake near Pucallpa, as reported by The Rio Times, sent tremors rippling across the border into Brazil. No damage, no casualties—just a deep, planetary reminder that all this building, all these adjudications and portfolios, occur on a living, restless crust. The quake was not a tragedy, but it was a metaphysical one. It punctured the illusion of control, leaving behind a mood of humbled awe. The day’s two stories—the soaring construction figures and the seismic shudder—are a perfect diptych of Peruvian existence: audacious ambition forever shadowed by the Andes’ ancient, unpredictable power.

The Shared Mood

The thread tying these six nations together on the last day of July is a shared act of renegotiation with reality. Brazil is renegotiating its debt maturities, Colombia its political accountability, Argentina its social contract with the dollar, and Chile its relationship with economic gravity. Even the earth in Peru seemed to be renegotiating its own internal pressures. This is not a continent in revolution, but in a vast, complicated, and deeply exhausting process of restructuring.

This points to a deeper regional psyche: a weariness with grand ideological experiments and a grudging turn towards the brutal, unglamorous work of technical management. From Tarcísio’s ‘management-focused’ campaign in Brazil to the Colombian central bank’s stoic rate hold, the day’s heroes are not caudillos but technocrats, not prophets but accountants. The shared mood is a collective, whispered confession that the miracles didn’t come, and now the bills are due. It is a sobering, adult feeling, as unglamorous and necessary as an 11% bond coupon or a plea deal signed in a quiet room.

What was the biggest corporate survival story in Latin America on Friday?

Mexico’s Orbia escaped a $1.14 billion cartel lawsuit, effectively wiping out a massive legal threat. Meanwhile, Brazil’s CSN launched a $1.3 billion bond exchange with a steep 11% coupon to push out its debt maturities, a costly but critical move to avoid a liquidity crisis.

How did Colombia’s political and economic realities collide on July 31?

The collision was stark. The central bank held rates steady at 12%, projecting an image of total institutional stability, while simultaneously, the recently departed CEO of state oil company Ecopetrol, Ricardo Roa, requested a plea deal over alleged campaign finance irregularities tied to President Gustavo Petro.

What natural event punctuated the economic news in Peru?

A magnitude 5.6 earthquake struck deep beneath the Amazon near Pucallpa, Peru. Tremors were felt across the border in Brazil, but no damage or casualties were reported. The event served as a powerful, humbling counterpoint to the country’s booming construction sector and infrastructure ambitions.

World.title: Costa Rica Approves Sharp Drop in Super Gasoline and Diesel Prices
World.content:
Drivers in Costa Rica will soon pay substantially less for super gasoline and diesel after regulators approved fuel-price reductions of up to ₡79 per liter. The Public Services Regulatory Authority (Aresep), approved the changes on Friday, July 31. The new prices will take effect the day after the resolution is published in the official government newspaper, La Gaceta.

Super gasoline will fall by ₡55, from ₡756 to ₡701 per liter. Diesel will receive the largest reduction, dropping by ₡79 from ₡683 to ₡604 per liter. Regular gasoline will remain unchanged at ₡755 per liter. The unusual price structure means super gasoline will cost ₡54 less per liter than regular once the adjustment takes effect. Drivers should still follow the octane recommendation in their vehicle’s owner manual rather than choosing fuel based only on price.

The reductions will produce noticeable savings for motorists and businesses that rely on diesel vehicles. Filling a 50-liter tank, equivalent to about 13.2 gallons, will cost ₡2,750 less with super gasoline and ₡3,950 less with diesel. A 60-liter diesel fill-up will cost ₡4,740 less than under the current price.

Households that use cooking gas will also receive some relief. The price of a standard 25-pound liquefied petroleum gas cylinder will fall by ₡451, bringing its price to approximately ₡6,989. The Refinadora Costarricense de Petróleo, Costa Rica’s state-owned fuel importer, attributed the reductions largely to lower international purchasing costs during the period used to calculate the adjustment.

An increase in global oil supplies and reduced pressure on international energy markets helped lower acquisition costs. The appreciation of the Costa Rican colón against the U.S. dollar also contributed because the purchases fuel internationally in dollars. Fuel prices in Costa Rica are regulated and generally remain consistent across service stations. Aresep calculates adjustments using international fuel costs, exchange-rate movements, taxes and the expenses involved in importing, distributing and selling fuel.

The latest reductions provide some relief after fuel prices rose sharply earlier in 2026 amid international market volatility and geopolitical tensions. Additional changes remain possible in the coming months. International conflicts, production decisions by oil-exporting countries, shipping costs and movements in the dollar-to-colón exchange rate can all affect future adjustments.

Drivers should double check that whatever service station they go to make sure they have updated their pumps after the new prices formally take effect.

World.title: Chris Hemsworth Shares Terrifying Costa Rica Flight
World.content:
Chris Hemsworth has shared frightening footage from a small-plane flight during his family vacation in Costa Rica, showing lightning flashing outside the aircraft as heavy turbulence shakes the cabin. The sequence appears in a five-minute video posted on the Australian actor’s YouTube channel. Hemsworth films the cockpit and dark storm clouds before several large flashes illuminate the sky around the aircraft.

He then turns the camera toward himself with a visibly alarmed expression. Text added to the video describes the experience as a “life-threatening plane ride,” while Hemsworth called it a “crazy plane ride through the lightning” in the video description. The aircraft landed safely, and no injuries were reported. Hemsworth did not identify the airline, flight operator, route or type of aircraft involved.

The footage also does not make clear whether his wife, Spanish actress Elsa Pataky, or their three children were aboard during the stormy flight. They appear throughout the rest of the vacation video. Hemsworth and his family spent much of their Costa Rica visit surfing, fishing, riding ATVs, climbing rocks, jumping from cliffs and exploring waterfalls. The actor described the vacation as one of the best trips the family had taken together.

The family was spotted in early July around Santa Teresa and Montezuma on the Nicoya Peninsula.. Hemsworth was photographed surfing, exercising with a Costa Rican trainer and posing with fans during the trip. The frightening flight footage has drawn particular attention because Hemsworth is best known for playing Thor, Marvel’s god of thunder. Several viewers joked that the actor appeared far less comfortable around real lightning than his superhero character.

Although several reports have described the aircraft as being struck by lightning, the publicly available footage only clearly shows flashes around the plane. It does not establish whether lightning directly hit the aircraft. The flight also appears to have been a domestic trip within Costa Rica rather than the family’s international journey into the country.

The remainder of the video returns to the family’s outdoor adventures, including deep-sea fishing, surfing and waterfall visits. Hemsworth ends the video on a considerably calmer note, describing Costa Rica as the setting for one of the family’s most memorable vacations.

World.title: Pura Vida and Property: How Costa Rica’s Traditional Way of Selling Homes Is Entering the Digital Age
World.content:
When people think about buying or selling property in Costa Rica today, they often picture property portals, real estate agents, Realtors and international buyers searching online for their dream home.

But that isn’t how Costa Rica built its property market.

For generations, Costa Ricans sold property through their communities. A simple “Se Vende” sign outside the gate. A conversation with a neighbour. A recommendation from a friend. Trusted lawyers handling the legal side of the sale. It wasn’t unusual. It was simply the Costa Rican way.

As Costa Rica became one of the world’s most desirable places to live, retire and invest, the property market naturally evolved. International buyers needed guidance through an unfamiliar legal process, language and culture, and real estate agents and Realtors became an important part of helping people buy property in Costa Rica with confidence.

For many homeowners, that remains exactly the right choice.

But somewhere along the way, one long-standing Costa Rican tradition quietly lost its place.

The professional private seller.

“Living in Costa Rica changed the way I looked at property,” says Wayne Johnson, founder of Slide’N Doors.

“I’d bought and sold property before, but Costa Rica felt different. There was a real sense of community. People trusted each other. Neighbours helped neighbours. That independent spirit is part of what makes this country so special.”

Wayne says he often met homeowners who weren’t trying to avoid real estate professionals. They simply wanted another option.

“Some people genuinely enjoy showing buyers around their home. They know every room, every fruit tree, every sunset from the terrace and every reason they fell in love with the property.

They weren’t asking how to avoid commission. They were asking why choosing to sell privately meant having fewer professional ways to market one of the biggest investments of their lives.”

That simple question stayed with him. Not as a business plan, but as an idea that refused to go away.

About a year ago, he decided to stop thinking about it and start building something.

“People often think the only alternative to using a Realtor is Facebook Marketplace,” Wayne says. “Facebook is brilliant at connecting people, and it proves there’s huge demand for private property sales. But selling a home there can feel a bit like selling a luxury watch at a busy flea market. The right buyer might be there, but your property is surrounded by sofas, bicycles and children’s toys. One of the biggest financial decisions of your life deserves a platform built specifically for property.”

For Wayne, that became the mission behind Slide’N Doors.

Not to replace real estate agents, but to stand alongside them by giving homeowners another professional option.

“The choice shouldn’t be whether your property gets seen,” he says. “It should simply be about choosing the way you want to sell your home.”

As our conversation continued, Wayne explained that the inspiration behind Slide’N Doors wasn’t technology.

It was Costa Rica.

“The longer I lived here, the more I realised Pura Vida isn’t just a saying. It’s a way of thinking. It’s about community, trust, independence and people looking after one another.

As Costa Rica grows, many people naturally worry about losing some of the traditions and culture that make this country so unique.

I didn’t build Slide’N Doors to change the Costa Rican way of selling property.

I built it because I was inspired by it.

I wanted to create a modern platform that reflects those same values. A business that puts people and choice at its heart. Technology that supports communities rather than replaces them. Giving homeowners more choice while continuing to respect the important role that real estate professionals play.”

Progress doesn’t have to mean leaving tradition behind. Sometimes the best ideas are simply old Costa Rican values, given the tools to thrive in a modern world.

Every day, buyers from around the world search for Costa Rica homes for sale, investment opportunities, retirement properties and beachfront homes. Wayne believes they should be able to discover professionally presented private listings alongside properties represented by experienced Realtors, giving buyers more choice while allowing homeowners to decide how they wish to sell.

As our conversation came to an end, one final question seemed obvious.

Is Slide’N Doors trying to change the way Costa Rica sells property?

Wayne smiles.

“No.

Costa Rica has always understood the value of community, trust and doing things your own way. Those values inspired every decision we made while building Slide’N Doors.

Technology should never replace a country’s culture.

It should help preserve it.

If people see Slide’N Doors as a modern expression of the values Costa Rica has believed in all along—people first, community first and always Pura Vida—then I’ll know we’ve built something worthwhile.”

Thinking of Buying or Selling Property in Costa Rica?

Whether you’re looking to buy a home, sell your own property or invest in Costa Rican real estate, Slide’N Doors brings private sellers and real estate professionals together on one platform.

• List your property in under 10 minutes.

• Reach buyers around the world.

• Pay zero commission if you find your own buyer.

Learn more at www.slidendoors.com

World.title: What the Judicial Coup Fight in Costa Rica is Actually About
World.content:
President Fernández accused four justices of the Constitutional Chamber of staging a coup d’état on Friday and announced that the governing-party legislative bench will file a criminal complaint against them on Monday over a ruling that provisionally extended the appointments of the court’s substitute justices.

The announcement was delivered in a video recorded at Casa Presidencial, where Fernández appeared alongside Legislative Assembly president Yara Jiménez and deputies of the governing Partido Pueblo Soberano. Fernández said the Chamber’s decision to extend appointments that expired on December 16, 2025 was illegal and unconstitutional, and that the power to appoint, remove or extend the terms of justices belongs exclusively to the Legislative Assembly. She cited articles 9, 11, 121, 154, 157, 158 and 164 of the Constitution in support of that position.

Jiménez said the complaint will be filed before the Secretariat of the full Supreme Court and will allege the offense of prevaricato against justices Fernando Cruz Castro, Paul Rueda Leal, Ingrid Hess Herrera and Jorge Araya García, the four who formed the majority. The Chamber rejected the coup characterization the same day, defending the ruling as grounded in law and describing the Executive’s statements as disproportionate.

What the Constitutional Chamber ruled

The ruling, adopted Thursday by a vote of four to three, resolved an appeal brought by a private citizen who argued that his cases had stalled because sitting justices had recused themselves and the court could not be properly constituted without substitutes to replace them.

The Chamber provisionally extended the appointments of the substitute justices whose terms ended last December and held that the extension remains in force until deputies elect replacements. It voided the Legislative Assembly’s agreement returning the candidate list to the Supreme Court and ordered Jiménez to bring the matter to a vote using the existing list of 18 candidates, from which at least nine substitutes must be chosen. The Supreme Court had sent that list to the Assembly, and the governing bench had returned it twice without voting.

Voting with the majority were Cruz, Rueda, Araya and Hess. Justices Fernando Castillo, Luis Fernando Salazar and Anamari Garro dissented and would have rejected the appeal.

What a substitute justice does

The Constitutional Chamber, known here more commonly as Sala IV, is made up of seven sitting justices. Substitute justices are elected by the Legislative Assembly to step in when a sitting justice is absent, disqualified or recused from a particular case. Recusal is routine rather than exceptional, and it occurs whenever a justice has a prior connection to a matter that would compromise impartiality.

Without a pool of substitutes, a case in which one or more sitting justices have recused themselves cannot be assigned a full bench, and it simply waits. That is the mechanical problem the ruling addresses. At the time of the decision, 123 case files were reported to be stalled for that reason, including claims involving pensions and access to health care. The Chamber described the extension as a transitional measure adopted to prevent the court from seizing up entirely.

What Prevaricato means under Costa Rican law

Prevaricato is an offense in the Costa Rican Penal Code that applies to judicial and administrative officials who issue rulings contrary to the law, or who base rulings on facts they know to be false. It is not a charge of simple legal error. It turns on knowledge and intent, which is what makes it both a serious accusation against a judge and a difficult one to prove.

The government’s filing takes the form of a querella rather than a denuncia. A denuncia routes an accusation through the Public Ministry, which decides whether to pursue it. A querella is a private criminal action advanced by the accusing party itself. Constitutional lawyer Marvin Carvajal noted that any official with decision-making authority can be accused of prevaricato, but said that filing an accusation does not establish that an offense occurred, and that the choice of a querella suggests the accusing side does not expect prosecutors to find a crime here.

Carvajal also said the complaint does not suspend the ruling. The order directing the Assembly to vote remains in effect while any complaint proceeds.

How the Chamber and legal scholars responded

In a written statement, the Constitutional Chamber said its decision responded exclusively to the constitutional mandate to protect citizens from the consequences of having no substitute justices available, and that its rulings are properly founded in legal norms and principles. It called the Executive’s remarks disproportionate and inconsistent with the respect that should prevail among branches of government, and said it would continue to act with firmness and independence.

Constitutional lawyer Hubert May said the ruling neither disregards nor violates the separation of powers, arguing that an invasion of powers occurs when one branch usurps the functions of another, and that the Chamber had instead ordered another branch to exercise a function it already holds. Rubén Hernández said the justices were correct to adopt an exceptional extension, describing extension as a general principle of law used to preserve continuity of service. Constitutional lawyer Manrique Jiménez also rejected the government’s characterization of the ruling.

Opposition figures backed the court. Deputy Claudia Dobles, who served as first lady between 2018 and 2022, said the Assembly is the body that has failed to meet its obligation to elect substitutes. Former president Luis Guillermo Solís described the government’s accusations as extremely serious.

What happens next

The querella is expected to be presented on Monday. Separately, the Assembly remains under the Chamber’s order to vote on substitute justices using the list of 18 candidates already in its hands, an instruction the governing bench has resisted for roughly seven months.

The confrontation continues a pattern that began under the previous administration, and it now places two branches of government in open dispute over which of them controls the composition of the highest constitutional court. How that dispute is resolved will say a good deal about where the boundary between them actually sits.

World.title: High Court affirms Firearms and Ammunition Control Board’s regulatory authority; Dismisses claim of being political biased and discriminatory
World.content:
High Court affirms Firearms and Ammunition Control Board’s regulatory authority; Dismisses claim of being political biased and discriminatory

By Jose Luis Cruz: Belmopan, Belize: The High Court of Belize issued a landmark judgment in late July, 2026, reaffirming the statutory authority of the Firearms and Ammunition Control Board (FACB) in the administration and regulation of firearms licensing under the Firearms Act.

The decision arose from judicial review proceedings brought by Abner Murillo and Lock N Loaded Guns and Ammunition Belmopan Limited against the FACB and the Attorney General, in Claim No. 823 of 2024, challenging several licensing decisions and administrative actions taken by the Board.

In its judgment, the Court upheld the FACB’s authority to administer the Firearms Act following the legislative transfer of licensing powers from the Commissioner of Police to the Board. The Court confirmed that licences issued after that statutory transfer by the Commissioner of Police were legally invalid because the authority to issue such licences had already been vested in the FACB.

The Court also dismissed allegations that the FACB acted with political bias or discriminated against the claimants. Applying the legal test for apparent bias, the Court found there was no evidence that the Board’s decisions were influenced by the Minister of Home Affairs or any improper consideration. Similarly, the constitutional claim alleging unequal treatment under section 6(1) of the Constitution was rejected.

In recognizing the nature of firearms regulation, the Court emphasized that the licensing of firearms, firearms dealers, instructors, and shooting ranges involves significant public safety considerations. The judgment acknowledged that the FACB is entitled to carefully scrutinize applications, verify supporting documentation, and ensure compliance with statutory requirements before granting licences.

While the Court made limited findings on certain procedural aspects of the Board’s administration, it largely upheld the FACB’s statutory mandate and dismissed the principal claims challenging the Board’s independence and regulatory authority. The Court awarded the claimants nominal constitutional damages of BZ$5,000 each, reflecting the limited nature of the findings, while declining to grant the broader constitutional relief sought.

The decision represents an important precedent for firearms regulation in Belize. By confirming the FACB’s legal authority, rejecting allegations of bias and unequal treatment, and recognizing the Board’s responsibility to regulate firearms in the interest of public safety, the High Court has reinforced the FACB’s role as Belize’s independent firearms licensing authority.

Former inaugural Chair of the Firearms and Ammunition Control Board and former CEO of the Ministry of Home Affairs, Sharole Carr-Saldivar, welcomed the Court’s decision, describing it as an important affirmation of the Board’s statutory role. “When the Firearms and Ammunition Control Board was established, it began with no dedicated staff or institutional infrastructure. Every policy, procedure, and licensing framework had to be developed while simultaneously assuming responsibility for a completely new regulatory regime. The Court’s decision confirms that the Board acted within its legal mandate on the principal issues before it and reinforces the importance of maintaining an independent firearms regulator committed to public safety.”

World.title: Horse found dead in Lord’s Bank as resident alleges ongoing animal cruelty
World.content:
Horse found dead in Lord’s Bank as resident alleges ongoing animal cruelty

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Warning: images accompanying this story may be disturbing to some readers.

A resident of Lord’s Bank Village is calling for action after a horse was found dead in the BDF housing area along Nim Li Punit Street, in what the resident alleges is part of a troubling pattern of animal abuse in the community.

According to the resident, who contacted Breaking Belize News on Saturday morning, young men in the area have been taking people’s horses and abusing them. The resident alleges the animal found dead was mistreated until it died overnight, and photographs shared with this newsroom show the horse lying in a grassy area with severe visible injuries.

The allegations have not been independently verified, no official cause of death has been determined, and no individuals have been identified in connection with the animal’s death.

Cruelty to animals is an offence under Belizean law, and the death of a working animal is also a real economic loss for families who depend on horses for transport and labour. The circumstances described, if accurate, would warrant investigation by police and the Belize Agricultural Health Authority, which also has a role where carcass disposal raises public health concerns for nearby residents.

Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact the nearest police station. Information can also be shared confidentially with Breaking Belize News and will be passed to the relevant authorities.

World.title: International News: El Salvador has new direct flight to Madrid, Spain
World.content:
International News: El Salvador has new direct flight to Madrid, Spain

By Zoila Palma: Today, President of El Salvador Nayib Bukele participated in the signing of the agreement formalizing Air Europa’s integration into the country’s connectivity network.

Air Europa added a new direct route between San Salvador and Madrid that will begin this December.

“This agreement is a commitment to further positioning El Salvador on the world stage, bringing us closer to Europe and opening the doors to more airlines, more visitors, and more investment,” a statement from the Government of El Salvador said.

The flights will be operated with Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner aircraft, offering greater efficiency and an experience aligned with the airline’s international standards.

Air Europa has been operating since 1986 and flies to more than 55 destinations worldwide.

World.title: “We are still mental slaves and true emancipation remains elusive” – Are we equally to blame?
World.content:
“We are still mental slaves and true emancipation remains elusive” – Are we equally to blame?

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

By Hugh O’Brien, San Ignacio, Cayo: Being the son of a wise black man, being married to a black woman, having black children, living amongst and interacting with black people, organizing, coaching and playing football at various levels, including semi-pro, with my black brothers, teaching black brothers and sisters at the Belize College of Agriculture and then Galen University, watching my black brothers hate on each other, seeing how we are full of envy especially against our own family, against our black neighbours, and watching our black brothers killing each other over red and blue colors, petty grievances, drugs, turf, etc., I have come to realize that a large majority of my BLACK PEOPLE ARE STILL MENTAL SLAVES…AND TRUE EMANCIPATION REMAINS ELUSIVE TO MOST OF US.

My father, George O’Brien, was a smart black man who married a wise Mestizo woman, named Romelia O’Brien nee Cruz. Together they raised seven (7) well educated, successful, independent and loving children. We are a close knit, loving family. My dad was very emancipated mentally but not fully emancipated. He transmitted the ethics of seeking peace, hard work and education to all of us, he believed in his capabilities and transmitted much of these to his children. However, he had two flaws he tried to transmit to me, which I never accepted. I can write a whole article about my dad, his experiences, what a great school teacher he was, and all the attributes he had, but today, I want to focus on the two flaws as they are crucial elements for the focus of this article.

One of the flaws my dad tried to transmit was to discourage me from studying agriculture as he wanted me to be a professional, an educated person who works for someone, a doctor or a lawyer or like profession. He said agriculture is hard work, and is not for the black man. This mentality prevails amongst most of us black people. Because our forefathers were slaves and were forced to work in the fields, we do not want to work the land. Even when we inherit land, the first thing that comes to most of our minds is to sell it. We have lost our connection to the land, and to some extent we also do not value hard work as the foundation for success. We will go as far as to say “Nobody wa work me like wa slave” to show how much we associate hard work with slavery.

The second flaw was to encourage me to marry someone that is fairer than me, in order to improve the color of my skin, he said, and to better the chances for my children’s success. My dad had essentially resigned himself to the idea that being black, you cannot succeed, or will have a hard time succeeding in Belize. I did not follow his advice and I married black, l love black, empowered my black children and will help to do the same to my grandchildren. I will not turn back on believing that black is beautiful, powerful and talented. Am saying all this, even though am fully aware that a large percent of my black brothers and sisters in Belize are still mental slaves, avoid farming and hard work, prefer the easy “Big Chill” life while other cultures around us are advancing.

Four hundred years ago, we ‘blacks’ lived as tribes in Africa, capturing our brothers from other tribes, and we sold them as slaves to the British and the French as their ships sailed by. The British put us in chains and shipped us across the Atlantic to the Caribbean and Belize where we were placed in the bondage of slavery. While we cast all the blame on the Europeans for our past as slaves and labeling us as ‘Chattels’, our black tribe forefathers are equally to blame as we sold our captured black brothers from other tribes as cheap ‘Chattels’.

Less than 200 years ago, we ‘blacks’ were still slaves in British Honduras working in mahogany and logwood camps, and we and our children were owned by white slave masters from a foreign land.

The history of our slavery and colonialism, have affected us significantly, and in a negative way. But should we continue to focus on the evils of the past, the enslavement of our forefathers and the slavery abuse of us blacks by our white slave masters?

It is my view that we must reflect on our slavery past to understand why we are where we are, but we must take responsibility for our future from now on. Rather than continue to blame and hate the white man, we need to accept that our black forefathers who captured us and sold us into slavery are to blame or are responsible as well. We need to move next to FORGIVENESS – forgive both the white man and our black forefathers for the evils of the past and focus more on the opportunities that emancipation, freedom and the future can offer. We must be like the Jews and the Israelites, who have the mentality that because they were enslaved in the biblical days, that they must never be slaves again. That because they were subjected to mass persecution and genocide during World War 2, that they must try to rule instead of be ruled. Their focus is to be their brothers keepers and protect their ‘peoples’ anywhere they are, to be progressive wherever they live, and to be rulers of the world in business and in politics.

In Belize, our black and ‘Kriol’ population appears to be the most challenged, and is the group that is not making full use of the opportunities around us. The state of affairs, particularly the mental state, of our black population can change. We all know too well that the leaders of the UDP or the PUP, whether Black, Arab or Spanish are not the solution…in fact, they have become part of the problem. In their own selfish or ‘unaware’ ways these leaders continue to promote dependency, political tribalism and deep down are content that we are a poor, dependent people, one that they can easily buy with some groceries and a few dollars.

Based on the scenario presented above, are we truly emancipated? Are we not still mental slaves? And is it not true emancipation remains elusive to most of us?

And to end on a positive note, do we want to remain where we are? If not, we gotta start thinking like the Jews and the Israelites. We gotta get rid of the ‘crab mentality’ and be more united and work together like the Mennonites.

I will follow up this article later today with some ideas on how to help get us out of mental slavery. It is time to talk about where we will go and how we can get there. In order to move forward, we have to develop the right mindset to overcome mental slavery and get rid of the dependency syndrome.

If we start to follow this plan as individuals, as families, as communities and as a people in general, the state of affairs for ‘black’ people in Belize will move towards positivity, growth and development, and from within the ranks of those who have changed will emerge real leaders…who will assist in breaking us out of the chains of mental slavery and pave the way towards true emancipation.

World.title: Beloved health advocate Milagro Garel in critical condition following stroke
World.content:
Beloved health advocate Milagro Garel in critical condition following stroke

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): For twenty years, Milagro Garel has been the person Belizean families turned to when a sick child needed care beyond our borders. Today, she is the one who needs help reaching it.

Garel, Country Director for World Pediatrics in Belize, suffered a stroke on July 28 caused by a ruptured brain aneurysm. Because the specialized neurosurgical care she urgently requires is not available in Belize, she was transported to Guatemala, where she remains in critical condition.

The news comes barely a week after World Pediatrics celebrated her extraordinary 20 years of service as Country Director, honoring the countless children and families whose lives she has touched. In its message sharing news of her condition, the organization wrote that Garel “has spent decades moving mountains to help children access lifesaving care,” and that it is now standing with its beloved colleague as she faces an unimaginable medical crisis.

Her family and friends have created a GoFundMe campaign, titled Support Milagro Garel’s Emergency Medical Care, to help cover her transportation, surgery, intensive care and hospitalization. World Pediatrics notes that the fundraiser is independently organized by Garel’s family and friends, and that the organization is sharing it in support but is not involved in collecting or managing donations.

Members of the public who wish to contribute can find the campaign on GoFundMe under her name, and are encouraged to donate, share, and keep Milagro and her family in their thoughts.

Few Belizeans have done more, more quietly, for the country’s sick children. Now the country has a chance to return the kindness.
