World.title: Fairytale denied: Late Eels try shatter Doueihi’s redemption story
World.content:
Wests Tigers 13 Parramatta 16 SportNRLMatch report Fairytale denied: Late Eels try shatter Doueihi’s redemption story Christian Nicolussi August 2, 2026 — 6:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

For a brief moment, the ultimate Adam Doueihi and Wests Tigers redemption story was on the cards. Yet another tumultuous week in Tiger Town was about to finish with a win against Parramatta courtesy of a try to Doueihi, and a wobbly 25m field goal. Loading But once again Tigers’ hearts were broken when Isaiah Iongi skipped through a yawning gap to seal a 16-13 victory at CommBank Stadium. The Sunday afternoon clash featuring two struggling western Sydney clubs was a contender for one of the worst games of the year.



The Eels completed at less than 50 per cent in the second half, while the Tigers never looked like scoring until prop Fonua Pole’s inspirational 48th-minute run brought the home side to life. The Tigers and Doueihi dominated the headlines after the playmaker refused to make himself available against Canberra the previous week. He was upset about being shifted out of the halves, then took the opportunity to tell coach Benji Marshall a few home truths about what he thought was going on at the club. Adam Doueihi reacts during the round 22 loss. Getty Images But Doueihi was welcomed straight back into the team, and the emotion was plain to see when he scored a try on the hour to level the scores. He ran hard from close range and carried three Eels defenders over the try line with him. His teammates celebrated as Doueihi, a spiritual man, took a moment to cross himself. When Doueihi stepped up to kick a field goal from 25m out, the Tigers looked set for snap a seven-match losing streak and score an unthinkable victory.



However, Iongi and the Eels had other ideas. Neither team will play in the finals, but you sensed this one meant more to the home side. Plenty of supporters had given up on their club a long time ago, and there were an alarming number of empty seats at CommBank Stadium. Not even a half-time performance by The Wiggles, whose frontman Anthony Field is a passionate Tigers fan, could energise the rusted-on faithful. What a contrast it was to the 30,000 fans who turned up to watch the same two clubs in round five when Jock Madden’s 84th-minute field goal handed the Tigers a thrilling win. Jordan Samrani opens the scoring for Parramatta. Getty Images



The Eels led 12-0 at the break, but could have been up by so much more. Jordan Samrani leapt for a Mitch Moses kick to score, and Tallyn Da Silva, a one-time Tiger celebrating 50 NRL games, scored next to the posts after a Samrani run the play before. The Tigers enjoyed plenty of possession and field position early, but not once looked like scoring. They fancied their chances whe going right, only for players to be caught with the ball, while a Doueihi pass sailed straight over the head of Sunia Turuva. It was not until Pole stormed on to the ball early in the second half and scored from 20m out that the Tigers woke up. The Tigers clicked into gear, and Doueihi kept the scoreboard ticking over.



The one passage that best summed up the fortunes of both clubs happened in the 57th minute when Doueihi dropped the ball cold, Ronald Volkman picked it up and looked ready to run the length of the field. He knew he did not have the pace, threw it to Josh Addo-Carr, who then spilled the ball down. The Tigers have the bye next weekend and will use the time to clear their heads and forget about the latest dramas surrounding Doueihi and claims of players receiving preferential treatment and a lack of accountability. Parramatta take on South Sydney. The quicker they forget Sunday afternoon the better.

World.title: Catholic Schools’ double standards a bit rich
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As a former NSW Catholic primary school teacher who spent the last 11 years of his career managing a music resourcing budget capped at $500 – unadjusted from 2011 to 2022 despite rising costs – I am incensed to read that at least $160,000 from Catholic Schools NSW was allegedly funnelled into Liberal Party branch stacking (“What we learnt from week one of ICAC’s Operation Rosny”, August 2). While teachers are forced to account for every cent and stretch meagre resources, leadership seemingly operates with impunity. The Catholic Church must face the same financial accountability and transparency with government funds that it demands from its hard-working educators. Anthony Frazer, Camperdown I almost choked on my morning coffee reading your editorial about Catholic schools (“Time for Catholics to be transparent about their use of other people’s money”, July 31). At first, I thought the editor must be mistaken. The millions of dollars channelled to Catholic schools are not required to “open their books” for the public gaze? As a public-school teacher for well over 40 years (and still going) I have to account for every rubber, pencil, book and kilometre travelled. Woe betide a public school or teacher that doesn’t “stack up”. As it is, up to 80 per cent of Catholic schools’ funds come from the public purse. It’s time the Catholic school system was incorporated into Department of Education. While we are at it, legislate that all politicians’ children attend public schools. Margaret Collins, Terrigal Dylan Whitelaw, Robert Assaf, Christian Ellis and Jean-Claude Perrottet were all members of the NSW Reformers. Monique Westermann So, in summary, a bunch of young, right-wing Christians seeks to deny the rights of certain fellow humans (“The secretive young men behind the Reformers”, August 1). They’re influenced by a man who opposed an initiative to reduce bullying of a significant number of school children. They’re funded in part by a shady land developer. They offer themselves as consultants and proclaim their mission to be a culture war. They call their gang The Reformers but insist they’re Liberals. Am I missing something, or is this old, gay atheist on the money? Peter Campbell, Potts Point If we stay very still, we might be lucky enough to observe the secretive Reformers and Catholics in their natural habitat. There, on the shady, murky waters, we glimpse their preening rituals and displays of marvellous plumage. The two breeds seem so different but work co-operatively as they go about the business of attracting handouts from passers-by and protecting their patch from other species. When we peer below the surface, however, we see all the sneaky shoving and the bitter squabbling over crusts. But life in the swamp is about to change forever. There has been a new arrival; the Greater Swooping ICAC. Dave Watts, Avalon United front Pasquale Vartuli’s observations (Letters, August 2) were an interesting sequel to your article earlier in the week on the refusal of the Presbyterian Church to allow women to become elders (“Stained glass ceiling for this Christian church”, July 27). The Uniting Church was formed on June 22, 1977 by almost all members of the Congregational Church, the overwhelming majority of the Methodist Church and the more thoughtful members of the Presbyterian Church. It’s therefore not surprising that the Presbyterian Church is not moving forward in relation to their female members. As I noted, the more progressive members moved on 46 years ago to the Uniting Church. It’s probably time for the rest of them to catch up. Elsie Gelling Merimbula



Fix the fiscus Peter Hartcher reminds us of the importance of reducing the national deficit (“It’s time to the PM to get fiscal”, August 1), while Caitlin Fitzsimmons makes the argument for a massive cut in fuel rebates for mining and resource companies (“Rewarding companies to do nothing is undermining Australia’s climate cuts”, August 1), which could be part of the solution Hartcher refers to. And if we also bring in the proposed 25 per cent tax for gas exports, a move that is widely supported across the community, then the task of reducing the national deficit will become significantly easier. If we are to have a country that has a chance of surviving and thriving through the coming years of climate disasters and international uncertainties, we must have governments that take the long view and are prepared to stand up to some of the corporate interests. Catherine Rossiter, Fadden (ACT) Photo: Badiucao Of course our national deficit is political, though it’s hardly all “baubles and charms”. We know most Australians support a real increase in taxes on our exports of fossil fuels and minerals to levels similar to that which have placed Norway among the wealthiest and happiest of nations. At the same time as undertaxing the resources sector, our governments continue to give them billions of dollars in fuel subsidies. If our government moved on those two issues alone our budget deficit could probably be fixed. Perhaps we could even increase spending on higher education, TAFE and university, that would both increase our skills level and end the massive debt and related disincentive for education that holds back those from less affluent backgrounds from improving their lives, and contributing to our nation as a whole. Colin Hesse, Nowra The “pollution paradox” forces taxpayers to fund the continued use of fossil fuels. The government is actively undermining its own climate policy by providing $3.3 billion in fuel tax rebates to major polluters, which outweighs emissions penalties by a 22-to-1 ratio. It is not just bailing out a boat with a teaspoon while water is added by the bucketload, as Caitlin Fitzsimmons suggests, but more like trying to empty a flooded room with an eyedropper while the government pumps water in with a fire hose. This is beyond absurd, profoundly counterproductive and needs to be addressed now. Daniela Catalano, Haberfield UN must act After a flurry of excitement that lasted five minutes, the Donald Trump-inspired Board of Peace plan for peace in Gaza is in trouble (“Hamas to disarm under deal for Gaza to get new government”, August 2). Too much water has flowed under the bridge to expect Hamas and Israel to trust each other. The only hope for peace is for a UN-authorised force to move in and end the violence, enabling rebuilding. Gaza could be declared a UN protectorate. This force must not include the US because it is too closely linked to Israel. It will be a long and difficult process, but the present death and destruction must not be allowed to continue. Ian Adair, Hunters Hill



Medicine isn’t politics After watching former US chief medical adviser Anthony Fauci facing a Senate committee accused of megalomania and invoking the Fifth Amendment over decisions he made during the COVID pandemic, it’s worth remembering that medicine isn’t politics (“The real takeaway from Fauci’s show trial is enduring rage”, July 31). A scientist can only tell you what the evidence supports at the time, and that advice shifts as the evidence does. That’s not deception, that’s the job working properly. Unfortunately, we’ve built a culture in which changing your mind in light of new evidence is regarded as proof that you had been lying all along. There’s real irony in a politician questioning a scientist’s judgment calls, when the reverse almost never happens. It’s easy to be angry about a lockdown in hindsight, especially if you didn’t lose anyone, but it’s much harder to have made that call, knowing people would suffer either way. Public health messaging isn’t undermined by rival experts, rather, it’s undermined by people who watched a podcast and decided that qualified them to add their opinions. The ones who pay for that arrogance aren’t the pundits, they’re the doctors and medical workers who kept showing up, exhausted, to look after the rest of us. Rani Sachdev, Cronulla Anthony Fauci, former director of the US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. Bloomberg Doctor poaching Correspondent Bruce Johnson argues that “We need immigration. How else do we put enough doctors and nurses into the regions?” (Letters, August 1). The truth is we actually need to train our own and use mechanisms such as university fee discounts to attract them to the regions. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke recently said half of Australia’s doctors and nurses were born overseas. Like other affluent countries, Australia recruits these professionals from countries which have paid for their training, “saving” Australia US$1.7 billion in the five years to 2023 alone. Thus, Australia maintains its ratio of 4.1 physicians per 1000 people for a population of 28 million. In contrast, South Sudan has no doctors and other poor countries have very few. The physicians they do train are often poached by the affluent West. The Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda are presently battling Ebola, with 0.2 physicians each per 1000 people for large populations. A strong medical system is a humanitarian imperative and the first global defence against pandemics. In short, poaching medical professionals is short-sighted, unethical and a false economy. Forewarned by the World Health Organisation (WHO) of a global shortage of 4.5 million nurses by 2030, Australia needs to be training more nurses, not relying on immigration. Barbara Chapman, South Yarra (Vic)



Petty politics It was fascinating to read Bevan Shields’ article about the political shenanigans in Finley, and then to check the AEC tally in that town in the recent by-election (“How Ley crushed a nasty coup”, August 2) – a massive 35 per cent swing against the Liberal Party. Politicians need to understand that politics is not a game between internal factions, nor a game between different parties. It is the way that we voters decide who is to govern our country how we want it governed. It is a serious occupation that requires full attention and must not degenerate into petty power squabbles and ideological indulgences. The proof is in the numbers. Richard Prosser, Armidale Picking on pensioners Doing away with the rebate to pensioners for having private health insurance is one of the worst ideas to have come from a Labor government (“Labor ignored internal report revealing toll of scrapping Baby Boomer health rebate”, August 1). It has nothing to do with equity. Seniors do not have the capacity to increase their income that younger, fitter people may have. The impact on pensioners will be enormous as it will increase the fees well beyond what most are paying now. Many already struggle to keep up with fees and the cost of living on their limited incomes. It will force many to suffer for longer as they will have to rely on an already overloaded public health system. The benefits to the aged-care system are not enough to warrant stopping these rebates. If aged care is underfunded, which everyone seems to agree it is, then increase it, but not at the expense of those who may then be forced into that system quicker. This is definitely a case of older people being disadvantaged by poor budgeting. Augusta Monro, Dural Puzzling policy Australia urgently needs more electricity, yet conservatives hold a bizarre double standard on how to deliver it. The Coalition and One Nation fully back “combustion” energy derived from burning finite polluting fossil fuels and clean “electron” energy if generated by nuclear, but less so or not at all if it’s solar or wind. Even stranger is their stance on transmission lines. Those transporting electrons created by fossil or nuclear power are uncontroversial. But lines transporting renewable electrons “scar landscapes” and “divide communities.” To the Coalition and One Nation: please explain. In whose interest is it to thwart, delay, and sabotage the transmission of abundant, inexhaustible clean power when an urgent supply crisis is already on our doorstep? Carlo Ursida, Kensington (Vic) Conservatives hold a bizarre double standard on power transmission lines. Bloomberg



IT merry-go-round I wonder if Waleed Aly has ever had to deal with Telstra over wifi problems, as many of us do regularly (“From food apps to help lines, tech is being used to frustrate us”, August 1). With a great sense of irony it seems that Telstra prefers you to contact them online about these issues. So begins a not-so-merry-go-round that circles for days, with repeated requests for all the details and to perform at-home modem resets. Eventually, you end up in the corner of a room curled up in the foetal position madly tapping a link on your phone that purportedly accesses your case. It really is the most effective remedy for internet addiction. So good on your Telstra for practising tough love and making us all go cold turkey. John Mizon, Collaroy No real test At last, we have a reporter who tells us the truth about how much a medal in Glasgow is worth (“We dominated in Glasgow, but the Olympics are a different beast,” August 1). Listening to the sports results each morning, the reporters were gushing about how the Australia swimmers and other athletes thrashed the rest of the Commonwealth, without mentioning the poor quality of the opposition. The PanPacs swimming event in California later this month will give us an idea of how good the swimmers really are. Victorian premier Dan Andrews was right to cancel the games due to the exorbitant cost. It’s time for them to be cancelled permanently. I feel sorry for the citizens of Ahmedabad, India, who will have to forgo services to pay for the third-rate event in 2030. Robert Pallister, Punchbowl Gold medallist Abbey Caldwell, silver medallist Jessica Hull and bronze medallist Claudia Hollingsworth after the women’s one mile final at the Commonwealth Games. AP Photo/Kin Cheung The Commonwealth Games medal tally shows Australia well out in front with 128 altogether. Next is England with 80. To put this into Olympic Games perspective, Team GB will include England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland as well as the Channel Islands and other British dominions. If we add the total medals won by these countries the total for all the British territories would be 177, well ahead of Australia. On the other hand, we would win hands down if you look at the per capita ratio of participants. Well done, Aussies. Brian Collins, Cronulla

World.title: Demons grind out win on Gold Coast; Tigers off the bottom as Lalor delivers knockout blow
World.content:
Loading

In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: A West Coast player went to ground in obvious pain after a gut punch from a Richmond opponent at the MCG.

Surgery for Swan after suffering a sickening lower leg injury. Melbourne have notched their 13th victory and climbed back into the top six after a hard-fought nine-point victory over the Gold Coast Suns in Queensland. The match was tight throughout but the Demons stepped up late to ensure their push for a top-four finish remains alive. For the Suns, it was simply more heartache – a 10th consecutive defeat the signs of a season to lament. John Noble and Matt Rowell led the possession-winners for both clubs, but Max Gawn was vying for best-on-ground honours with 25 possessions and 10 marks.



In a dynamic and absorbing match, Melbourne 18.6 (114) defeated Gold Coast 16.9 (105). Kysaiah Pickett of the Demons shows plenty of dash, finding space ahead of Matt Rowell. Getty Images More to come



Tiger in the gun for behind-the-play blow Marc McGowan Richmond took a major step towards dodging a second wooden spoon in three years with a second win this season over a wayward West Coast as Tigers defender Luke Trainor faces match review scrutiny for a gut punch. Adem Yze’s men had lost eight matches in a row by an average of almost 50 points, and were on the bottom, behind Essendon on percentage, with a miserable 2-17 win-loss record before Sunday’s 11-point victory.



Richmond took advantage of the Eagles’ yips in front of goal at the MCG to climb above the Bombers and within one win of 16th-placed West Coast, who had kicked 3.17 at one stage before losing 12.12 (84) to 9.19 (73). The result eases pressure on coach Yze, who has presided over only 10 victories in 66 matches in what is a full-blown rebuild at Tigerland. “We’re rebuilding, so when you rebuild, you need games into younger players,” Yze said. “We get a win today, but we still need Jonty Faull, Harry Armstrong and Tom Sims [to get back from injury] … we’ve still got guys we need to gel together. But at the same time, if we can scratch out some wins while we’re going through what we’re going through with unavailability – it’s terrific. “We know what we’ve got within our four walls … we’ve dealt with more than what other teams have dealt with.



“But when you see Sammy [Lalor] do what he does today; he’s [only] scratching the surface. When those lads start to grow together; it’ll be really exciting.” Footy with feeling: Richmond’s Sam Lalor after kicking the sealer. Getty Images Yze re-signed until the end of 2028 in November last year, and chief executive Shane Dunne said last month he had the club’s backing. There were only 12 points between the sides at three-quarter-time, but goals to Richmond premiership veterans Tom Lynch (20 disposals, 2.4) and Toby Nankervis blew the margin out before they withstood a late fightback. The Eagles, who have been competitive most weeks despite their lack of success, have plenty to rue, with Jake Waterman’s 2.6 day – on top of putting another kick out on the full – headlining their woeful goalkicking.



Elliot Yeo had a chance to slice the difference to six points with a set shot inside the last two minutes, but sprayed it to the left, only for No.1 draft pick Lalor to seal the contest with his third major after winning a test of strength. View post on X West Coast were trying to beat Richmond at the MCG for the first time since 2015, but the 33,737 crowd instead were able to celebrate a rare Tigers triumph this season. Tim Taranto led Richmond’s charge with 32 disposals and a game-high 11 clearances, while Harley Reid was outstanding in a losing cause with 34 touches, 20 contested possessions and nine clearances. Mid-season draftee Marcus Herbert (34 disposals) was also prolific for the Eagles. Yze said he had not seen Trainor’s behind-the-play gut punch to West Coast’s Jack Williams in the second quarter. They were engaged in a standing wrestle before Trainor struck the Eagle with a clenched left fist.



The second-year Tiger, playing his 30th career game, instantly jogged away while Williams went to ground in obvious pain and went to the bench soon after. Richmond captain Toby Nankervis and Nathan Broad celebrated a rare win in 2026. Getty Images “I’m not too sure how hard the impact was, but if he’s gone and done something wrong, we’ll look at it,” Yze said. “I think there have been a few fines over the last few occasions when things like this have happened, so hopefully, we can get that type of result. “We don’t want to be losing players through stupidity [when we have so many injuries], so hopefully, it wasn’t too bad. We’ve educated our players, and they understand what’s right and wrong.”



It is the type of incident the AFL aimed to stamp out when it announced tribunal changes in February, revealing that incidents where a player strikes another in the chest or stomach were more likely to be graded medium impact and result in suspension. Match review officer Michael Christian has typically graded these incidents as low impact, which led to fines rather than bans. Richmond’s lengthy injury list includes key defensive options Noah Balta, Josh Gibcus and Campbell Gray, while prized draftee Sam Cumming (ankle) was the latest addition on Sunday. Surgery for ‘devastated’ Swan after leg injury



Peter Ryan Sydney Swans defender Will Edwards had surgery on Sunday after suffering a sickening lower leg injury against the Saints on Saturday. Will Edwards was taken from the ground with a broken leg. AFL Photos Edwards appeared to dislocate his ankle and was carted from the field having received pain medication during the Swans’ 19-point win at Marvel Stadium. Coach Dean Cox described the injury as “devastating” for the 23-year-old, who made his debut this season following a series of leg fractures and infections.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 If the Crows fade away yet again, could this Essendon contender step up? The club is expected to provide more information about the injury and his prognosis after the operation. Midfielder James Rowbottom will also have surgery to repair a broken hand sustained during the match against St Kilda. For the Saints, Jack Silvagni (dislocated shoulder) and Tom De Koning (hip pointer) are in doubt for next Sunday night’s match against their former team, Carlton.

World.title: Everything you need to know about Ekka 2026, including discounts, transport and showbags
World.content:
NationalQueenslandThe Ekka Everything you need to know about Ekka 2026, including discounts, transport and showbags Nick Dent August 2, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Suzy Dekker is an Ekka superfan. She’s 55 now, and reckons she has only missed three since her first visit, way back in the 1970s. In those days, showbags were called ‘sample bags’, food was either a scone from the Country Women’s Association or a dagwood dog, and there was a novel approach to waste collection. The Ekka, AKA the Royal Queensland Show. Bradley Kanaris “You could register and get a bag, then as you’re going around you would pick up rubbish and put it in your bag,” the Mount Cotton resident says. “You would take it back when it was full, and they would give you a little toy or something.”



The Brisbane Exhibition is 150 years old this August, and expecting an even larger crowd than the 428,000 who attended in 2025. As usual, Dekker will be coming with her mum, sister, nieces and nephews, and she has her routine all planned out. “The first thing we do is go straight to the Butter Board and buy some turkey sandwiches,” Dekker says. “Those turkey sandwiches have always been our favourite.” Her next stop is Dog Pavilion for the prize pooches. “I always look to see what dogs are on,” she says.



“We do the showbags for the kids, and we take them to the Kids’ Carnival, and they play the games.” Her favourite competition is the woodchopping: “When I was a kid, I would collect a chip from every woodchop every year – I [wrote] the year on the woodchips and everything.” The Ekka turns 150 in 2026. Royal Queensland Show She has two pieces of advice for Ekka first timers: grab a map as soon as you arrive, and take your time – you’ve got all day. “Don’t rush from one thing to the next, thinking that you’re gonna miss out. There’s so much going on. Don’t stress! Something else will be on.”



Here is all the other essential information you need about visiting the Ekka in 2026. When is the Ekka on? It’s on for nine days, from Saturday, August 8 until Sunday, August 16. Opening hours are 9am-9pm. Most exhibition pavilions close at 6pm, but Sideshow Alley, the Showbag Pavilion, the Gourmet Plaza and the Main Arena stay open till late. When is the People’s Day Holiday?

If you work in Brisbane, the public holiday is on Wednesday, August 12. If you work in Logan, Moreton Bay, Redland City or Scenic Rim, you get a long weekend, with your show day occurring on Monday, August 10. Ipswich, Gold Coast and Sunshine Coast don’t get a day off.



How do I get to the Ekka? Exhibition train station is open for the Show, and you can join the Ekka Loop at Roma Street, Central or Fortitude Valley stations. Buses stopping nearby include M1, M2, 330, 333, and 340 – plan your journey on public transport here. Exhibition station has been upgraded to better accommodate large crowds. Queensland Government If driving, the five main parking stations are at King Street, Herston, Royal Women’s Hospital, Valley Metro and McWhirters. A dedicated drop-off/pick-up zone for cars and taxis is on Costin Street. Can I buy tickets at the gate?



Nope. Online only. How much does it cost and how can I save money?

Pricing all depends when you buy and what day you want to go. Non-discount days are $42.95 adult (15 years and over), $31.95 concession, $27.95 child (5-14 years) and $92.95 family. Toddlers under four are free. Adult entry after 4pm is $27.95. Discount days – on August 10, 11, 13 and 14 – are a full 20 per cent cheaper. The new Back for More Pass gets you in on another day for $23.



Can I get a passout?

Yes, before 8pm to return on the same day – but each ticket holder can only get one passout. Is the Ekka accessible?

Exhibition Station has elevators and ramps, and ramps are provided between roads, footpaths and pavilions. The Main Arena has two wheelchair-accessible viewing areas. Scooter, wheelchairs and strollers can be hired from the John Macdonald Stand. How do I pay for rides?





You can only pay for rides with Fun Pass Credits. For this, you can download the app, or buy a physical Fun Pass card at an Information Booth or self-serve kiosk at the Show and load it up. Pre-purchased credits on the app come with discounts, and if you buy too many credits you can get a refund if you apply by August 30. How can I save money on rides?

Two-for-one ride sessions are on 9.30-10.30am every morning. The classic Bertie Beetle bag is one of the cheapest showbags, but upgrades are available. Courtney Kruk What’s new in showbags?





There are 93 new bags this year including Vegemite ($32), The Mandalorian ($32), F1 Kit Kat ($14), Onikuma ($35), Ovaltine ($6) and Hershey’s and Reese’s ($15). What are the cheapest showbags?

A Rainbow Freeze showbag (sour candy) is just $2, and there are some $5 ones available including the Bertie Beetle Blue. What are the most expensive?

The dearest one we can find is the Morish Nuts Showbag for $55, and no doubt it’s the macadamias that are pushing up the cost of that one.



There are also a half dozen $38 bags ranging from Derwent x Home Studio (art equipment) to the Perfume Collection or the Miss Coco Showbag – a collection of beachy fashion items. How can I pay less for lunch?

More than 110 vendors are offering a “value” food item priced at $10 or less. Some are offering Family Bundles – deals from $25 designed to feed a family of four. Profits from sales of strawberry sundaes are invested back into the Ekka’s agricultural education programs. Ekka What about Strawberry Sundaes?





Get them at the corner of Gregory Terrace and King Street, or four other locations around the Ekka. When buying tickets online you also have the option to pre-order a sundae for a discounted $7, or four for $26. Where do the big shows and fireworks take place?

From 6-8pm every night there are two hours of performance, storytelling and spectacle in the Main Arena, culminating in fireworks at 7.50pm. The Main Arena will also have army bands, dance eisteddfods, kids’ shows, stunt shows, woodchopping, circus and more. You can also find entertainment at the Main Stage, the XXXX Stockman’s Bar and Grill Stage, the Plaza Music Stage and the Royal Queensland Cooking Stage.



I’ve lost my kid, what do I do?

Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics Bleijie insists Ekka station will stay open during Olympics The Lost Persons station at the Gregory Terrace Police Station is open 9am-8.30pm. Parents are encouraged to write their phone number on a free wristband from the police marquee on Gregory Terrace as soon as they arrive in case of unplanned separations. Yes, but what if my phone dies?

Charging stations are located under the John Mac Tunnel.



Technology infuriates me, is there an information phone number with a person on the end?

Yes, it’s (07) 3253 3900. How do I avoid a child sugar meltdown?

Don’t buy them junk food? Sorry, you’re on your own there. The Ekka runs August 8-16, 2026 at the Royal Exhibition Grounds, Bowen Hills. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Cronulla cement reputation as real premiership deal with Rabbitohs rout
World.content:
Cronulla 32 South Sydney 16 SportNRLNRL 2026 Cronulla cement reputation as real premiership deal with Rabbitohs rout Dan Walsh Updated August 2, 2026 — 5:30pm ,first published 4:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

“I’m telling you, Cronulla can win the competition if they want it.” But then Sharks premiership winner Mick Ennis would say that, wouldn’t he? Loading With every win – and Sunday’s 32-16 defeat of South Sydney at Ocean Protect Stadium made it nine from their past 10 outings – you have to put more stock in Cronulla’s premiership credentials. Particularly, when despite being reduced to 15 by Kayal Iro’s head knock and a biceps injury to Siosifa Talakai, they barely missed a beat. Coach Craig Fitzgibbon has been at pains to point out his side hasn’t achieved anything yet.



“We’re going good, but there’s a bit more to go. It’s round 22,” he said as he noted how Cronulla finished last year’s regular season with seven wins from eight games as well. “So what’s different is maybe the perception of the way we’re doing it. I’ve never felt any different about the group in the last five years, to be honest. “Maybe I believe in [the players] more than they believe in themselves, but we’re working hard towards something and we’ve been building that for a little bit.” The year-on-year difference is getting harder to ignore, though. Million-dollar No.7 Nicho Hynes is playing a more rounded game than when he won the 2022 Dally M medal as his run of 32 consecutive goals closes in on Hazem El Masri’s all-time record of 35. Blayke Brailey and Addin Fonua-Blake have both returned from Origin in compelling form too. The latter especially is coming off Fitzgibbon’s bench in devastating fashion from the 20-minute mark, and is the last thing an opposition wants to deal with on their try line – per his classic big-man try from a superb angled run midway through the second half.



So it proved for a gutsy but outgunned South Sydney at Shark Park. Cronulla’s 18-6 half-time lead came after a clutch of penalties for high shots and late hits by the home side. Cronulla celebrate an Addin Fonua-Blake try on Sunday. NRL Photos Discipline has been their biggest issue all year, though Teig Wilton seemed unlucky to be sin-binned for contact that split Jack Wighton’s ear open – despite replays suggesting the contact was almost exclusively head-on-head. Both had to pass HIAs and while the Sharks lost their shape while playing down a man, Trindall came into his own once it was 13 on 13 again. After almost scoring himself from close range, the man with more try-assists than anyone else added another to his tally by piloting Briton Nikora through. His kick for Mulitalo then finished in a milestone try to Talakai in his 150th NRL game. And even though the Rabbitohs hung in grimly, the contest was only heading one way when Brailey scurried over from dummy-half before half-time.



A second half that started with Campbell Graham polishing off a right-edge overlap briefly kindled hope of a Rabbitohs comeback. But with Latrell Mitchell, Cameron Murray, Tallis Duncan, Euan Aitken and David Fifita all sidelined, the Sharks always had their measure. All but Mitchell will return next week against Parramatta as Wayne Bennett spelled out South Sydney’s next hurdle once their best and brightest are on the field. Cronulla halfback Nicho Hynes braces for heavy contact. Getty Images “We can run deep any day of the week if we can just get over the rubbish that gets into our game,” Bennett said. “I’m not disappointed with our effort... Our Achilles heel is when we don’t execute, then we play a bit of a price for it and that’s been consistent all year with us.”



And for the umpteenth time this season, Fitzgibbon had a scrambling defensive effort – which the warhorse coach prizes above all others – to hang in his pool room. This week it was Will Kennedy producing a superb long-range chase and cover tackle on Jye Gray. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 NRL ‘media cop’ to crack down on negative coverage of game Danny Weidler Sport columnist Late tries to Mulitalo and Alex Johnston made no difference in the final wash-up. And the Rabbitohs casualty ward is a reasonable counter to Ennis and his suggestion “Cronulla can win the competition” during commentary. The old Cronulla hooker noted exactly that, along with the enduring question of how the Sharks stack up come finals time against the Panthers, Roosters and Warriors. Right now though, they can only beat the team in front of them each week. And right now, they look like legitimate contenders doing it.

Tackled Group 3 opposition at only his second start as a two-year-old before being turned out, and fitted with two metropolitan trials. Drawn to get a handy enough run on or near the speed and this shapes as a nice starting point for bigger targets in spring. 5. Stronghold is another metro visitor that can improve into his second start after an even effort on debut at the provincials. 8. Savvy Diamond is a filly by Savabeel and a big market watch on debut for the Waterhouse-Bott stable. Progressed to win her second trial and drawn to get a soft run. 10. Visna, a filly by Rebel Dane in the Gary Portelli yard, also makes her debut off a recent trial win on the synthetic, while 7. Legaselli resumes for a second prep, with blinkers coming off and behind two progressive trials.

1. Orange Tsunami hits peak fitness fourth-up from a handy draw in a very moderate race. Drops back from provincial level and was scratched from the opener at Wyong on Sunday to be saved for this. Watch the betting on 2. Gentle Giant, a four-year-old by Maurice in the Waterhouse-Bott yard, which debuts with blinkers on behind two improving trials. 4. Who I Think I Am is another improver that missed narrowly here last start when reloading off a month-long freshen. 3. Milchel did his best work late first-up at Gosford over a mile, and relishing the bigger circuit can run into the money at good odds.

Glenn’s Legacy is over the odds dropping back from a much steeper BM 72 metro race.

Building a nice record at the track and the drier the surface the better she is. 3. Dancer’s Delight is a progressive four-year-old that hit the line late in a better Class 3 here second-up after beating home the top selection the start before. The handicapper hasn’t missed him up to 62kg rising to a Class 3, although it’s a weak line-up for this level. 2. Stormbringer swept home to win a BM 66 here two starts ago before doing nothing in a deeper provincial grade. Is a different galloper at home, although also has to carry a big weight. 9. I Am Brave is drawn to get an economical run dropping back from provincial level fourth-up and can run into the money.

Charged home late to miss narrowly at Wagga before going one better at that course a fortnight ago. Up 2kg, but hard fit, loves the courses with long runs home, and this isn’t strong. 7. Roonami dug in hard to win a weak country BM 58 when resuming and normally holds that form into her next run. 3. Astrogazer is well over the odds second-up from a handy on-speed draw and coming back from a tougher provincial race. 1. Sir Tua is a big watch second-up since late summer. 5. Lucky Star, deep into his prep, goes in all trifecta and first fours.

6. Flywire is a lightly raced and versatile Canberra three-year-old emerging as the one to beat, second-up as a gelding, and in a thin race for this grade. Superior Style bounced to the front and kept going here on debut when well in the market. Is up to repeating the dose over the same trip and draw. 2. The Main Event can improve sharply second-up back on firmer ground and coming off a fair effort in tougher Class 2 Highway company. Big watch on 3. Bosco, which resumes behind a nice trial win on the synthetic. Big weight offset by a 4kg claimer booking but has to overcome the outside draw. 8. Vainstream is another Canberra raider over the odds deep into his prep, while 7. Showtime Maggie, back on drier ground third-up, can add plenty of value into wider exotics.

How to play it: Flywire to win. Best bets Race 2: (1) Orange Tsunami

World.title: Fairytale denied: Late Eels try shatter Doueihi’s redemption story
World.content:
Wests Tigers 13 Parramatta 16 SportNRLMatch report Fairytale denied: Late Eels try shatter Doueihi’s redemption story Christian Nicolussi August 2, 2026 — 6:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

For a brief moment, the ultimate Adam Doueihi and Wests Tigers redemption story was on the cards. Yet another tumultuous week in Tiger Town was about to finish with a win against Parramatta courtesy of a try to Doueihi, and a wobbly 25m field goal. Loading But once again Tigers’ hearts were broken when Isaiah Iongi skipped through a yawning gap to seal a 16-13 victory at CommBank Stadium. The Sunday afternoon clash featuring two struggling western Sydney clubs was a contender for one of the worst games of the year.



The Eels completed at less than 50 per cent in the second half, while the Tigers never looked like scoring until prop Fonua Pole’s inspirational 48th-minute run brought the home side to life. The Tigers and Doueihi dominated the headlines after the playmaker refused to make himself available against Canberra the previous week. He was upset about being shifted out of the halves, then took the opportunity to tell coach Benji Marshall a few home truths about what he thought was going on at the club. Adam Doueihi reacts during the round 22 loss. Getty Images But Doueihi was welcomed straight back into the team, and the emotion was plain to see when he scored a try on the hour to level the scores. He ran hard from close range and carried three Eels defenders over the try line with him. His teammates celebrated as Doueihi, a spiritual man, took a moment to cross himself. When Doueihi stepped up to kick a field goal from 25m out, the Tigers looked set for snap a seven-match losing streak and score an unthinkable victory.



However, Iongi and the Eels had other ideas. Neither team will play in the finals, but you sensed this one meant more to the home side. Plenty of supporters had given up on their club a long time ago, and there were an alarming number of empty seats at CommBank Stadium. Not even a half-time performance by The Wiggles, whose frontman Anthony Field is a passionate Tigers fan, could energise the rusted-on faithful. What a contrast it was to the 30,000 fans who turned up to watch the same two clubs in round five when Jock Madden’s 84th-minute field goal handed the Tigers a thrilling win. Jordan Samrani opens the scoring for Parramatta. Getty Images



The Eels led 12-0 at the break, but could have been up by so much more. Jordan Samrani leapt for a Mitch Moses kick to score, and Tallyn Da Silva, a one-time Tiger celebrating 50 NRL games, scored next to the posts after a Samrani run the play before. The Tigers enjoyed plenty of possession and field position early, but not once looked like scoring. They fancied their chances whe going right, only for players to be caught with the ball, while a Doueihi pass sailed straight over the head of Sunia Turuva. It was not until Pole stormed on to the ball early in the second half and scored from 20m out that the Tigers woke up. The Tigers clicked into gear, and Doueihi kept the scoreboard ticking over.



The one passage that best summed up the fortunes of both clubs happened in the 57th minute when Doueihi dropped the ball cold, Ronald Volkman picked it up and looked ready to run the length of the field. He knew he did not have the pace, threw it to Josh Addo-Carr, who then spilled the ball down. The Tigers have the bye next weekend and will use the time to clear their heads and forget about the latest dramas surrounding Doueihi and claims of players receiving preferential treatment and a lack of accountability. Parramatta take on South Sydney. The quicker they forget Sunday afternoon the better.

World.title: Demons grind out win on Gold Coast; Tigers off the bottom as Lalor delivers knockout blow
World.content:
Loading

In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: A West Coast player went to ground in obvious pain after a gut punch from a Richmond opponent at the MCG.

Surgery for Swan after suffering a sickening lower leg injury. Melbourne have notched their 13th victory and climbed back into the top six after a hard-fought nine-point victory over the Gold Coast Suns in Queensland. The match was tight throughout but the Demons stepped up late to ensure their push for a top-four finish remains alive. For the Suns, it was simply more heartache – a 10th consecutive defeat the signs of a season to lament. John Noble and Matt Rowell led the possession-winners for both clubs, but Max Gawn was vying for best-on-ground honours with 25 possessions and 10 marks.



In a dynamic and absorbing match, Melbourne 18.6 (114) defeated Gold Coast 16.9 (105). Kysaiah Pickett of the Demons shows plenty of dash, finding space ahead of Matt Rowell. Getty Images More to come



Tiger in the gun for behind-the-play blow Marc McGowan Richmond took a major step towards dodging a second wooden spoon in three years with a second win this season over a wayward West Coast as Tigers defender Luke Trainor faces match review scrutiny for a gut punch. Adem Yze’s men had lost eight matches in a row by an average of almost 50 points, and were on the bottom, behind Essendon on percentage, with a miserable 2-17 win-loss record before Sunday’s 11-point victory.



Richmond took advantage of the Eagles’ yips in front of goal at the MCG to climb above the Bombers and within one win of 16th-placed West Coast, who had kicked 3.17 at one stage before losing 12.12 (84) to 9.19 (73). The result eases pressure on coach Yze, who has presided over only 10 victories in 66 matches in what is a full-blown rebuild at Tigerland. “We’re rebuilding, so when you rebuild, you need games into younger players,” Yze said. “We get a win today, but we still need Jonty Faull, Harry Armstrong and Tom Sims [to get back from injury] … we’ve still got guys we need to gel together. But at the same time, if we can scratch out some wins while we’re going through what we’re going through with unavailability – it’s terrific. “We know what we’ve got within our four walls … we’ve dealt with more than what other teams have dealt with.



“But when you see Sammy [Lalor] do what he does today; he’s [only] scratching the surface. When those lads start to grow together; it’ll be really exciting.” Footy with feeling: Richmond’s Sam Lalor after kicking the sealer. Getty Images Yze re-signed until the end of 2028 in November last year, and chief executive Shane Dunne said last month he had the club’s backing. There were only 12 points between the sides at three-quarter-time, but goals to Richmond premiership veterans Tom Lynch (20 disposals, 2.4) and Toby Nankervis blew the margin out before they withstood a late fightback. The Eagles, who have been competitive most weeks despite their lack of success, have plenty to rue, with Jake Waterman’s 2.6 day – on top of putting another kick out on the full – headlining their woeful goalkicking.



Elliot Yeo had a chance to slice the difference to six points with a set shot inside the last two minutes, but sprayed it to the left, only for No.1 draft pick Lalor to seal the contest with his third major after winning a test of strength. View post on X West Coast were trying to beat Richmond at the MCG for the first time since 2015, but the 33,737 crowd instead were able to celebrate a rare Tigers triumph this season. Tim Taranto led Richmond’s charge with 32 disposals and a game-high 11 clearances, while Harley Reid was outstanding in a losing cause with 34 touches, 20 contested possessions and nine clearances. Mid-season draftee Marcus Herbert (34 disposals) was also prolific for the Eagles. Yze said he had not seen Trainor’s behind-the-play gut punch to West Coast’s Jack Williams in the second quarter. They were engaged in a standing wrestle before Trainor struck the Eagle with a clenched left fist.



The second-year Tiger, playing his 30th career game, instantly jogged away while Williams went to ground in obvious pain and went to the bench soon after. Richmond captain Toby Nankervis and Nathan Broad celebrated a rare win in 2026. Getty Images “I’m not too sure how hard the impact was, but if he’s gone and done something wrong, we’ll look at it,” Yze said. “I think there have been a few fines over the last few occasions when things like this have happened, so hopefully, we can get that type of result. “We don’t want to be losing players through stupidity [when we have so many injuries], so hopefully, it wasn’t too bad. We’ve educated our players, and they understand what’s right and wrong.”



It is the type of incident the AFL aimed to stamp out when it announced tribunal changes in February, revealing that incidents where a player strikes another in the chest or stomach were more likely to be graded medium impact and result in suspension. Match review officer Michael Christian has typically graded these incidents as low impact, which led to fines rather than bans. Richmond’s lengthy injury list includes key defensive options Noah Balta, Josh Gibcus and Campbell Gray, while prized draftee Sam Cumming (ankle) was the latest addition on Sunday. Surgery for ‘devastated’ Swan after leg injury



Peter Ryan Sydney Swans defender Will Edwards had surgery on Sunday after suffering a sickening lower leg injury against the Saints on Saturday. Will Edwards was taken from the ground with a broken leg. AFL Photos Edwards appeared to dislocate his ankle and was carted from the field having received pain medication during the Swans’ 19-point win at Marvel Stadium. Coach Dean Cox described the injury as “devastating” for the 23-year-old, who made his debut this season following a series of leg fractures and infections.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 If the Crows fade away yet again, could this Essendon contender step up? The club is expected to provide more information about the injury and his prognosis after the operation. Midfielder James Rowbottom will also have surgery to repair a broken hand sustained during the match against St Kilda. For the Saints, Jack Silvagni (dislocated shoulder) and Tom De Koning (hip pointer) are in doubt for next Sunday night’s match against their former team, Carlton.

World.title: Everything you need to know about Ekka 2026, including discounts, transport and showbags
World.content:
NationalQueenslandThe Ekka Everything you need to know about Ekka 2026, including discounts, transport and showbags Nick Dent August 2, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Suzy Dekker is an Ekka superfan. She’s 55 now, and reckons she has only missed three since her first visit, way back in the 1970s. In those days, showbags were called ‘sample bags’, food was either a scone from the Country Women’s Association or a dagwood dog, and there was a novel approach to waste collection. The Ekka, AKA the Royal Queensland Show. Bradley Kanaris “You could register and get a bag, then as you’re going around you would pick up rubbish and put it in your bag,” the Mount Cotton resident says. “You would take it back when it was full, and they would give you a little toy or something.”



The Brisbane Exhibition is 150 years old this August, and expecting an even larger crowd than the 428,000 who attended in 2025. As usual, Dekker will be coming with her mum, sister, nieces and nephews, and she has her routine all planned out. “The first thing we do is go straight to the Butter Board and buy some turkey sandwiches,” Dekker says. “Those turkey sandwiches have always been our favourite.” Her next stop is Dog Pavilion for the prize pooches. “I always look to see what dogs are on,” she says.



“We do the showbags for the kids, and we take them to the Kids’ Carnival, and they play the games.” Her favourite competition is the woodchopping: “When I was a kid, I would collect a chip from every woodchop every year – I [wrote] the year on the woodchips and everything.” The Ekka turns 150 in 2026. Royal Queensland Show She has two pieces of advice for Ekka first timers: grab a map as soon as you arrive, and take your time – you’ve got all day. “Don’t rush from one thing to the next, thinking that you’re gonna miss out. There’s so much going on. Don’t stress! Something else will be on.”



Here is all the other essential information you need about visiting the Ekka in 2026. When is the Ekka on? It’s on for nine days, from Saturday, August 8 until Sunday, August 16. Opening hours are 9am-9pm. Most exhibition pavilions close at 6pm, but Sideshow Alley, the Showbag Pavilion, the Gourmet Plaza and the Main Arena stay open till late. When is the People’s Day Holiday?

If you work in Brisbane, the public holiday is on Wednesday, August 12. If you work in Logan, Moreton Bay, Redland City or Scenic Rim, you get a long weekend, with your show day occurring on Monday, August 10. Ipswich, Gold Coast and Sunshine Coast don’t get a day off.



How do I get to the Ekka? Exhibition train station is open for the Show, and you can join the Ekka Loop at Roma Street, Central or Fortitude Valley stations. Buses stopping nearby include M1, M2, 330, 333, and 340 – plan your journey on public transport here. Exhibition station has been upgraded to better accommodate large crowds. Queensland Government If driving, the five main parking stations are at King Street, Herston, Royal Women’s Hospital, Valley Metro and McWhirters. A dedicated drop-off/pick-up zone for cars and taxis is on Costin Street. Can I buy tickets at the gate?



Nope. Online only. How much does it cost and how can I save money?

Pricing all depends when you buy and what day you want to go. Non-discount days are $42.95 adult (15 years and over), $31.95 concession, $27.95 child (5-14 years) and $92.95 family. Toddlers under four are free. Adult entry after 4pm is $27.95. Discount days – on August 10, 11, 13 and 14 – are a full 20 per cent cheaper. The new Back for More Pass gets you in on another day for $23.



Can I get a passout?

Yes, before 8pm to return on the same day – but each ticket holder can only get one passout. Is the Ekka accessible?

Exhibition Station has elevators and ramps, and ramps are provided between roads, footpaths and pavilions. The Main Arena has two wheelchair-accessible viewing areas. Scooter, wheelchairs and strollers can be hired from the John Macdonald Stand. How do I pay for rides?





You can only pay for rides with Fun Pass Credits. For this, you can download the app, or buy a physical Fun Pass card at an Information Booth or self-serve kiosk at the Show and load it up. Pre-purchased credits on the app come with discounts, and if you buy too many credits you can get a refund if you apply by August 30. How can I save money on rides?

Two-for-one ride sessions are on 9.30-10.30am every morning. The classic Bertie Beetle bag is one of the cheapest showbags, but upgrades are available. Courtney Kruk What’s new in showbags?





There are 93 new bags this year including Vegemite ($32), The Mandalorian ($32), F1 Kit Kat ($14), Onikuma ($35), Ovaltine ($6) and Hershey’s and Reese’s ($15). What are the cheapest showbags?

A Rainbow Freeze showbag (sour candy) is just $2, and there are some $5 ones available including the Bertie Beetle Blue. What are the most expensive?

The dearest one we can find is the Morish Nuts Showbag for $55, and no doubt it’s the macadamias that are pushing up the cost of that one.



There are also a half dozen $38 bags ranging from Derwent x Home Studio (art equipment) to the Perfume Collection or the Miss Coco Showbag – a collection of beachy fashion items. How can I pay less for lunch?

More than 110 vendors are offering a “value” food item priced at $10 or less. Some are offering Family Bundles – deals from $25 designed to feed a family of four. Profits from sales of strawberry sundaes are invested back into the Ekka’s agricultural education programs. Ekka What about Strawberry Sundaes?





Get them at the corner of Gregory Terrace and King Street, or four other locations around the Ekka. When buying tickets online you also have the option to pre-order a sundae for a discounted $7, or four for $26. Where do the big shows and fireworks take place?

From 6-8pm every night there are two hours of performance, storytelling and spectacle in the Main Arena, culminating in fireworks at 7.50pm. The Main Arena will also have army bands, dance eisteddfods, kids’ shows, stunt shows, woodchopping, circus and more. You can also find entertainment at the Main Stage, the XXXX Stockman’s Bar and Grill Stage, the Plaza Music Stage and the Royal Queensland Cooking Stage.



I’ve lost my kid, what do I do?

World.title: Cronulla cement reputation as real premiership deal with Rabbitohs rout
World.content:
Cronulla 32 South Sydney 16 SportNRLNRL 2026 Cronulla cement reputation as real premiership deal with Rabbitohs rout Dan Walsh Updated August 2, 2026 — 5:30pm ,first published 4:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

“I’m telling you, Cronulla can win the competition if they want it.” But then Sharks premiership winner Mick Ennis would say that, wouldn’t he? Loading With every win – and Sunday’s 32-16 defeat of South Sydney at Ocean Protect Stadium made it nine from their past 10 outings – you have to put more stock in Cronulla’s premiership credentials. Particularly, when despite being reduced to 15 by Kayal Iro’s head knock and a biceps injury to Siosifa Talakai, they barely missed a beat. Coach Craig Fitzgibbon has been at pains to point out his side hasn’t achieved anything yet.



“We’re going good, but there’s a bit more to go. It’s round 22,” he said as he noted how Cronulla finished last year’s regular season with seven wins from eight games as well. “So what’s different is maybe the perception of the way we’re doing it. I’ve never felt any different about the group in the last five years, to be honest. “Maybe I believe in [the players] more than they believe in themselves, but we’re working hard towards something and we’ve been building that for a little bit.” The year-on-year difference is getting harder to ignore, though. Million-dollar No.7 Nicho Hynes is playing a more rounded game than when he won the 2022 Dally M medal as his run of 32 consecutive goals closes in on Hazem El Masri’s all-time record of 35. Blayke Brailey and Addin Fonua-Blake have both returned from Origin in compelling form too. The latter especially is coming off Fitzgibbon’s bench in devastating fashion from the 20-minute mark, and is the last thing an opposition wants to deal with on their try line – per his classic big-man try from a superb angled run midway through the second half.



So it proved for a gutsy but outgunned South Sydney at Shark Park. Cronulla’s 18-6 half-time lead came after a clutch of penalties for high shots and late hits by the home side. Cronulla celebrate an Addin Fonua-Blake try on Sunday. NRL Photos Discipline has been their biggest issue all year, though Teig Wilton seemed unlucky to be sin-binned for contact that split Jack Wighton’s ear open – despite replays suggesting the contact was almost exclusively head-on-head. Both had to pass HIAs and while the Sharks lost their shape while playing down a man, Trindall came into his own once it was 13 on 13 again. After almost scoring himself from close range, the man with more try-assists than anyone else added another to his tally by piloting Briton Nikora through. His kick for Mulitalo then finished in a milestone try to Talakai in his 150th NRL game. And even though the Rabbitohs hung in grimly, the contest was only heading one way when Brailey scurried over from dummy-half before half-time.



A second half that started with Campbell Graham polishing off a right-edge overlap briefly kindled hope of a Rabbitohs comeback. But with Latrell Mitchell, Cameron Murray, Tallis Duncan, Euan Aitken and David Fifita all sidelined, the Sharks always had their measure. All but Mitchell will return next week against Parramatta as Wayne Bennett spelled out South Sydney’s next hurdle once their best and brightest are on the field. Cronulla halfback Nicho Hynes braces for heavy contact. Getty Images “We can run deep any day of the week if we can just get over the rubbish that gets into our game,” Bennett said. “I’m not disappointed with our effort... Our Achilles heel is when we don’t execute, then we play a bit of a price for it and that’s been consistent all year with us.”



And for the umpteenth time this season, Fitzgibbon had a scrambling defensive effort – which the warhorse coach prizes above all others – to hang in his pool room. This week it was Will Kennedy producing a superb long-range chase and cover tackle on Jye Gray. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 NRL ‘media cop’ to crack down on negative coverage of game Danny Weidler Sport columnist Late tries to Mulitalo and Alex Johnston made no difference in the final wash-up. And the Rabbitohs casualty ward is a reasonable counter to Ennis and his suggestion “Cronulla can win the competition” during commentary. The old Cronulla hooker noted exactly that, along with the enduring question of how the Sharks stack up come finals time against the Panthers, Roosters and Warriors. Right now though, they can only beat the team in front of them each week. And right now, they look like legitimate contenders doing it.

World.title: ‘How can it be?’ Church leader turns Albanese’s words against him
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGambling ‘How can it be?’ Church leader turns Albanese’s words against him Rob Harris August 2, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anthony Albanese’s gambling reforms are facing a fresh backlash from church leaders, child advocates and broadcasters, with critics arguing the government’s crackdown still leaves the vulnerable exposed to betting s while creating costly new burdens for Australia’s media industry. A Senate inquiry into Labor’s gambling advertising laws will this week reveal growing pressure on the Albanese government from groups that say the reforms are a significant retreat from the landmark Murphy inquiry, alongside warnings from broadcasters that key provisions risk unintended consequences for public interest journalism. Reverend Sandy Grant is critical of the federal government for avoiding a phased ban on online gambling advertising and a prohibition on gambling inducements. Dominic Lorrimer Among the most pointed criticisms came from Anglican Dean of Sydney Sandy Grant, who questioned how Albanese could reconcile his promise to protect children with reforms that would still permit gambling s during live sport. “How can it be that the prime minister, who says he is ‘making sure Australian children don’t see betting ads everywhere they look’, still considers it appropriate for children to see three gambling adverts every hour on TV, including during pre-game and half-time broadcasting associated with live sporting matches?” Grant wrote in a submission to the inquiry.



Grant welcomed Labor’s ban on gambling advertising on sports uniforms, grounds and through celebrity endorsements but urged parliament to fully implement all 31 recommendations of the bipartisan Murphy inquiry, including a phased ban on all online gambling advertising and a prohibition on betting inducements. Related Article Exclusive

Gambling Labor’s millions in gambling donations revealed amid last-ditch push for reform “The parliament should never put the vested interests of big-business gambling and broadcast companies and big sporting codes over the public health and welfare of ordinary Aussies, especially our children, youth and young adults,” he said. “As the Reverend Tim Costello said, we wouldn’t accept capping cigarette ads shown to children to three per hour so why would we say it’s OK for gambling ads?” Albanese has defended his government’s approach to the issue, saying it sought to balance protecting children from gambling advertising with preserving adults’ freedom to bet.



He said last month he was “not against someone having a punt on a Saturday” but wants to tackle problem gambling – which he said was mainly pokie machines and regulated by state governments. “I think we have gone far enough,” he said, adding that the approach was the right balance between doing nothing and a full ban. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at Labor’s recent national conference. Dominic Lorrimer The Murphy inquiry, chaired by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy, recommended a comprehensive phase-out of gambling advertising across television, radio, online platforms and sporting broadcasts after concluding pervasive betting promotion was contributing to gambling harm. Instead, Labor opted for a narrower package announced in April that bans gambling advertising on sports uniforms, at venues and through celebrity endorsements while restricting, rather than eliminating, betting s around live sport.



Children and Media Australia, the national peak body representing children’s interests as media consumers, also urged the government to revisit its approach, describing the legislation as only “a first step”. The organisation warned there would still be “significant exposure” to gambling advertising and argued only a full ban would adequately protect children. Its submission cited growing evidence that childhood exposure to gambling advertising increased the likelihood of developing gambling problems later in life, while smartphones and online betting had brought wagering into family homes in ways unimaginable a generation ago. It criticised Labor for failing to prohibit online gambling inducements and warned young men using sports apps and gaming platforms would continue to be bombarded with betting promotions. The group also questioned why the government’s proposed public education campaign would target young men, First Nations Australians and culturally diverse communities but not children, parents or carers.



But while health advocates say Labor has not gone far enough, broadcasters warned the legislation risks overshooting its objectives. SBS, a hybrid public broadcaster that carries limited commercial advertising, backed stronger gambling ad restrictions but warned the bill as drafted would effectively create a blanket ban on wagering ads across its digital services because it could not implement required age-verification technology before the proposed January start date. Related Article Exclusive

Gambling Labor’s streaming carve-out for gambling ads is a step backwards, says chief reform advocate SBS said its existing self-declared age system on SBS On Demand should satisfy the legislation, warning more sophisticated identity checks would be costly, complex and raise privacy concerns. The broadcaster also cautioned the reforms could remove commercial revenue that helps fund trusted news, current affairs and Australian content, while disadvantaging local broadcasters against global digital platforms with established account systems.



It urged an 18-month implementation period, exemptions for free news websites and protection from liability for gambling content produced by wagering companies. Free TV, representing commercial broadcasters including Nine Entertainment - the owner of this masthead, has argued the measures will have a “material impact” on advertising revenue that supports free services relied on by millions, while imposing significant compliance costs for online platforms. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.
